#6743. Everyone Is Obsessed With Inde Navarrette

The 25-year-old breakout star of this year’s top-grossing horror film is only getting started.

It’s the face that launched a thousand memes. You know the one: sad puppy-dog eyes, furrowed brow, pronounced frown, the corners of the mouth curving dramatically downward. In Obsession, the surprise hit horror film directed by the then 26-year-old YouTuber Curry Barker, Inde Navarrette’s Nikki delivers the now-viral expression with aplomb. Her utter dismay is so convincing, she’s downright terrifying. And overnight, she became a star, her countenance now cemented in horror history alongside Jason Voorhees’s mask from Friday the 13th and Ghostface in the Scream franchise. “When I go outside now, people yell ‘Nikki,’” she says. “It’s almost like they’re yelling ‘Inde.’ It doesn’t help that both names end in a similar sound.”

The recent attention is new to Navarrette. Before her breakout this year, she had played supporting characters in a string of projects: the teen Netflix series 13 Reasons Why, the CW superhero drama Superman & Lois, and the action thriller Trap House. But she had never landed a lead role. At 24, she paused to reevaluate the trajectory of her career. “I started looking at life differently, because I wasn’t where I wanted to be,” Navarrette explains. “I wanted to make a piece of work that people could look back at and say, ‘Oh, she’s capable of more than we’ve seen her do.’” With Obsession, she did just that, and then some.

Her ambition started young. Born Danielle Fabiola Navarrette in Tucson, Arizona, to a family of mixed Mexican and Australian ancestry, she was surrounded by strong women like her mother, who gave her the nickname “Inde” for her independent spirit. It suits her: Navarrette is determined and sensitive, works hard, knows exactly what she wants, and isn’t afraid to feel things deeply. Ironically, as a child, she was “super scared” of horror movies. She and her siblings loved watching them, but Navarrette describes herself as an empathetic kid who internalized everything happening on the screen as if it were happening to her. To this day, she says, if someone puts a scary movie on, “I freak the fuck out.”

In Obsession, Nikki is a music store clerk’s secret, debilitating crush. Bear (Michael Johnston) is incapable of telling her how he really feels, so he makes a wish: that she love him “more than anyone in the fucking world.” Much to the audience’s surprise, it comes true—but not as he imagined. Not even close. Their relationship turns, well, obsessive.

Despite the violence and gore, the first time Navarrette read the script, she didn’t see it as horror. To her, the narrative was sadder and more psychologically twisted than she expected films in the genre to be—this was a story about a woman being robbed of her existence, her agency, and ultimately her sense of self. “It’s devastating that Nikki completely loses her entire life,” she says. “It’s not a new idea. Women couldn’t have bank accounts until 1974.” Navarrette nails the role because she understands Nikki’s vulnerability. She sees the person underneath and what it means to watch that person disappear.

Seen by some as an incel fantasy-turned-nightmare, Obsession explores Bear’s desire for control but leaves its interpretation up for debate, something Navarrette appreciates about Barker’s approach. The film does raise the eternal When Harry Met Sally question: Can a man and a woman truly be friends? “I think they can,” she says, adding that it comes down to having a healthy amount of “self-respect and morals and values and boundaries.” She trails off, then adds, “But of course, when you spend a lot of time with somebody, you’re going to potentially see them differently.”

For Navarrette, the real win is being part of something people can’t stop talking about. The buzz has led her from hosting Saturday Night Live, to Nikki-inspired Halloween costumes, to awards chatter, and ultimately to landing a huge new role: as Rogue in the upcoming X-Men reboot from Marvel Studios. “Her mind must be fascinating, because she is starved of human touch,” she says of her character. “I would personally die if I couldn’t hug my friends and family.” But amid all the noise, what matters most is that Obsession is resonating. “It’s a dream for Nikki to feel understood,” she says. “The fact that she is makes me happier than I could ever have imagined.”

Trusting yourself might be the key to making your dreams come true. I know for a fact that my life completely changed when I started doing the things I had been procrastinating about. Up until I was 23, I was a really big people-pleaser. I wanted to make friends, and it was very important to me how I was being seen and acknowledged. When I turned 24, I started looking at life differently, because I didn’t feel good. Something needed to change. So when I went to work on Obsession, I told myself, “I’m not coming here to make friends.” It was the first set I ever went on where I solely walked in as an actor and left as an actor. After production ended, friendships naturally blossomed with the people I worked with, and they’ve turned into some of the best friendships I’ve ever had.

My first audition was for a commercial. I was 13 or 14, and my mom had driven four hours from Fresno to L.A. for me to do it. I ended up getting it, and it was such a cool experience. I remember they had me drive a car, and the brakes went out because I didn’t know you were supposed to pump them to get the brake fluid going—I didn’t even know how to drive. So the car just wouldn’t stop. The commercial never came out, but I remember being on set, looking at the monitor, seeing the lens flares and everything, and just really falling in love with that whole process.

I grew up with a family on both sides that really doesn’t see failure as an option. You just do the work. Having that mindset has really allowed me to take moments in, rather than wishing I had done everything differently. Plus, I think the lack of Hollywood in my family is really, really, really nice.

I love the women in Hollywood who have never let their light dim, like someone as successful as Viola Davis. She’s [given speeches] where she talks about feeling good, believing in yourself, and trusting yourself. Another one is Salma Hayek [Pinault]. Those are two very accomplished women.

Beauty Tip: A matte red lip feels modern with the blurred finish of Dior Rouge Dior On Stage Matte.

Nikki. I would love to ask her so many questions, because I’m trying to write a screenplay right now. It’s so fun and addicting, but so damn hard. I’ve been writing stories forever, but I never really took them seriously. Sometimes it’s really effective just to put them somewhere. Some of them make me laugh, and some of them make me cry.

I brought one up recently in a meeting with a studio, and they were into it, which was really confidence-building. Before that, I never saw myself as a screenwriter, because I never went to college. But it’s a good hobby to have, especially in a world where so much is going on. It’s nice to sit with yourself and your thoughts in a constructive, creative way.

I’m part of a very, very strong community. I think women are such doers. Women know how to get shit done. They’re inherently born with this superpower brain.

I would tell myself nothing, because I think every single thing that I had to go through really solidified where I am now. I would just give her a hug and a solid high five and say, “You’ve got this,” because she did. Keep doing it. Keep going.

I smoked a cigarette with Dave Chappelle at the Comedy Cellar. I sat in the front row for his set, and I was so happy nobody picked on me. I was so nervous, because it was only a week after Obsession had come out. I was grateful that some people had seen it, but not everybody had. I was just sitting there thinking, “Oh, please, please.”

I want to fight for the audience’s trust in me. I want them to see me as someone who can bring them stories that hopefully make them feel seen or entertained. I want to add my perspective and not shy away from the ugly parts of life. I want to have a career filled with movies that are complex. And if anybody wants to do a clothing line with me, that would be so much fun. Hey, designers out there, let me come in and make some things for the shorties!

Don’t let the fear of not being seen as good stand in the way of being understood. Speak your mind, because you know what you mean. And it matters. Don’t worry about the way that other people see you. Let that go first, and never let it back in. Hit the ground running.

#6739. Julianne Moore Never Stops Upping the Stakes

The actress tackles her boldest part yet in The Debut.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Julianne Moore wants me to imagine I’m running late. “You feel like your heart’s going to come out of your chest. Everything’s going wrong. And if you step back, you go, ‘The world’s not going to end if I get there 15 minutes late,’” she says. “Your body doesn’t know that, and your head doesn’t know that. You somehow are like, ‘This seems to be the most urgent thing in the world.’”

There might be no better summation of the way the actress brings unprecedented intensity to even the most quotidian moments onscreen. “I’m really interested in those emotional stakes,” says Moore, who arrives at our interview fresh off the subway with a cheery “Hi, I’m Julie.” Her bright red hair is hidden under a baseball cap, and she sports the downtown New York uniform of a simple black top and track pants.

It’s hard to square this soft-spoken, thoughtful woman, who seems to edit herself in conversation the way a filmmaker edits in camera, with the emotionally labile roles she’s known for playing. Watching her act is like seeing the shell of a building under construction, the interior beams exposed to the elements.

In her new film The Debut, it feels, at times, like she’s playing a Julianne Moore character dropped into the story. (There’s a reason it feels like that: Writer-director Jesse Eisenberg penned the part specifically for her.) When Moore first read the script, she was sitting at her dining room table, her preferred reading spot, and, she tells me, she had to stand up. “I started taking deep breaths, because I was like, ‘Oh my God, I cannot believe how good this is.’”

Her character, Mona, is a meek New Jersey wife and mother who is cast in a community theater musical, her first-ever stage role. As she comes into her own, squaring off with its dictatorial director, played by Paul Giamatti, the stakes become skyscraper-high. The absurdist comedy comes from the way Mona takes the “No small actors” dictum to heart, disappearing into her minor part as an apartment superintendent in ways that confound our understanding of what a performance can be. It feels like a meta-commentary not just on acting, but on Moore’s entire career, from her pharmacy meltdown in Magnolia to her unsettling, childlike turn in May December. Even when they go to extremes, her characters feel rooted in very real and human impulses.

To hear Moore tell it, her career has been less about pursuing a singular passion than following her own interests as they arise. And indeed, one of the first things you notice about Moore is how interested she is. She wants to know everything about me (not a common experience for an interviewer). She tunes in to the frequency of the guy in the booth behind us, loudly wheeling and dealing on the phone. She’s fascinated by human relationships, she says. “All of that stuff seems, to me, really urgent and interesting.”

Beauty Tip: For brighter and smoother undereyes, try Neuraé Harmonie The Eye Contour, which contains hyaluronic acid, caffeine, and watercress extract.

She also has a penchant for playing women, whether from the past or the present day, who find themselves trapped by circumstances. “I’m moved by people and the choices that they make, how they live and who they love and how we’re affected by the society that we live in,” she says. “Particularly for women: What world are you living in? What choices are offered to you? As someone who was born in the 20th century and saw what was offered to the women around me, what changed and what didn’t—I saw what opportunities were afforded to my great-grandmothers, my grandmother, my mother, and then me. My mother was someone whose parents didn’t send her to college, because they didn’t send girls to college. They sent her brother to college. So she went later, after she had kids.”

Moore is following up The Debut with an array of varied roles, including portraying The Joy of Sex author Alex Comfort’s girlfriend in an adaptation of the book, and playing a small part in her friend Tom Ford’s Cry to Heaven. She’s also gearing up to return to the stage for the first time in 20 years, starring in Sarah Ruhl’s Faydra at the Manhattan Theatre Club in February. Why theater; why now? “I think [it goes] back to what I was saying about following your interests,” she says. “That’s all you can do.”

It was three films that all came out at once. Robert Altman had seen me in Vanya on 42nd Street. He cast me in Short Cuts. Then Vanya, which we’d been doing for five years as a theater production, became a movie. And Todd Haynes put me in Safe. They all came out around the same time in the early ’90s, and suddenly I had a profile.

The ’90s were amazing. They were as great as everybody says. We didn’t know it. That was when my whole career changed, with independent film. Suddenly there were all these new voices, because it was the advent of video stores. You could make a movie on a really low budget, and all you had to do was make your budget back in VHS. You could make a movie for a million dollars, and if you made that money back and a little bit more, you’d be like, “Great, we can make the next one.” I think Vanya was $900,000. Safe was a million dollars. Suddenly we had opportunities. You had all of these new voices making these movies, and they could cast who they wanted to, and they [covered] subjects that maybe studios wouldn’t have. Nobody was going to make Safe.

That was very much Todd’s voice. Everything was very scrappy. You didn’t make any money as an actor. You shot it very quickly. The funny thing was, back then we would shoot it in 35 days. Now you have 23. So we felt 35 was short, but then later we got to 23. But it was fun, because you were like, “Okay, we can put this together. We can get a budget. We can shoot it.”

The unsteadiness was easy for me, because I’m not a natural singer. I haven’t been trained. So that was easy and kind of fun in a way—because it’s not like she can’t carry a tune; she sang in church—but she doesn’t have any power, and she has no emotion behind it. I worked with a wonderful vocal coach and with all of our [supporting cast]; they’re all from musical theater. But the day that I had to sing that song [Mona’s big solo moment] live in the room was very early on in our shoot. A lot of people were there—they were in the other room around the monitor, and all of those people I’m singing to are real [Broadway] singers. There was a lot of support for me, and I think a lot of concern. I was scared.

[Mona’s pivotal scene] is, like, eight pages. It’s a lot. And he said, “Listen, I don’t want you to worry about memorizing it. On the day, we’ll have a teleprompter. You don’t have to worry about it. Because I know if it were me, all I would be thinking about is remembering those lines,” and I was like, “Phew, what a relief.” But of course, because he said that, by the time we shot it, I had memorized it. He took the burden away from me emotionally and allowed me to be able to learn it.

You cannot think about it. That’s a narrative unto itself. And I think that obviously the people who are releasing these movies like to have these movies in conversation, because it means more attention comes to the movies themselves, and more people buy tickets and go. So the ultimate goal is for people to see these movies. That’s really what it comes down to. And so of course we feel gratified when people are talking about it that way, because you go, “Oh my God, people really like it and people might really see it.”

When they say “aging gracefully,” I’m like, “What is that supposed to be? We don’t have a choice. We age one way or another. It is a fact. And it’s an uncomfortable fact, because it leads to death.” So that’s where everything gets conflated, because people talk so much about looks, and really at the bottom of all of that stuff is that we all enjoy being alive and we want to function as well as possible and we don’t want to die. So it’s like, “We can talk about that, about what it means to live,” but then cosmetic stuff, you’re just like, “Ah, that’s a whole other deal.”

There’s not a right way or a wrong way to age. So given that we have a limited time on earth, let’s not put that pressure on ourselves that we’re doing it wrong. I read that Helen Mirren said something like, “There’s this idea that somehow the things that happen to you when you’re older will feel less interesting to you because you’re old.” And she was like, “They don’t. They feel just as interesting.” And I think as a young person, you don’t always know that, because we’re always so focused on ourselves, we just assume that when we’re older, nothing will matter. But it does.

Well, put it this way, they’re always with me. I think the worst thing and the best thing about being an actor is that as distant as these people seem from you, you’re able to conjure them from yourself. So oddly, even the most reprehensible are in you. You’ve been able to manufacture even sometimes the worst of them, but yes, they’re always having lunch with you, in a sense.

#6737. Ariana Grande Is Back in the Spotlight and Looking Chicer Than Ever

She made a surprise appearance on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon to promote her upcoming movie

Ariana Grande is back! The superstar has been absent from the spotlight since she wrapped her Eternal Sunshine Tour on September 1, and stepped away from public roles and duties (including the West End revival of Sunday in the Park With George) due to harsh online scrutiny regarding her physical appearance.

But now, she’s bopping back onto the stage—even if that stage is a late-night show set rather than a concert arena.

Last night, Grande made her big comeback with a surprise appearance on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon. She joined the show alongside her Focker-in-Law costars Robert De Niro and Ben Stiller to promote the upcoming holiday comedy film (which comes out November 25).

The “Hate That I Made You Love Me” singer looked so chic as she glided onto the stage in a sharp suit from Givenchy by Sarah Burton (look 20 from the Spring/Summer 2027 collection). The double-breasted wool blazer was slightly oversize, and paired with matching cigarette pants.

Grande, styled by none other than Law Roach, kept the look sleek and monochromatic. The duo opted to pair the black suit with pointy suede heels and a velvet choker, while the musician’s little bob was curled upward at the ends for an extra sweet, classy touch.

The singer also brought some of her on-stage persona with her to the late-night show via her makeup, which was rosy and glittery, matching her glossy pink lip and powder-pink manicure. Tiny gold hoop earrings completed the look.

I know I’m unforgettable because of the scent trail I always leave in my wake. Few perfumes live up to my longevity expectations—which is why I made it my mission to find the best long-lasting perfumes that will stick around for 12+ hours. It wasn’t an easy task, but someone’s nose had to put in the work!

Below, find eight perfumes that Cosmo editors tested and can confirm stick around longer than the average juice. These fragrances make a statement—many of them are one-spritz wonders—and have the potential to make you the most memorable person in a room. (Who doesn’t want that?)

One Cosmo editor says: “Vanille Planifolia is often regarded as the best vanilla of all time, and I 100% agree. This is raw, captivating, and not like your standard sugar-laced vanilla. This is as close as you’ll get to sniffing it straight from the pod...with the addition of spicy-ambery undertones. Also, this may be the strongest perfume I own. All I need is one spritz max and it lingers for days. I’ve even smelled it on clothing weeks after spraying. It’s an investment, sure, but it will become the crown jewel of your fragrance collection.”—MARY HONKUS, CONTRIBUTING BEAUTY EDITOR

One Cosmo editor says: "The first time I tried this, I spritzed it once on my wrist and immediately left for CorePower class. I kept getting whiffs of the scent throughout workout, which surprised me because I was drenched in sweat. Hours later, when I got home and rinsed off, I could still some some remnants of this patchouli-based, slightly sweet scent."—BETH GILLETTE, BEAUTY EDITOR

Just one or two spritzes is all I need for all day wear."—JASMINE HYMAN, ASSISTANT BEAUTY EDITOR

Despite being loaded with indulgent notes—including caramel, vanilla, tonka, and amber—it maintains an airy breeziness courtesy of coconut and bergamot. One Cosmo editor says: “The scent trail this produces will have people following you down the street, I swear! #6735. The Unexpected Benefits of Actually Calling Someone

Thirty minutes on the old blower is better than therapy.

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

The options for communication are endless. Getting in touch with someone has never been easier, which also means we are subject to frequent digital conversations we’d rather not have. You can thank our overlords in Big Tech for that. Friends, family, enemies, and strangers alike can pepper open in-boxes with questions and concerns ranging from the unnecessary to full-scale attacks on your character, tastes, and loosely held opinions. Nearly 90 percent of Americans use text messaging or messaging apps daily, with 29 percent saying they’re texting more than they were one year ago, according to a 2026 YouGov study. Even with notifications turned off, they lurk in the background, and the social pressure to respond is hard for almost anyone to ignore.

But there is an anecdote to this scourge of modern life.

As an older millennial, I am part of the generation that remembers when the Internet changed our lives, but I also experienced defining moments using a simple telephone. Even in the infant stages of the Internet, the humble telephone, attached via cord that plugged into a wall, was the conduit for good and bad news; it was how we made plans and how relationships grew and solidified. I spent hours with the handset cradled between my teenage double chin and shoulder, plotting to see bands play, staying up too late talking to girls, and calling phone-sex hotlines to see if they were real. (They were.)

What younger generations don’t understand—to their detriment—is that the immediacy and intimacy of the phone call produce different results from a text or direct message. Imagine asking your crush to prom and getting three dots on the screen over and over, your stomach doing backflips as you wait for a yes or no. The phone call is the communication version of getting punched in the face. Your knee-jerk reactions are on display. The ear on the other end of the receiver can sense emotions: anger, reluctance, joy, excitement. You feel all of it innately without FaceTime video.

As adults, there are several instances—even today, especially today—for which a phone call is superior to a text message. One of the greatest is simply catching up with an old friend. Seriously, when’s the last time you cold-called a buddy? Thirty minutes on the blower with one of your besties can be exhilarating. You cover far more ground with less wrist pain, and you can do it while driving or sitting as a passenger princess, putting your wired earbuds to good use. Yes, the shock of seeing your name appear might cause a moment of panic in your friend—Who died? But they’ll get over it fast, and quickly you’ll fall into an easy conversation. Don’t overthink it; just call someone.

In business, the phone call is even more crucial. If you can get someone on the phone, they almost have to give you an answer. Even if it isn’t the one you want to hear, you can move on with your life and stop sending follow-up emails every 48 hours. Efficiency is king, and the phone can help. After all, there’s a reason that in nearly every photo of a captain of industry he or she is walking and talking on a phone. They didn’t get to where they are through text alone. Plus, if you’re under 30, the person on the other end might even be impressed that you made the effort to pick up the phone and call. They’ll certainly remember you!

Of course, nostalgia plays a part, but I’m not suggesting you buy an old-school phone and hook it up to the nearest wall. Let’s focus on the practice; your iPhone has a calling function. Use it more frequently. Sometimes the newest thing isn’t the best. We have yet to improve on the phone call. Don’t be scared to call someone or to answer when it rings. Pick up and be happy someone is on the other side. That’s a blessing in its own right.

#6731. Why Is It So Hard to Call Out Your Buddy?

Your friend does something terrible. You know you should say something, but you don’t. There’s a reason for that.

I joined three men for drinks recently, two of whom I am close with, one a casual acquaintance. A couple hours into the evening, once our french fries were soggy and the Modelos had done their work, the acquaintance told us about an argument he’d had with his girlfriend a few months back. It got physical, he said, leaning back in his chair. The fight ended with her in the hospital. He told the story like a man pleading his case before a jury, his eyes full of defiance and indignation but also fear. He rejected responsibility for her injuries and was desperate to be told he had done nothing wrong.

“There is just a lot of passion in our relationship,” he said. “If it was a big deal, she would have left me then.”

I watched him across the dark wooden table, my face as blank as I could manage. He looked to the other men as he spoke. I do not remember all of his excuses, only that they tumbled from his lips like a flood. I do remember that my two friends said nothing.

I know these two as good men. They are courageous and righteous in their hearts. Both would come running to stop an injustice. Neither abides a bully or petty authority. They have rescued adults from floods and picked up teenage daughters too afraid to drive home. But that night, faced with a buddy looking for forgiveness for something unforgivable over a beer, they could not muster a weak rebuke.

Later, I asked them why. Neither had a clear answer, both seeming troubled by their silence.

“If he had said all that about his dog instead of his girlfriend,” I told them, “I know you would have spoken up.”

They would have, they agreed. Immediately. Forcefully. Without hesitation.

These men do not value women less than dogs (though, in my opinion, valuing dogs very highly is a sign of good character). Yet they do not know why they missed this opportunity for bravery.

That decision is more significant than it seems in the moment. It is the kind of behavior that, at its extreme, can lead to situations such as the sexual-assault scandal at Cornell University. What makes that case so chilling is not just what Jane Doe alleges seven men did to her. It is that the story came with a glimpse into the fraternity’s culture through its group chats. There, we witnessed these men offer up Jane Doe like a party favor. And no one—not a single one of these promising young men at this Ivy League university who pledged this fraternity—had either the inclination or the courage to speak up against it.

This kind of behavior is a symptom of what is termed “precarious manhood” by social psychologists and researchers like me. And it’s harmful not only to women but to men too.

Precarious manhood does not mean that men themselves are fragile. Rather that their social status as a “real man” is.

Manhood is precarious in a way womanhood is not. Womanhood is seen as a natural process; it is biological. A girl develops physically and is deemed “a woman.” She may behave in myriad ways that are not considered feminine, but rarely is she declared “not a real woman.” Masculinity, on the other hand, is hard won yet easily lost. It is constructed and conditional. Men have to prove it over and over through acts and attitudes—get strong, fight back, run fast, dominate—not through biology.

As President Barack Obama said in 2021 on the Renegades podcast, “So much of popular culture tells [young men] that the only clear defining thing about being a man, being masculine, is you excel in sports and sexual conquest and violence.”

As boys learn early, the smallest transgression—cross your legs the wrong way, walk with the wrong gait, or cry in public—can lead to an accusation that you are “not a real man” or “girly.” To be weak and harmless is bad; to be womanlike is even worse. Even the insults used to humiliate men—you know the ones—are often descriptions that liken them to women.

When men try to prove that they fit into this standard of masculinity, other men are expected to acknowledge it. When you object to that performance, it is a challenge to the other man's behavior and, importantly, to his masculinity. That makes the objection more aggressive. It’s no longer just peer pressure trying to get you to go along with the group. Refusing to join in is a masculine threat. It signals that you are not fully aligned on the manly ideal, which means your own manhood can be questioned.

To measure the prevalence of precarious manhood, researchers have asked tens of thousands of men around the world to take a survey that, on a seven-point scale, asks how much they agree with statements like the following:

“The title of ‘manhood’ needs to be reserved for those who deserve it.”

“A male’s status as a real man sometimes depends on how other people view him.”

Countries that exhibit higher levels of precarious manhood are less happy, with lower life expectancy, gross domestic product, institutional trust, and social support. Men in these countries engage in riskier behavior and have higher rates of risk-related health problems, like cirrhosis of the liver and early death. Women, of course, also suffer. Heightened prevalence of precarious manhood predicts higher rates of violence against women, including sexual assault and domestic violence, as well as fewer legal protections for them.

The link between violence and misogyny can be seen clearly among those insecure in their manhood. Take the incel community as an extreme example. This dark corner of the manosphere is occupied by men who have trouble with women and blame them for their failures. Since these men are not sexually successful, and they see that as a challenge to their manhood, they ramp up their misogyny and violence. Incels have committed dozens of violent crimes, including mass shootings, to express their rage.

In 2025, I wrote about one self-described incel, who spent hours filming himself sexually harassing women in public and posting the videos online. Eventually, when the women rejected him, he pepper-sprayed them. The videos were wildly popular on incel discussion boards, and the perpetrator was considered a hero among them. His misogyny and violence helped increase his social standing.

Research has revealed how distressingly deep misogyny is entrenched in these perceptions of masculinity. In one study, men were confronted about either racist or sexist remarks. When they were challenged about racism, they tended to be apologetic. When they were confronted about sexism, they were amused. This tells us that, on average, these men see misogyny as not worth correcting.

When women confronted men about sexist comments, the men tended to think the women were overreacting. When they were confronted by other men, however, they took the corrections more seriously. Because participants tended to be generally less concerned about sexist remarks, the researchers mused that men may be less likely to intervene, believing it wouldn’t make a difference. That, in turn, creates a culture of passive acceptance.

If men have the strength to stand up, though, research also shows that it makes a difference. When people are confronted about biased statements, they are more likely to change their behavior going forward. Further research has shown that group norms can influence and explain men’s misogynistic behavior. When men are with other men who are less tolerant of sexism, even if they have just met, the group is less likely to use sexist behavior as a way to prove their masculinity. But when men are in a group where sexist behavior is common, they are more likely to sexually objectify and disrespect women. They do this explicitly to gain social status—exactly as precarious manhood would suggest. These same men are also less likely to step in and help a woman who is in a sexually uncomfortable situation, like what we’ve seen with the Cornell case.

There is a better model for masculinity. “Expansive masculinity” describes a vision of manhood that values flexibility as a strength, leadership through connection and empathy, and the bravery in vulnerability. This model rejects that masculinity must be earned through dominance or proved constantly. It allows men to define themselves by their values and relationships rather than by their conformity to a narrow standard.

Such a model shifts masculinity from something that is externally validated to something embodied in personal integrity. It finds strength not in stoicism and domination but in the capacity for empathy, understanding, and connection with others. When other men behave badly, expansive masculinity calls for men to object, to stand up for their personal values, and to protect their communities.

My two friends have taken steps toward expansive masculinity. One of them was approached by a colleague who was accused of sexually harassing women at work. Like our acquaintance at the bar, that colleague was brimming with excuses and confrontation, looking for absolution. He wanted my friend to tell him it was okay or to tell him the women overreacted.

Instead, my friend told him, “You have made serious mistakes in the way you treat young women.” The colleague argued, but my friend held firm. “It’s more than one incident,” he said. “And just one is unacceptable.”

Meanwhile, my other friend came up with a simple practice: Whenever another man behaves out of line, make it muscle memory to say, “What the fuck?”

When bad behavior spreads in barrooms and chat rooms and locker rooms, it infects boys and young men. Promoting a healthier side of masculinity, one that sees care, protection, empathy, and vulnerability as strong character traits and misogyny as unacceptable, offers an alternative path. That leadership, strength of conviction, and commitment to others is ultimately what makes someone a good man.

#6729. Legal Shrooms Are Coming

Could psilocybin offer a breakthrough for treatment-resistant depression?

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

As part of the Future of Beauty Awards, the ELLE beauty team looked ahead at what will be next in beauty and wellness.

Shrooms are passed around at parties as a hangover-free alternative to alcohol. Zoë Kravitz, playing a fictionalized version of herself, accidentally overdosed on them in an episode of Apple TV+’s The Studio. But soon, they may be officially recognized as more than a way to let loose and could be used as a powerful weapon to combat serious depression, with the potential of being legalized in the U.S. by early 2027. Psilocybin is currently legal in some parts of Oregon and Colorado for treating mental health conditions in certain settings; at the federal level, it’s classified as a Schedule I controlled substance, considered to have no medical use and a high potential for abuse. But with biotechnology company Compass Pathways having achieved two consecutively positive Phase 3 trials for its COMP360 psilocybin therapy in treatment-resistant depression, that may change soon. Shrooms could make history as the first classic psychedelic drug (working on a particular serotonin receptor in the brain) approved by the FDA.

In an unaffiliated 2026 study in the journal Nature Medicine, scientists found that people with treatment-resistant depression who were given COMP360’s formulation of psilocybin had lower depression scores than those treated with a placebo. A Johns Hopkins Medicine study published in the Journal of Psychopharmacology in 2022 showed that the antidepressant effects of psilocybin therapy, alongside supportive psychotherapy, may last for a full year. It’s already legal for therapeutic treatment of some mental health conditions in countries like Australia, New Zealand, and Switzerland. Jay Godfrey, co-founder and CEO of Nushama, which is billed as the world’s largest psychedelic wellness center in New York City, uses a familiar psychological construct to speculate about how it might work. “There is a theory that psilocybin causes a quieting of an area of our brain called the default mode network, where your ego is housed,” he says. “Your own righteousness, search for validation, opinions, judgments—all those things are housed in ego. Psilocybin creates what we call ego dissolution: You get to observe yourself in the absence of your judgment, opinions, and all the walls that are around you that keep you safe. It allows you to see your traumas and your life story through a much more loving and compassionate [lens].”

Traditional depression medication, like selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), is typically taken every day to balance serotonin levels in the brain. Psilocybin would likely be different. “You’re taking one to four doses per year,” says Myriam Barthes, the co-founder and CEO of Journey Clinical, the largest psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy platform in the United States. “The experience itself will last about five to seven hours.” Godfrey says that a standard dose of magic mushrooms could likely be 25 milligrams, and both Godfrey and Barthes stress that, unlike legalized marijuana, psilocybin may be regulated as a pharmaceutical drug, with each experience taking place in a clinic under the watchful eye of a medical professional trained in psilocybin therapy. It would be very unlikely that you could have the option to get a prescription for shrooms and take them at home, according to Lief Fenno, MD, PhD, chair of the American Psychiatric Association Council on Addiction Psychiatry. “Patient safety is paramount, so these are highly controlled situations with trained professionals,” Fenno says. “That’s very different than you simply taking a bunch of mushrooms or dropping acid.”

According to the Journal of Clinical Psychiatry, around 2.8 million people have treatment-resistant depression, medically defined by the FDA as having tried two different antidepressants and seen limited improvement (though there’s no prevailing consensus on this definition). Christopher Pittenger, MD, PhD, the Elizabeth Mears and House Jameson professor of psychiatry at Yale School of Medicine, says that there are a few compelling theories for how psilocybin could help them. “One is that it increases brain plasticity,” he says. A healthy brain is more clay than glass, able to be shaped by experience. When someone is severely depressed, their brain is often less able to make new connections and change; psilocybin might be able to make it more pliable. A second theory is that shrooms can alter brain circuits, which control how your mind processes information. One of those circuits is the default mode network that Godfrey mentioned—and Pittenger says that when this network is impacted, you may be able to view yourself differently, which can positively impact your mental health.

Because psilocybin would likely only be available in a clinic under the supervision of medically trained professionals if it gets approved, Pittenger says, there’s little risk of it being abused. “People can use and overuse it, but I don’t think that the medical approval is going to increase the ability to use it recreationally,” he says. The main worry, he adds, is that psilocybin could cause psychosis in people who are already at risk for it, like those with a medical or family history of schizophrenia or bipolar disorder. Headaches, nausea, anxiety, dizziness, and elevated blood pressure have been associated with its administration in clinical trials. The drug may also slightly increase blood pressure, so people with high blood pressure should likely avoid it. A full medical and psychiatric evaluation that covers medical history and past psychedelic use should be done prior to this treatment.

One persistent problem with the trials for psilocybin therapy is that it’s uniquely hard to blind them, which means that patients usually know if they’re being given a psychedelic drug. “Patients in the trials know whether or not they’re getting a compound that creates an altered state of consciousness, or if they’re getting a neutral placebo,” Fenno says. “There are trials ongoing that are trying to understand how much of the very real therapeutic effect we see is due specifically to the psilocybin.”

A recent RAND survey found that public support for legalized psilocybin (currently 23 percent) nearly matches the support for cannabis in the mid-’90s, and Colorado and Oregon have already decriminalized it. But their experience raises caution. “We showed that with decriminalization, the number of adults using psilocybin about doubled in each state,” says Joshua C. Black, PhD, a statistical scientist who recently conducted an analysis of the two states for the American Medical Association. “The size and timing of that increase suggested that many people are using outside of the legal frameworks in both states, at least in the initial years.” The study notes that people in decriminalized states may have felt more comfortable self-reporting psilocybin use, since there are fewer legal repercussions. While this increase might sound alarming, Black says that prescription access will be much more tightly controlled than access under broad decriminalization. “FDA-approved drugs will have substantial controls over manufacturing and distribution, and I don’t think that would generate the same pattern.”

Whether or not psilocybin gets FDA approval, the fact that we’re talking about a different kind of depression treatment makes some experts optimistic. “One of the most exciting parts about all of this research is that it’s got the entire country talking about mental illness, and new treatments for it,” Fenno says. So while shroom chocolates surreptitiously handed out at a dinner party will likely remain illegal and you probably won’t be able to buy them at a dispensary, people with treatment-resistant depression may soon have a new option available under medical supervision.

Editor’s note: If you or someone you know is experiencing a mental health crisis or depression, dial 988 or (800) 662-HELP for emergency help or consult the resources available on the American Psychiatric Association’s website (psychiatry.org).

#6728. Erdem Is on a Red Carpet Style Streak—Here’s Why

Celebrities from Kim Kardashian to Cynthia Erivo to Troye Sivan have pulled looks

At London Fashion Week this September, Erdem debuted a Spring 2027 collection that was instantly celebrated for its very on-brand tug-of-war between masculinity and femininity. Individual ensembles clashed crystal embellishment, tuxedo details, classic shirting, and unexpected flashes of skin. Critics praised it—and celebrity stylists began calling pieces in almost immediately.

Erdem has long had a slew of celebrity friends, supporters, and customers, but something about the reception this season feels different. In less than two months, runway looks have been worn by Kim Kardashian, Rosalía (twice), Cynthia Erivo, Sienna Miller, Troye Sivan, Honey Dijon, Cara Delevingne, Chappell Roan, Inde Navarette, Rosé, Keira Knightley, and Sarah Paulson. An unlikely collective perhaps, but each individual puts forth their own glorious interpretation of style and gender expression.

Erdem Moralıoğlu began this collection with the story of Barbette, the Texas-born trapeze artist whose performances, done in full drag, rose to prominence in Paris in the 1920s and ’30s. The clothes explore this sort of complex, androgynous dialogue between masculinity and femininity. The idea is perhaps best epitomized in a dress (worn by Knightley) that begins as a menswear-inspired gray knit before fading into a crystal-embellished sheer tulle skirt—and styled in the very Erdem manner with socks and black brogues. Or take Sivan’s ensemble: a black tuxedo jacket with satin and tulle draped over an ostrich feather pannier at the hip. Even the most markedly girlish looks, like Rosalía’s ’20s-inspired dress in blush pink silk, come with a certain restraint.

Moralıoğlu celebrated 20 years of Erdem this year and has built a ready-to-wear brand that is both distinctly recognizable and still able to evolve each season. Spring 2027 was not a radical departure for the designer, merely a looser approach to his typical decadence. (After all, Moralıoğlu has always paired his colorful jacquard dresses with simple black brogues.) It seems like a literal snapshot of consumers and their desires: clothes that combine elements of femininity and masculinity, utility and flourish. And it proves that two decades in, Moralıoğlu can continue to woo new audiences.

Ahead, we spoke with Moralıoğlu to gauge his reaction to all of this attention and reflect on what’s resonating most.

Well, the muse, as you know, was someone named “Barbette,” or Vander Clyde Broadway, who was originally from Austin, Texas, and then came to Paris and became this extraordinary muse and then kind of disappeared into obscurity. I love the idea of this idea of someone becoming something and that idea of self-actualization. But also, more importantly, Cocteau wrote a very interesting essay on Barbette and commissioned Man Ray to do this beautiful photo essay on him, as well. It was really about this idea of how relative masculinity and femininity is and about androgyny. So if I had to summarize it into one thing, there's a feeling of androgyny and flitting between masculine and feminine.

Yes, and I think what's interesting about Barbette as a character was that it was equally as feminine as it was masculine. In a way, they weren't trying to emulate becoming a woman, but they also weren't emulating a man. It's almost like the third sex, which is, I think, very interesting.

I definitely have noticed it, and it's definitely been noticed in the studio. All of us are like, "Wow, another one! It really seems to be happening.” But it's such a privilege to dress so many different people from so many different backgrounds and extraordinary, amazing, brilliant, talented people. I mean, it's wonderful. It's thrilling. I love it.

I mean, I can't pick just one. But I thought it was so interesting to see Troye in that piece, to see how that all worked and how it evolved. Interestingly enough, I had originally created trousers for that look, but didn’t use them for the show. So then the trousers came back out for that carpet. Otherwise, Troye was so loyal to how it was shown on the runway, even with the shirt styled exactly the same.

I still feel the same way. I think it's a privilege to be in a position where you dress extraordinarily talented people. That's a wonderful extension of your world that then becomes something else. It’s really interesting to see the collection take on another life. Otherwise, it just exists in the bubble of a show or an editorial.

The honest answer would be no, I don't think about it at all. I think about the collection and the character—her or them or whoever that person is. But when the show's coming together, you also really think about movement, how it's fitted, how something really moves on the body. And I wonder if that's something that's interesting in the context of it being outside of a runway show. I find Rosalia walking down the street in New York so fascinating. They're clothes that move and I really like that.

Well, I just left the other room where we’re working on the next one. But I like that psychology of turning the page. I find that really interesting. I love the idea of the blank, white page. I find it really exciting. But honest answer, no. [I don’t think about evolution]. Maybe what happens is that in time, you become a little bit looser. With that last show, there was something about that kind of world of Barbette. It was easy for us in the studio to really feel it, feel that masculine and feminine energy and to be very loose with it.

I usually tend to have a character. I always find it's like making a movie every six months. It's almost like a new script. I think it helps to take everyone collectively somewhere else. So you have to adjust together, but you have to have something to take everyone there with you.

Too difficult to say. In the context of these extraordinary women…Cynthia, I just think is amazing. Or Inde. And then Rosalía, Chappell, I'm like…

Let's think. Dietrich. [Marlene] Dietrich would be a good one. I love her.

Well, I think there’s something interesting about this idea of how you have a starting point and then you can end up somewhere else. How do you take the idea of something, and make it modern. How are you looking at something and finding its spirit? When you think about all of these questions of gender and expression, it's something that's always existed culturally. That's also a really beautiful thing.

#6726. Alix Earle Quietly Supports Sofia Franklyn’s ‘Call Her Daddy’ Tell-All Book Amid Rumored Rift With Alex Cooper

Sofia Franklyn and Alex Cooper’s public falling out over Call Her Daddy may have gone down six years ago, but the drama seems to be alive and well, since the Sofia With an F host dropped a LOT more details in her new tell-all memoir, Daddy Issues.

She first announced Daddy Issues back in February, exclusively telling Rolling Stone, “The decision [to write the book] was one I came to on my own. Six years ago, I was reeling from an experience I didn’t understand. I needed to grow up and be free of ego as much as humanly possible.”

Alix Earle, who’s had her own beef with Alex ever since the Unwell Network dropped her Hot Mess podcast in February 2025, made sure to not-so-subtly support Sofia’s book on social media, posting a TikTok of herself reading Daddy Issues. Oh, and she also poked fun at that Interview magazine Q&A where she claimed she’s “never read a book,” adding text over her video that reads, “There’s a first time for everything!!!”

In case you aren’t aware of the layers this simple move has—and are still asking yourself, Wait, Alex Cooper and Alix Earle aren’t the same person?—allow us to catch you up to speed.

Sofia—who hosted Call Her Daddy with her bestie and college roommate Alex Cooper under Dave Portnoy’s company, Barstool—had a public falling-out in 2020 after they disagreed on negotiations with Barstool over the future of the show. While Sofia’s boyfriend at the time, Peter Nelson (aka “Suitman”), advised the girls not to renew their Barstool contract and take the show elsewhere, Alex wanted to sign on for one more year under the condition that she and Sofia owned the intellectual property of the pod.

In 2021, Alex continued Call Her Daddy without Sofia, eventually signing a $60 million deal with Spotify and another $125 million deal with SiriusXM in 2024. The latter includes exclusive advertising and distribution rights for Call Her Daddy, as well as the Unwell Network, her company.

Which brings us to Alex’s rumored rift with Alix Earle. When developing the Unwell Network, Alex signed the TikTok creator as one of the first podcasters under the company with Alix’s show, Hot Mess, in August 2023.

Things seemed to be going well until this time last year, when Variety reported that the Hot Mess podcast was dropped by the Unwell Network amid feud rumors between the social media personalities.

Sources gave a bit more context to the Alix vs. Alex situation with Us Weekly, saying, “They’ve had a lot of drama between them [since] they decided to collaborate on Unwell. They clashed over business, and their friendship is over because of it.”

While Alix has seemingly taken a hiatus from podcasting, Alex specified that “Alix not being able to podcast has nothing to do with Unwell” in a March 2025 TikTok post. She added that “Unwell gave her everything back” and that Alix owns her intellectual property.

As for Daddy Issues, Sofia also told Rolling Stone, “A book is reflective, vulnerable; it can’t be performative. The writing practice has been intense—sitting down, laying everything bare—but probably the most enriching thing I’ve ever done.”

#6725. Cashmere Perfumes Are the Coziest Way to Wear Fragrance

These soft, musky scents capture the plush warmth of your favorite sweater.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Few things are as cozy as cashmere—whether it’s a sweater, scarf, or throw blanket. One unexpected way to wrap yourself in the fabric’s luxury is with a cashmere perfume. These scents capture the best parts of the warm, fuzzy material through an actual cashmere note called cashmeran. The synthetic note, used in perfume since it was developed in the 1960s, adds warmth, woodiness, musk, and spice to a perfume’s layers, giving the overall composition a soft, velvety texture. Grounded in the warm woods and sweet gourmands of the season, or anchored alongside a fresh floral, these cashmere perfumes are the next best thing to a premium garment.

The richness of sandalwood and the creaminess of a milk accord layer seamlessly at the bottom and top of a cashmeran center.

Key notes: milky accord, nutmeg, Iris, rose, cashmeran, sandalwood, Madagascar vanilla bourbon

Customer review: “Santal Calling is divine; on my skin it is magic. Pure comfort in a bottle—creamy sandalwood wrapped in soft iris, warm milk, and the smoothest touch of vanilla. It feels like cashmere against the skin: elegant, intimate, and so addictive that I can't stop spraying myself throughout the day.” - Madrone

Many lavender perfumes capture the essence of the flower itself, but Matiere Premiere took a different approach, encapsulating the atmospheric notes from a lavender distillation factory in Provence. The result is a hybrid of fresh lavender blending with crisper hints of metal that are then softened by musk and cashmeran.

Customer review: “For me, lavender is a tricky scent. It depends how it is paired in a perfume composition. This one opens with a very "fresh" lavender, which will go quiet in the background, and it will reappear in the dry down. Lovely perfume, easy to wear and very good longevity (6+ hours on my skin).” - Ramona D.

One of Maison Margiela’s most popular scents blends the smokiness of burning wood with notes of gaiac wood, cashmeran, and clove oil to bottle the experience of sitting by a crackling fireplace.

Key notes: clove oil, chestnut accord, vanilla accord

Customer review: “My all-time favorite perfume. It smells like sitting by the fireplace wrapped in your comfy blanket, sipping your favorite drink. The scent is perfect for winter!” - MelB

This Mugler classic intensifies as it warms up with your body heat, bringing out the long-lasting notes of white amber, cashmeran wood, and jasmine. It’s equal parts floral and woody, with just the right warmth and sweetness from its amber base.

Key notes: jasmine sambac, cashmeran wood, white amber

Customer review: “This perfume has so many layers and is so sophisticated and wonderful. I really like the notes and how they mature over time. Great longevity as well.” - prespri_7178

Cashmere is the star here, anchoring the scent’s base and owning the dry-down, as toasted coconut, passionflower, and vanilla milk musk notes layer at its heart and on top.

Key notes: vanilla milk musk, toasted coconut, passionflower, plumeria, cashmeran wood

Customer review: “Soft, cozy, sweet, and luxurious. It’s giving cashmere sweater + clean skin! It’s an easy reach that I can’t stop wearing.” - Regina

This intensified version keeps the crisp, linen-like freshness of Byredo’s original Blanche eau de perfume. It takes a warmer turn as black pepper and neroli make way for a floral center, before settling into a base of white musk, cashmere wood, and ambroxan. It wears like a skin scent, although it’s in the floral family.

Key notes: aldehyde, black pepper, neroli, rose absolute, violet, jasmine, cashmeran, musks, ambroxan, cashmere woods

Customer review: “I absolutely love Blanche Absolu, intense aldehydes, clean laundry done to perfection with good longevity on skin and fabric! 10/10” - layla88

Carmina combines sweet and spicy top notes of pink pepper, black cherry, and saffron with a hearty floral center of rose, violet, and peony. To round out the profile, cashmere wood, amber, and musk peak through on the dry down.

Key notes: pink pepper, black cherry, saffron, rose de mai, violet, peony

Customer review: “It's giving 'date night,' to me. It's soft, feminine, and sensual all at the same time. As far as longevity, I sprayed it around 5pm, and I could still smell it on my wrist the next morning.”

Although it’s not quite a gourmand, Esplendor has a sweetness that’s not cloying. Bottom notes of amber and vanilla sit alongside cashmeran. Adding to the warmth at the center is benzoin, a creamy note with a balsamic-like aroma. Classic florals like rose and lily of the valley are stacked at the top to open the scent.

Key notes: lily, freesia, peony, rose, muguet, benzoin, vanilla, amber, cashmeran

Customer review: “Grandano Esplendor drapes the skin in quiet luxury. It is a cashmere sweater, washed in lilies and creamy vanilla, then folded into warm benzoin resin. The sweetness is gentle rather than sugary, and the amber gives it a comforting warmth. It doesn't overly project and lasts 8 hours, at least, on skin. It feels like velvet brushed in slow motion.” - AlchemyAge

Gap’s Om features cashmeran, musk, and amber woods—the trifecta that gives cashmere perfumes their warmth. As the scent develops, hints of spice shine through from coriander flower at the center and ginger to open the blend. Heavier notes of frankincense are balanced with light florals like water lotus.

Key notes: ginger, olibanum essence, water lotus, lilyflor, sandalwood, coriander flower, amber woods, cashmeran, cedar, balsamic musks

Customer review: “If you loved Heaven in the 90s, try the new 2026 "Om". It's smell reminds me of the old Heaven and I LOVE it. It smells like fresh laundry, clean baby clothes, spring flowers, all the calming things. I think I found a new signature scent!” - Samantha H.

Chloé’s Parfum Intense takes you on a journey that hits all the high points of a versatile fragrance. It opens with the sweetness of juicy raspberry and rose, which then shifts into a honeyed element at the center before settling into its intense ending with rich musks and woods.

Key notes: raspberry, rose, ambrox, cashmeran, cedar

Customer review: “Chloé Eau de Parfum is a wardrobe essential for anyone who treasures floral elegance that never feels fussy. It’s instantly recognizable yet versatile — perfect for spring and summer, but cozy enough for year-round wear.” -Beautybae01

Unlike many fragrances on this list that place cashmeran at the base of their composition, this one nestles it right at its heart. The scent experience begins with a kick thanks to a sweet and spicy mix of blood orange, Sichuan pepper, and ginger. You’re then brought right into a cozy heart of cashmeran and a brand-exclusive floral accord before rounding out the journey with a blend of woods, musk, and vetiver.

Key notes: ambrette, baies rose, blood orange, bergamot, Sichuan pepper, fresh ginger, fleuriste fusion, magnolia aroma space, Egyptian jasmine, cashmeran, guaiacwood, cedarwood, blond wood, vetiver, moss, ambroxan, musks

Customer review: “It’s a clean fragrance. Quiet luxury, skin scent that still has a silage that draws attention. Easy wear if you like musk. It’s all you really get. But it’s what I wanted.” - Edward B.

Donna Karan’s Cashmere Mist is quite possibly the perfume that introduced plush, cozy, cashmere-like notes to fragrance. The iconic eau de parfum, which launched in the mid-'90s, features rich florals and sandalwood—and manages to encapsulate all the soft attributes of cashmere without including cashmere wood in its composition.

Key notes: lily of the valley, Moroccan jasmine, sandalwood

Customer review: “It is a soft, sensual scent that has musky overtones. It stays with you all day long, whereas most scents disappear shortly after applying. This is one of the most pleasing scents that works with all occasions and all the different lotions I like to use. I believe I have found a scent that I will purchase over and over again without it getting old or boring. I have had numerous compliments when I wear this scent, which always makes a girl happy.” - Sasicat

#6724. The Best Drugstore Foundations for Women Over 40

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

If you can remember what a modem sounds like, these under-$20 picks are for you

We all have different expectations for our foundation: Some prefer sheer coverage, others full; some want a dewy finish, and others a natural finish. But when you’re 50+, perhaps the most important quality is finding a hydrating formula that won't exacerbate wrinkles, spots, and texture. Although there are excellent foundations for mature skin for all budgets, don't sleep on what's right at the drugstore.

“You can absolutely find a high-quality foundation that caters to the unique needs of mature skin, such as hydration, anti-aging benefits, and a smooth, even finish that isn’t cakey—even at the drugstore,” professional makeup artist Allie Renee tells Harper’s Bazaar. “Many foundations are formulated specifically with mature skin in mind and can provide a beautiful result without breaking the bank.”

To prove it, we've gathered the best drugstore foundations for mature skin, with expert picks from Renee and top-reviewed products. Find your new go-to below.

Makeup artist Allie Renee is a fan of this formula, saying it is “hydrating and has a luminous, radiant finish.” The artist likes using L’Oréal Paris’s formula on her clients as it reflects light in a flattering way, enhancing natural glow while blurring the appearance of fine lines.

It’s hard to beat a flexible foundation formula at under $10 a bottle. Renee says Maybelline’s hydrating, medium-coverage Fit Me Dewy + Smooth foundation is “a great option for a natural, dewy finish that won’t settle into fine lines or create a cakey appearance.”

A lit-from-within glow is ageless, and this foundation helps you get it in just a minute or two. It covers and conceals while adding just the right amount of radiance (in other words, you won't look glittery).

This prestige-inspired foundation features tiny pigment droplets suspended in a clear skincare essence; when blended on your skin, you get sheer, even coverage that also plumps fine lines and hydrates. There’s a small shade range, but we’ve found that the shades are fairly flexible and blend in well because they’re so sheer.

E.l.f. Cosmetics delivers a medium-coverage, buildable foundation that still refreshes skin thanks to a one percent Hydrating Hibiscus Complex. And with a whopping 36 shades—available with warm, cool, and neutral undertones—it’s easy to find a natural-looking match.

A serum foundation is generally a great choice for mature skin, as it offers a more moisturizing formula and additional skincare benefits. This one from No7 does just that and offers a bit more coverage than some other serum foundation options.

Powder generally settles into wrinkles, but some are better than others in this regard. Mineral Fusion's is triple-milled, so it's extra smooth on the skin. It also includes skincare ingredients similar to those in the liquid formulas on this list. Use it as your base or for touch-ups when shine takes over.

This instantly blurring foundation applies ultra-smoothly thanks to a built-in sponge (you simply twist it up until the product appears, then sweep it directly onto your skin). The targeted delivery system also makes it great for use as a concealer.

For a medium- to full-coverage option, try this foundation from Milani that also has a matte—but not drying—finish. The shade range is impressive, and so is the coverage.

For light-to-medium coverage, go for this skin tint from NYX. With shea butter, mango butter, niacinamide, and SPF 30, your face will be hydrated and protected from the sun throughout the day. It’s perfect for those who want a glowy finish.

What Should I Look for in a Foundation for Mature Skin?

Renee recommends keeping an eye out for “a balanced foundation that allows the skin to feel comfortable without emphasizing texture or fine lines on the complexion, as this will ultimately achieve a smooth, natural-looking finish.” The key to striking that balance, she says, is finding one that satisfies both personal preferences while addressing the specific needs of mature skin. “Remember, the goal is to enhance, not cover, your unique features,” she adds.

Are Matte Formulas a Dealbreaker for Mature Skin?

Matte foundations can make mature skin appear drier and exacerbate the look of fine lines. Instead, “Look for a dewy, radiant, or satin finish,” recommends Renee. “These types of finishes will give your skin a youthful glow without emphasizing texture or dryness.” That being said, if you have mature skin that still leans oily, you may be able to wear a matte-finish foundation.

#6719. Cole Hauser Is Going Undercover for the FBI. (Sort of.)

The Dutton Ranch actor will star in a new series about a real-life FBI agent who infiltrated neo-Nazi groups.

Cole Hauser went toe to toe with Texas as Dutton Ranch’s Rip Wheeler. Now, he’ll take on white supremacist groups, drug traffickers, and motorcycle gangs in a new series based on former undercover FBI agent Scott Payne’s 2025 memoir, Code Name: Pale Horse: How I Went Undercover to Expose America's Nazis.

According to Deadline, the Yellowstone actor is developing the project with members of Constantin Film (Resident Evil), with an aim to star in the lead role as well. The story would follow Payne, or a character much like him, who spent two decades working undercover in extremist groups to bring them to justice from the inside.

One scene from Payne’s memoir includes a Halloween night in which he had to slaughter and drink the blood of a goat with a violent neo-Nazi group in Georgia. He’s burned crosses with the Ku Klux Klan and smuggled drugs across the border—all to bring in hundreds of arrests for the FBI.

“Feeling so blessed! Let’s go!!!!” Payne reacted to the news on social media.

Dubbed “The Hillbilly Donnie Brasco,” Payne’s memoir also details the struggles of undercover work, as well as how he managed his marriage, his faith, and fatherhood throughout some of the most dangerous operations in FBI history.

“These are the type of stories that I am drawn to as a producer and as an actor,” Hauser told Deadline. “Scott Payne is a real-life hero, with the kind of moxie and edge you would need to risk your life to fight evil. I am looking forward to producing this movie and getting a chance to bring him and his story to life on the screen.”

Elsewhere, Hauser is also working on a series about the origins of modern-day poker with Sylvester Stallone titled Blood Aces: The Wild Ride of Benny Binion. He told Esquire in 2023 that he was in the early stages of a series where he and Matthew McConaughey would play brothers, written by True Detective’s Nick Pizzolatto. (Brothers may have gotten in the way of that one.) But Hauser’s also gearing up for the release of Dutton Ranch season 2, which will likely air sometime in 2027.

#6718. I Asked Nail Artists in New York and LA—These Are the Most Popular Shades for Fall

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

As an editor, it’s my job to report on beauty trends, whether that’s the buzzy skincare ingredient about to take over shelves or the haircut every celebrity will have in a few months. This year, I’ve reported countlessly on the biggest nail trends of 2026, from the minimalist designs all over Instagram to the nail colors on red carpets and runways. But what are real people actually asking for at the salon?

Now that we’re in the middle of fall, I asked a few nail artists all around the U.S. for the fall nail colors their clients are constantly requesting. “Fall’s nail palette is rich, nuanced, and far more versatile than the usual seasonal script,” says nail artist Elle Gerstein. Among the top trends, which I’ve outlined below, Gerstein says most people want shades that “look polished without feeling predictable and flatter a wide range of skin tones.”

Every single nail artist I spoke to called out deep browns as the most-requested nail color this fall. “Chocolate shades, from milk chocolate to rich espresso, are particularly trending,” says nail artist Vikki Swan. “These colors feel elegant and perfectly capture the fall aesthetic,” she says, noting that “brown tones are increasingly becoming an alternative to classic black, offering a softer, warmer look.”

Nail artist Viktoriia Voloshyna agrees, noting that “clients love it because it feels warm and cozy, but still very elegant, and it goes with all the fall neutrals people are wearing.”

Although dark nail colors are everywhere right now, don’t count out the classics. “Light nails are still having a major fall moment,” says Gerstein. “Sheer pinks and ashen lavender—especially in translucent, glassy finishes—feel fresh rather than summery,” she says. “Old rules of seasonal color are open to interpretation.”

For Voloshyna, “Milky and soft neutral shades are still very popular too. A lot of my clients have busy schedules and want a manicure that looks clean and polished for weeks.”

We apparently can’t get enough of all types of chocolate, including this burnished deep-red shade. “Chocolate cherry is particularly seductive because it combines the warmth of brown with that almost-vampiric red,” says Tucson-based nail artist Max Estrada.

“Browns and reds have a timeless appeal and can be a more interesting alternative to blacks and whites,” says Wong. She loves the MiniLuxe Pure Polish in shade Mexi-Cocoa for an in-between brown-and-red shade.

“Emerald is a fabulous wildcard; I love an unexpected jewel green when everyone else reaches for burgundy,” says Estrada. “But I want more than a flat coat of color. Give me dimensional velvet, reflective chrome, glassy shine, and glitter. Even a basic nude can become opulent with the right sparkling finish.”

“I’m seeing a continued love for effortless, barely-there manicures, and I expect that trend to carry into the holiday season, with subtle touches of sheer chrome and glitter for a festive feel,” says Wong. In fact, even Taylor Swift is trying it out, with a recent nude-and-glitter manicure. “Her look is a lovely reminder that the base color can be simple; add dazzling texture and extra length, and the look becomes something glamorous and memorable,” says Estrada.

“I’ve been seeing a lot of people ask for darker, moodier shades,” says Nicole Wong, nail artist and lead nail designer at MiniLuxe. “I think people naturally gravitate toward these colors as the weather gets cooler because there's this richness and warmth we associate with fall, while still feeling sophisticated and easy to wear.” If you want to opt for those deep shades but try something different, the experts say go for a cat-eye finish. “I expect to see more deep shades with interesting textures and finishes in the latter half of fall,” says Swan.

“Cat-eye nails continue to be one of our most requested styles, and we've noticed clients becoming more intentional about how they wear them,” says nail artist Sandra Wei. “Rather than going for an all-over, dramatic shimmer, many are gravitating toward softer, more diffused magnetic effects that subtly catch the light.”

“Clients are choosing cool blue shades this fall, both deep navy and soft light blue,” says Voloshyna. “Blue isn't a typical fall color, but the darker shades feel just as cozy and elegant as brown or burgundy, and light blue looks fresh and a little icy. It's a nice change for people who want something different from the classic fall palette.”

Beth Gillette is the beauty editor at Cosmopolitan with eight years of experience researching, writing, and editing skin, hair, makeup, nail, and fragrance stories.

Prior to Cosmopolitan, she wrote and edited beauty content as an Editor at The Everygirl for four years. Follow her on Instagram for makeup selfies and a new hair 'do every few months.
