#6702. ¡Vamos, España!

With Spain fresh off a World Cup win, there’s no better time to visit Madrid and the cooler northern regions of Asturias and Galicia

I lived in Spain in the early aughts, when the country was experiencing a mic-drop moment. The shiny, futuristic Frank Gehry–designed Guggenheim Museum had gone up in Bilbao a few years earlier, setting off what is now known as the Bilbao effect: a phenomenon that describes how investing in a visionary architecture project can transform a place. Food-obsessed travelers were flocking to a small beach town in a remote corner of northern Spain just to experience a meal at El Bulli, the legendary, now closed, three-Michelin-star restaurant headed up by Ferran Adrià.

Spain is now in the midst of another glow-up, thanks in part to its World Cup win, and Madrid is front and center. A recent influx of expats from South and North America has locals calling the city the “Miami of Europe.” But don’t let that dissuade you. Mallorquín designer Rosa Esteva, who designs the elegant, made-in-Spain fashion brand Cortana, emphasizes “the charm of those glorious old places that have survived through time.” That means staying at hotels like the intimate Hotel Orfila, booking a table at La Parra, wandering through El Rastro, Madrid’s legendary flea market, and checking out a late-night flamenco show at Tablao de la Villa. At the same time, contemporary places like Esteva’s new shop in the Salamanca neighborhood, the modern tapas bar Sala de Despiece, and the contemporary-art gallery Albarrán Bourdais are worth checking out.

The typical Spanish itinerary often includes a few days in Barcelona to take in the Gaudí before heading south to the beaches of Andalusia. But Vella González, the founder of fashion brand Boxcalf, which has a flagship in Madrid’s Malasaña neighborhood, extols northern Spain’s charms and cooler climate. “For non-Spaniards, it’s an undiscovered paradise,” she says. Start in San Sebastián, one of the world’s most celebrated gastronomic capitals, and eat your way through its pintxos bars, finishing with a steak at the Basque grill house Portuetxe.

In Bilbao, discover the next generation of art spaces, such as the light-filled expansion of the Bilbao Fine Arts Museum, designed by Norman Foster and Luis María Uriarte. The Bilbao effect can be felt in nearby Santander, thanks to the new Faro Santander museum and cultural space, a historic building reimagined by David Chipperfield and currently showcasing the works of surrealist painter Leonora Carrington. Move on to the pristine beaches, green hills, and exceptional dining scene of the Asturias and Galicia regions. In Asturias, splurge on a stay at the remote wabi-sabi styled Solo Palacio and explore the old-growth forests and prehistoric rock shelters of Las Ubiñas-La Mesa Natural Park. Cozy up in the Casa Beatnik Country House hotel in Galicia, and walk the last 10 miles of the famed Camino de Santiago trail to Santiago de Compostela and its Old Town, a UNESCO World Heritage site. It’s an idyllic ending to a new kind of Spanish pilgrimage.

Spoil her with little luxuries she didn’t know she needed.

Shopping for the maximalist woman can feel trickier than shopping for anyone else on your list. Her beauty routine is set, her wardrobe is filled with pieces she adores, and her home is precisely curated. So how do you surprise someone who seems to have it all? As a maximalist with a circle of fellow maximalists, I’ve taken the guesswork out of it and rounded up presents she’ll be delighted to receive.

Look for thoughtful, personal gifts that won’t take up much space but will hold plenty of sentimental value, like a petite signet ring engraved with her initials, a silver frame holding a favorite photo of the two of you, or laundry detergent infused with her signature scent. Everyday luxuries are another lovely option, from an electric wine opener to ultra-cozy slippers or pajamas embroidered with her name. Ultimately, focus on meaningful little treasures or luxurious upgrades to the things she already uses and loves.

Ahead, discover the gifts she’ll remember long after unwrapping.

A dainty, personalized signet ring is sure to earn a permanent spot in her everyday jewelry stack. Choose from 14K yellow gold, sterling silver, or gold vermeil, and make it uniquely hers with an engraved monogram, initial, or meaningful date.

This hand soap smells divine and works like magic to whisk away lingering odors from garlic, onions, and the like, thanks to its gentle exfoliating beads. It’s quickly become a permanent fixture by my kitchen sink, and I haven’t looked back.

Bombas may be best known for its stylish, ultra-comfy socks, but the brand also knows a thing or two about making cozy slippers. And how sweet is this fleecy pair in a neutral check pattern? Whether she’s lounging around the house or stepping out for a quick errand, she’ll have a hard time taking them off.

With so much attention devoted to skin and hair care routines, lashes and brows often get overlooked. So why not treat her to Cécred’s cult-favorite Lash and Brow Builder, a little luxury she can easily incorporate into her daily beauty regimen.

Make the often-dreaded laundry routine feel a little more luxurious with detergent and dryer sheets that infuse her clothes with DedCool’s dreamy fragrance. With notes of bright bergamot, soft vanilla, and warm amber, the scent is reason enough to fall in love, but these laundry essentials go beyond smelling irresistible, helping lift stains and soften fabrics, too.

Eberjey is beloved for its buttery-soft pajama sets in the chicest colorways, and I’m a firm believer that one can never have too many pairs of luxurious PJs. Make her gift feel all the more special by adding a personalized monogram—complimentary, might I add.

There’s always room for another gorgeous pair of earrings in a jewelry lover’s collection, especially when they’re as exquisite as Fope’s designs. For a truly unforgettable gift, spoil her with the brand’s gold Prima earrings, embellished with glittering diamond accents.

Whether she loves hosting or just enjoys unwinding with a nice bottle of wine, an electric corkscrew makes opening her favorite vintage a breeze. No more struggling with a traditional bottle opener or wondering whether the screw is in far enough. Plus, it’s much easier on the wrists.

Elevate her winter wardrobe with an elegant, supremely soft cashmere poncho she can effortlessly slip on for an extra layer of warmth, whether she’s lounging at home, out and about, or braving the office air conditioning.

I’ve been raving about Gemi’s serum-infused hand sanitizers, which keep hands clean without leaving them feeling dry or stripped. This adorable keychain version clips right onto her handbag or keys for easy access, making it a practical yet charming gift for the woman on the go.

For a gift she’ll adore showing off on date nights and at glamorous evening affairs, look to couture designer Zuhair Murad’s new collaboration with footwear brand Aldo. Known for avant-garde creations and intricate embellishments, Zuhair Murad brings a couture-inspired touch to Aldo’s stylish, affordable designs in a collection of party-ready accessories. Among the gorgeous pieces is this patent bag, finished with Murad’s signature logo detailing.

These glimmering studs have earned a spot on actress and style icon Claudia Sulewski’s Nice List at Mejuri, and it’s easy to see why. Not only are they dainty enough for everyday wear, but they’re also available in every birthstone, allowing you to personalize her pair with a gem that corresponds to her birth month—or simply choose her favorite stone.

If you’re looking to make a major impression, a designer handbag is a surefire way to earn yourself the title of her favorite gift-giver. Gucci is known for its sumptuous leather, and this understated shoulder bag is destined to become her new go-to for work and beyond.

A luxurious silver photo frame holding a cherished memory is a sentimental present she’ll be proud to display. For an extra-personal touch, have it engraved with a meaningful date, sweet message, or heartfelt sentiment.

ELLE beauty director Kathleen Hou praises this tortoiseshell hair pin as “an elegant adornment to any updo,” noting how its silver accents catch the light and enhance hair’s natural shine. And considering how often hair ties seem to mysteriously disappear, this chic alternative makes a useful gift for any stylish woman who loves keeping her hair swept out of the way.

Here’s a little luxury guaranteed to make her smile: a Chanel travel fragrance spray housed in a sleek case finished with a limited-edition, jewelry-inspired chain.

When in doubt, a gourmet box of chocolates is a gift that’s unlikely to last long once unwrapped. Compartés is a name to know in the world of luxury confections, and this generously sized gift box is brimming with chocolate-covered nuts, fluffy marshmallows, dipped fruits, and more.

If she takes her makeup routine seriously, she’ll love Simplehuman’s 5x magnifying mirror, which folds up for easy travel and makes perfecting every detail easy.

Transform her bathroom into a five-star spa retreat with this plush, fluffy robe. Whether she’s slipping it on after a shower or wearing it while getting ready for the day, she’ll feel like she’s enjoying a luxurious hotel stay without even leaving home.

Myles Price’s super-soft pull-on pants make an ideal gift for the woman who’s always on the go or simply appreciates lounging in style. I can personally vouch for the comfort—I own a pair myself, and between the exceptional quality and flattering fit, it’s hard not to want to wear them everywhere.

#6700. 11 Best Cowboy Boots in 2026, According to GQ Editors

You might think that cowboy boots are a privilege reserved for ranch hands and folks who can actually ride a horse. But with a little chutzpah, the best cowboy boots are just as adept on a saddle as they are on the subway. Is that so surprising? Before they blossomed into their fashionable forms, much of menswear’s most riffed on garments were rooted in function: cargo pants, work jackets, even suits. With enough time, they were adopted by civilians and adapted to their second lives as symbols of self-expression and creativity, not just job uniforms. Cowboy boots are no different.

In terms of styling, the classic move for western boots is to lean into their rougher side. Toss them on with some well-fitting jeans (preferably vintage boot cuts) and with a snap shirt. And that's still a great approach. But if you open up your mind and step outside of the saloon, the possibilities are practically endless. A slick pair of exotic leather cowboy boots matched with a ‘70s-inspired suit screams filthy rich oil tycoon if not Alessandro Michele-era Gucci. Or, why not mix up a preppy pair of chinos with a grungy graphic tee and some roughed-up suede ropers? The point is, you don’t have to pretend to be a cowboy to wear their boots. So treat them like any other pair of shoes in your closet and wear them however you want. Hell, we’d go so far as to call them an essential pair of boots for every wardrobe.

And if you’re having trouble, well, that’s why you’re here. We’ve wrangled together the best cowboy boots west—and east—of the Mississippi, from the budget-friendly to the ostentatious and every vibe in-between.

The good folks at Tecovas are living, breathing proof that direct-to-consumer brands aren’t all operated by algorithms tasked with solving imaginary problems. The DTC upstart might be the youngest of the bootmakers on this list, but it's quickly endeared itself to budget-strapped swashbucklers with a hankering for democratically-priced kicks.

Take, for example, the Cartwright, a handsome riff on a classic western silhouette made in Leon, Mexico, a bona fide cobbling capital of the world with over a century of expertise to draw on. It boasts hand-laid cording at the shaft, a resoleable Goodyear-welt construction, and a slew of colors and leathers to choose from, including genuine cowhide and goat leather. They’re not the cheapest boots on this list, but the relatively approachable price belies the craftsmanship involved. For $375, they’re one small step up from our favorite budget cowboy boots—but one giant leap in overall quality.

You can think of roper boots as the chilled-out version of the average western boot. Originally designed for calf roping, roper boots feature a shorter shaft and a shorter, squared off heel. These details made it easier for cowboys to dismount their horse and run after the calves they roped. Coincidentally, they also make roper boots easier to walk in which is why some people prefer them over other cowboy boots for everyday wear.

Our pick for the best roper boots currently goes to Red Wing. (Perhaps no surprise, given the brand also makes our favorite trend-proof boots.) Part of Red Wing's Heritage line, they're crafted with premium S.B. Foot Tanning Company leather, and feature Goodyear welt construction so you can have them resoled and keep ‘em going for a long time. Plus, if you’re just dipping your toes into the cowboy boot world, the minimalist uppers forgo the decorative western stitching which makes them easier to style.

If you’re after that western look but need a pair of boots that can handle the demands of a jobsite, a lot of guys will tell you to look to Ariat. That’s because they manage to blend classic cowboy style with modern-day features, and a palatable price point in perfect proportion. While they do offer a range of work boots in lace-up styles, their Groundbreaker boots are a standout with classic cowboy boot looks.

They’re made of full-grain leather, include a supportive and comfortable insole, and meet ASTM standards for slip resistance and electrical safety. Because it’s among Ariat’s most popular styles, it’s also available in a wide range of colorways, toe shapes, and even steel toe versions. Some more traditional cowboys will poo-poo the fact that these aren’t made stateside, but if you’re on a budget, you’ll get more than what you pay for.

Cowboy boots aren’t all rough-and-tumble affairs. In fact, the right pair can easily strut the red carpet or waltz into a fancy restaurant with panache. You’ll want a pair with leather that shines up well and in a darker colorway. For date nights and more formal affairs, these Tony Lamas will impress thanks to the exotic lizard skin uppers and low-key embroidery. They’re the kind of boots that can play well for the in-laws with a tailored suit or play a rock-’n’-roll star with some vintage jeans and a tight white tee.

These days, most boot brands walk in the shadows of one brand: Lucchese. They’ve been outfitting American presidents, high-profile celebs, and the Dallas Cowboy Cheerleaders for decades and it’s all thanks to their commitment to high-quality craftsmanship. Though any pair of Lucchese’s would earn you more than a few approving head nods, the most coveted are the boots that they make in their Texas workshop.

Using a range of full-grain leathers and exotic leathers like caiman alligator and pirarucu fish skin, each pair is crafted by master bootmakers using time-honored techniques. The Gavin, in their iconic Black Cherry, is a picture-perfect style featuring smooth Santini goat leather uppers with intricate embellishments, welted construction, and lemonwood pegs—made the old-fashioned way, basically. They’ll cost you a pretty penny, of course, but they'll last pretty much forever, and the drip you’ll get in return is priceless.

From Ralph Lauren’s western-inspired sub-label, these RRL boots meld high-end materials with old-world craftsmanship and feature American-tanned leather uppers, Goodyear-welted construction, and vintage-style rubber soles—all crafted in a multi-generational Texas bootmaking factory.

Frye is another American brand with proven boot quality chops. (In fact, it claims to be America's oldest continually-operating boot company.) Its Roper boot has all the same strengths as Red Wing's, and comes in a non-roughout leather.

We don't typically include the same designers twice on one list, but Tecovas are that good. The Johnny is for anyone who wants a softer, slightly more charming boot than the eternal Cartwright up top.

For fellas whose style skews a little more regular-guy than rodeo, these lower-profile, lower-priced Ropers have a Goodyear welt and Vibram outsole. Bang for your, ahem, buck.

Wythe's playing-card-inspired boots feature all the bells and whistles, including premium leather inside and out, hand-applied details, lemonwood pegs, and second-to-none construction all-around. While some brands tap the expert bootmakers in Léon, Mexico to pump out high-quality mass-appeal boots, Wythe tapped these artisans to really let them cook.

All of Yuketen's shoes are perfect, which is a big part of the reason Drake's now carries them. And while they're best known for their moccasin styles, the brand makes an exceptionally handsome cowboy boot too. Really, they're just showing off now.

The classic move for western boots is to lean into their rougher side. Toss them on with well-fitting jeans (preferably vintage bootcuts) and a snap-button shirt. But open up your mind and step outside of the saloon and the possibilities are practically endless. A slick pair of exotic leather cowboy boots matched with a '70s-inspired suit screams filthy-rich oil tycoon—if not Alessandro Michele-era Gucci. Or why not mix up a preppy pair of chinos with a grungy graphic tee and some roughed-up suede ropers? The point is, you don’t have to pretend to be a cowboy to wear their boots (though you certainly can). So treat them like any other pair of shoes in your closet and wear them however you want. Hell, we’d go so far as to call them an essential pair of boots for every wardrobe.

Peter Middleton knows a thing or two about the lifestyle having cut his teeth at Ralph Lauren and used it as a springboard for his own western-inspired brand, Wythe. “To me the beauty and shape of the Cowboy Boot (and a lot of the original design intent) lies in its curves and that’s what makes a great boot SEXY. There isn't a lot of men's footwear that has these dramatic curves, leather, and a high heel but the right cowboy boot has them all.”

He says that good cowboy boots should be made with natural leathers that age well with wear, mould to the wearer’s feet, and can be recrafted repeatedly. His non-negotiables include full leather construction from the insole to the outsole, linings, uppers, and heels. Look for Goodyear welted construction which will allow you to have the boots resoled and extend their life. The toe bug (the fancy stitching at the toe), should sit right where your foot flexes to help cover up the crease that comes with each step. Preferably, this would be corded by hand, of course.

Price points will vary, and you can get some well-made boots for around $300. The really great stuff will often be twice that much. Middleton says, “the best thing to do is wait and save up until you can buy the version you actually want because its impossible to cut corners and still deliver the product you want.” So if you can be patient, save up. If you can’t, try buying secondhand. But if you simply can’t wait, you’ll do well enough with plenty of the mid-tier brands until you’re ready to upgrade.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you.

#6699. My Fall Outfits Were Feeling Stale—12 November Outfit Ideas I’m Trying Instead

Now that the weather is cooling off, leaving the house involves grappling with the internal struggle: will I be cute or will I be comfortable today? On chilly days, the heaviest coats or most weather-proof shoes are all-too-appealing, but they don’t always show off your style in the way you might hope. Luckily, this month there are some clever ways you can meet in the sartorial middle: ensuring you don’t freeze, but still putting your outfit first.

With darker evenings here, football season in full swing, and Thanksgiving around the corner, think of these 12 November outfits as the puzzle pieces to help you check the boxes for everything coming up on your calendar. Playing with bold colors, contrasting textures, and even sneakily comfy silhouettes are some of the simple ways you can make November your best-dressed month of the entire year. Check out some of my favorite looks below.

An on-trend striped rugby sweater is the kind of dress-up-or-down staple you might usually style with jeans and sneakers. But for any dressy events on the calendar, try playing with texture and structure by styling it with a full, sequin skirt. It’s a look that reads dressy without trying too hard.

One way to make comfy pieces like oversized knits and track pants feel instantly dressy? By going bold with color. For days when you want to look polished but will mostly be relaxing on the couch, this is a great place to start.

It’s prime football season, which might mean your Sunday afternoon is devoted to keeping up with your favorite team. A pair of relaxed jeans and a suede jacket is a combination that’s cute enough to wear to brunch with your girlfriends, but won’t feel out of place at a sporty party.

If you’re the type to dress up for Thanksgiving (or any occasion really), a trim satin suit is a dressy look in stark contrast to the usual oversized staples. The shiny fabric gives the look a festive touch, while styled back to a simple black top and shoes, the overall effect is very ‘90s Prada—who can complain about that?

Odds are you’ll be headed out of town to spend some time with family. Your travel day look should always put comfort first, but a few small styling choices can make the outfit feel purposeful instead of schlubby. A crew neck tee paired with a V-neck sweater, a trench coat, and chunky Dad sneakers are what make Zoë Kravitz’ outfit look so good.

As winter approaches, there’s something enduringly chic about a white-on-white look. Even if your outfit is as simple as jeans and an oversized sweater, the matchiness pulls everything together. Black accessories are an easy pick, but you could also add a pop of contrast by styling the outfit with red shoes.

Call it genius, call it sneaky; there’s no need to wear full-on sweats to the Thanksgiving table. A dressy matching set can be just as comfortable. Look for styles with a soft, stretchy plissé fabric, which has a dressed-up, flowy air but feels as easy as your coziest loungewear.

This time of year, fashion is all about rich, sumptuous textures and hues. Gigi Hadid’s party look puts a soft, check flannel skirt in contrast with leather boots and a matching jacket, and the effect is greater than the sum of its parts. Cozy yet chic.

When you don’t want to think too hard about your look, an all-black outfit is an easy fallback with polish. Try opting for an oversized knit, styled with tailored trousers and loafers for a look you could wear to the office, but would feel just as comfortable in for a Saturday spent shopping with your most fashionable friends.

Breaking up a tailored look with a cummerbund or even a scarf can be an easy way to repurpose pieces you might usually relegate to the office. This dressy yet comfortable look is versatile, so throw it on for post-work martinis or even a night at the orchestra.

Fringe is a trend to know this season, and Nara Smith’s Kallmeyer dress is the blueprint for a festive Thanksgiving party or wedding when you want to dress to impress. The fringe detail adds movement, which makes it ideal for a situation with a dance floor. Layer a leather jacket or a black trench coat on top for your time in transit.

A great pair of jeans should always be in heavy rotation, but how you style them is an easy way to make them feel fresh. Here, mixing feminine pieces with more classic menswear details gives this a casual-yet-effortful effect. Try a blazer and little heels with socks for a playful spin on pieces you likely already have sitting in your closet.

Aemilia Madden is a freelance writer, editor, and consultant with over 10 years of experience in the fashion industry. She’s written for publications including Vogue, Harper’s Bazaar, Elle,The Cut, and The Wall Street Journal.

She also writes a newsletter called Taeste Bud, that covers stuff we buy, places we go, and the people we want to be. Previously, she held roles at The Zoe Report, WhoWhatWear and Popsuagar. Aemilia attended the University of California, Berkeley where she majored in Political Economics. In her time away from the internet, Aemilia is probably out on a hike.

#6697. Julie Curtiss Captures Snapshots of New York City in Her Paintings

Her latest exhibit, “UNREAL,” is on view at Gagosian

New York City hides its wonders in the folds of everyday life. A crowded deli collage, the quirky decorated interiors of tiny apartments, aquariums lining the windows of Chinese restaurants, and the bustle of crowds all offer small joys for anyone looking closely enough—and artist Julie Curtiss is taking it all in. “I love walking around looking at those big food photo montages that are so gross and grotesque,” Curtiss says. “For painters, it’s such rich material.”

On one of these outings in 2025, Curtiss was walking around the Upper East Side when she caught sight of a peculiar pair: two women wearing fur coats and sporting postoperative compression face masks. The resulting painting, Makeover (2026), features the two mysterious figures standing with their backs to the viewer, one of whom is smoking a cigarette, rendered in Curtiss’s distinctive lurid graphic style. This encounter, which sparked her solo show “UNREAL,” on view at Gagosian through December 19, is a bittersweet meditation on the weight of growing older and the creeping suspicion that life is becoming increasingly uncanny as the city—and the world—changes around her.

“[New York] is always about the facade and constantly rebuilding or changing yourself and about things in a state of disrepair and how you feel on the inside and on the outside,” she explains a couple of weeks before the show in her East Williamsburg studio. Curtiss explains that Makeover marked the start of this New York–focused exhibition, though she needed to shelve the project while completing projects for her show at White Cube in Seoul, focusing on motherhood, and, for Gagosian in Paris, a meditation on domesticity. This new project borrows ideas from both of those shows, distilling them into an examination of her life in New York and how it forged her art and her life over the past 16 years.

Curtiss, now 43, first moved to New York in 2010, after growing up in Paris in a French-Vietnamese household. She worked at Jeff Koons’s studio before moving to work as a studio assistant for KAWS. All the while, she toiled away on her paintings: hyper-stylized, colorful portraits marked by a sharp illustrative sensibility. “You have so much doubt; it’s so full of despair sometimes,” she says of her first years in the city. It wasn’t until 2017 that Hein Koh curated a booth for Curtiss at the Spring/Break Art Show. The show received glowing praise, catapulting her to art-world-darling status and leading to solo shows at Anton Kern, White Cube, and, more recently, Gagosian.

“It sounds cliché, but you just have to persevere and be a little strategic,” she says. “New York is fascinating because it is a place of constant change, and nothing ever feels really secure. Things are always going to move, and you’ve got to adapt to it.”

Life recently changed drastically for Curtiss. She welcomed her first child with her husband, abstract painter Clinton King, in 2024. This newfound motherhood pops up in her painting Kitchen Appendages (2026), a brightly colored illustration of a chaotic household kitchen. The woman is barely present, bent over and nearly out of frame, as a pressure cooker spouts steam and smoke leaves the open oven. This mid-century aesthetic is inspired by Chantal Akerman’s film Jeanne Dielman, 23 Commerce Quay, 1080 Brussels (1972). “[The painting is] a portrait of a woman, but through her kitchen accessories,” she says. “It’s me poking fun at a part of me, the housewife part of myself.”

This playful spirit resurfaces across the exhibition. Intimate reflections are often rendered through magical realism, as in Squid and Whale (2026). This bedroom scene features the two titular animals contorted together in some act of intimacy or violence on a far-too-small bed. “Without really thinking about it, I was making a comment on intimacy and relationship,” Curtiss says, emphasizing how she works by transmuting images she encounters into strange places. This image in particular came from an entirely different place: a diorama at the American Museum of Natural History in New York.

During our studio visit, she is reflective, often mentioning the passing of time and the strangeness of everyday life. “As you get older, things start to feel less real,” she explains to me. “They don’t really go the way you expected them to go. They go off in a weird, surreal place. On a personal level, you look at yourself in the mirror and the way you’ve aged, and you’re like, ‘Is this still me?’ You have this identity crisis because you still see yourself as a young person.” I ask, then, are the faceless black-haired women populating several of her new works—doing gymnastics in Arachne (2026) or nearly carried away by the wind in Before the Storm (2026)—meant to be her?

“They’re always an extension of the self, in a way,” she says. “They are fictional archetypes and characters that embody an experience or side of myself I’m interested in.… I like not giving a face because it keeps people a little frustrated, I’m sure. But at the same time, I find it a more interesting dynamic. It puts the viewer in a voyeuristic position.”

A final glance at the paintings in her studio reveals their purpose: Curtiss wants us in her shoes, to see the world as she does, if even for a moment. In each painting, she crafts a story, leaving us with an occasionally frustrating mid-action snapshot. Each builds a distinct sense of cinematic suspense, as if you might blink and the painting will change.

“I’m as inspired by movies as I am by paintings, [but] I like the ideas that come with the still image,” she proclaims. “You can actually tell a whole story that’s quite complex. There’s a lot going on. People will keep wondering about what happened before the frame and what’s going to happen after the frame.”

#6696. Abdul El-Sayed Is a ‘Retinol King’

Experts review the senator-elect’s skin care routine.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Now that the midterms are over and we’ve seen a blue wave, the way people are talking about the candidates who won has shifted. Instead of policy, we’ve been able to focus on other issues: namely, how hot many of the candidates are (a welcome change). My social media feeds have been littered with photos of newly elected politicians like James Talarico, Jon Ossoff, Rob Sand, and Abdul El-Sayed. And while Sand may have modeled for Prada back in the day, El-Sayed’s complexion is near-perfect. As it turns out, the doctor-turned-politician has a killer skin care routine.

In a video from May that resurfaced and went viral on X last week, El-Sayed revealed his skin care regimen in a video with comedian Suzanne Lambert. Though at first El-Sayed tried to pass off his glowing complexion as “good genetics,” he has a full routine to help. The senator-elect begins his day with CeraVe Facial Cleanser. After that, he uses EltaMD AOX UV Elements SPF 50 sunscreen, which he reapplies halfway through the day. At night, he washes his face with the same CeraVe cleanser. Every other day, he uses Differin, a retinoid, to increase cell turnover. El-Sayed is a fan of the “sandwich method,” where you use moisturizer both before and after retinol (he opts for EltaMD PM Restore Moisturizer). It’s clear that El-Sayed has done his homework (he is a doctor, after all). Below, I asked three skin experts to give their thoughts on his skin care routine.

“Okay, I’m obsessed. A retinol king with a strong SPF commitment—extremely impressed. The only thing missing in my opinion is a low and slow daily exfoliation to help shift some of that cell buildup that can occur with retinol use. I’m of course going to recommend Sofie Pavitt Face Mandelic Clearing Serum. If he’s ever in New York City I’d love for him to come in for a facial with me, my treat.”

“Of course he has an evidence-backed routine. He’s using a cleanser in the morning and then a sunscreen which can double as a moisturizer (although the EltaMD one is not super moisturizing). Reapplying that around 12 P.M. or 1 P.M. is fantastic advice. The one thing that he is wrong on—and I hate that I’m using that term—is that adapalene is not tretinoin. He keeps calling adapalene retinoic acid, and they are not the same thing. They are both vitamin A derivatives, approved for drug use, but adapalene is approved for acne, while tretinoin is approved for acne and antiaging. They’re same-same but different. Adapalene is great for acne, but if you’re worried about acne and aging, you’re probably going to be using retinoic acid. Other than that, my man, he’s got it. He’s gold.” [Editor’s note: you could also try the Dieux Firm Revival HydroRetinal Firming Serum.]

“Starting with a CeraVe face wash? A bipartisan choice if I’ve ever seen one. It’s gentle, effective, accessible, and works for a wide range of skin types and ages. Honestly, one of the few things I think we can get both sides of the aisle to agree on. Following that up with SPF that he actually reapplies? Now that’s the kind of commitment to prevention I can get behind. A politician who understands the value of protecting against future damage? How refreshing. But where Senator Abdul really earns my attention is when he casually drops the retinol sandwich method into the conversation. It’s an excellent strategy for people whose skin doesn’t tolerate retinol directly. I have one friendly amendment to the senator’s skin care legislation: If your skin can tolerate it, consider applying retinol directly to clean, dry skin before moisturizing. That can allow for more direct delivery of the active ingredient, although the sandwich method can still be effective.”

It’s certainly not your standard autumn hue

Kermit the Frog once famously declared that “it’s not easy bein’ green,” but Jennifer Lawrence seems to disagree.

#6690. 18 Best Raincoats for Men 2026, According to GQ Editors

Decades ago, your only options for rainy weather coverage were some kind of trench coat, a coarse wool overcoat, or, if you really needed to be out in it, a thick rubber sack that kept you dry but didn’t breathe. Thankfully, material science has advanced.

There are, of course, umbrellas? And we won’t stop you looking into those. But ask anyone from the Pacific Northwest, and they’ll tell you their rain jacket does all that work with ease. That’s because raincoats aren’t an accessory to your outfit: they’re the main focus. A good raincoat can turn your sad ensemble into head-turning Paparazzi fodder, or at the very least, keep you dry and stylish when it’s wet out.

Still not convinced? We figured—so we tested the best rain jackets and coats for men on the market right now, from the tried-and-true natural-fabric mainstays to the buzzy, newfangled riffs, and everything in between. Here they are.

Arc'teryx's Beta LT jacket is the pinnacle of no-BS rain defense, beloved by wannabe Everest climbers, GQ Recommends editors, and meme-savvy TikTokers alike. Its custom Gore-Tex fabrication will keep you from getting soaked during the harshest of downpours, while its breathable pores work overtime to let water vapor (a.k.a. sweat) escape. That sleek, streamlined silhouette also lends itself naturally to a range of pairings, from straight-fit jeans and sneakers to a full-on “Scaling Kilimanjaro” kit—cargos, backpack, hiking boots—perfect for all of your wildcard outdoor activities.

It’s an investment, but hundreds of guys were showering in theirs for a reason: If you need top-tier weather protection and long-term durability—and are willing to invest—this is still the best rain jacket for serious outdoor use. That said, most dudes chasing the clout that Arc’teryx affords won’t need to max out its capabilities. Still, it’s good to know that if you’re ever caught in a downpour that won’t let up, the Beta’s the one waterproof jacket that won’t leave you high and, uh, wet.

When it comes to outdoor gear that keeps up with Mother Nature, Patagonia’s among the first to come to mind. The OG gorpcore label has more than its fair share of bangers for every climate from the iconic Baggies shorts to its range of plush fleece jackets, and when it comes to rainy weather, there’s the Torrentshell jacket. It’s a canonical piece of kit for Patagonia and has kept customers dry and fly for years.

The latest version features a three-layer shell system that maximizes water-repellency and breathability with a 100% recycled nylon face fabric. It features toasty microfleece-lined handwarmer pockets, welted zippers for water protection (plus pit zips for ventilation), and the entire thing can pack down into itself. So pack it up, throw it in your bag, and bust it out whenever the weather turns out to be worse than what the weatherman says. With a feature set like that, you’d expect to pay through the nose, but we’re thrilled to say that it doesn’t even break $200.

The advancements in rain-wicking technology tickles our lizard brains as much as watching a rock-crushing machine turn a boulder into pebbles. But as much as we appreciate multi-layered DWR-coated materials and heat-sealed seams give us joy, we also have a great reverence and appreciation for rain coats of yore. Enter the waxed jacket, a time-tested fabric used by sailors off the British coast since the 1800s.

If you’re gonna get a waxed jacket, you’d best get a Barbour, the reigning champ of waxed jackets. Barbour has more options and collaborations than ever, so it can be tricky to get your head around what’s what but for our money, the classic Beaufort is the Goldilocks of wax jackets. Where the Bedale is shorter and styles like the Border run down to the mid-thigh, the Beaufort is just right but still long enough to layer over your sport coats. Whichever you choose, don’t forget to re-wax at home after a few seasons. Guys seem to be nervous to do it, but it’s easy, and everytime I’ve re-waxed mine, people compliment me on how great it looks. The reward for your grunt work is a jacket you'll keep for decades to come.

This season, J.Press has unearthed a Rare Barbour: the Burghley. It hasn’t been in the brand’s regular rotation for a number of years, earning it a following among collectors in places like Japan. But now it’s back in all its sweeping, full-length glory.

Originally designed to extend past the knees (and over the saddle and tops of riding boots) the Burghley protects the rider from rain and thorns. It’s a dramatic silhouette that will set you apart from all the cropped Transport and Bedales out there. Sure, it has equestrian heritage, but you needn’t be keeping a stable to wear one. It’s a great alternative to a trench, at home in the city as well as the country. And yes, it’s still made in England.

The perfect trench coat does exist, and Burberry, inventor of the style's signature gabardine fabric in 1879, cracked the code on it long ago. In the nearly 150 years since, surprisingly little has changed about the silhouette, and for good reason. The classic fit means it's roomy enough to layer over your slouchiest Armani-inspired suiting, while the belted design gives it instant sophistication. Plus, the lining and under-collar check pattern is unmistakably Burberry—an investment-worthy flex since the coat was invented.

Its WWI heritage is well-documented—British officers wore it in the trenches, using details like the shoulder flap for rifle recoil and belt rings for canteens and grenades serving real military functions. Today, it’s less about battlefield utility and more about how that water-resistant cotton gabardine will keep you dry in light city rain. I like the black, but the classic tan is always an option for you too.

Another entry from Vancouver—what can we say, they know a few things about rain up there. Indie label James Coward sources fabric from mills known for their quality and considered production practices, then makes its garments locally in its workshop. This coat is cut from the brand’s durable, waterproof ‘Mastershield cloth, a dense weave that offers protection from the elements. A generous silhouette and roomy raglan sleeves give it natural gravitas in gloomy weather, all while keeping the look relaxed and easy to layer.

Whereas the Arc’teryx Beta is the brand’s versatile all-mountain shell, the Alpha SV is built for technical climbing and severe weather. A helmet-compatible hood, harness-ready chest pockets and pit zips make it the top dog of storm shells.

HAVEN puts a GORPcore spin on the refined, city-ready trench made from three-layer GORE-TEX PRO, a more rugged fabric typically found in shells for climbing and backcountry skiing. It’s serious storm gear with a city sensibility, ready to make you feel invincible during a rainy commute.

The wrap coat is Lemaire’s runaway hit. But this Ventile-cotton style is a rainy-day flex: densely woven, breathable cotton that swells when wet to help keep wind and rain out, without synthetic fibres or coatings. Chic.

Menswear can get a little obsessive about fabric specs and provenance. But when a jacket is this cool, you get why. 100 percent Giza cotton, woven at maximum density in Saitama, Japan and originally developed for the British Air Force and later recommissioned by Japan’s Coast Guard. Yeah, that’s the good stuff.

Prep never left, but J.Press is certainly on its way back. The label’s updated take on a classic hooded parka keeps the familiar military shape sans PFAS with natural Ventile cotton. Choose classic army green, or eye-popping orange.

Haider Ackermann's take on Canada Goose is coming into focus. The brand’s Snow Goose sub-label is more Milan than Manitoba, trading logo-heavy designs for cool colours and modern silhouettes that go well beyond down parkas.

Making a good rain jacket might not take a degree in nuclear science, but Outdoor Research’s founder was actually a nuclear physicist turned avid mountaineer. This stripped-back shell sheds weight and packs small without skimping on protection. Stash it and forget it.

Marmot, meanwhile didn’t pull back on features to shave weight. This soft, quiet waterproof shell is built for movement, with an “Angel-Wing” design that lets you reach overhead without the hem riding up and putting your backside on display.

Reigning Champ has also gone well beyond sweats and tees. This workhorse of a rain jacket is more downtown than summit in style but still meets the moment with GORE-TEX construction and a very digestible price.

Italian fabric. Fifth-generation Portuguese construction. New York City design. That’s the mix behind Knickerbocker’s full-length trench. Its tightly woven, water-repellent fabric helps keep rain out all with the kind of easy, downtown cool Knickerbocker does so well.

Uniqlo’s even more affordable sister brand, GU, delivers a lot of jacket for the money The throwback piping and punchy colours nod to the ’90s, while the water- and wind-resistant fabric makes it practical, too.

A waxed Harrington probably isn’t for a downpour unless your trousers are waxed, too, but it’s ideal for breezy, drizzly, and sunny fall days alike. And, aye, the waxed fabric comes straight from Scotland. No messing about.

Who wants to drag a sopping wet umbrella around only to forget it at the restaurant or in the back of a cab? When you’ve got a trench coat with your cell and headphones in the pockets, it’s almost impossible to lose. Through light mists, heavy rain, and even torrential downpours, the best rain coats are, ironically, the drippiest too. They’ll prevent you from showing up to the function like a poor wet dog and instead make your arrival a warm, dry welcome.

Trench coats that aren’t the only coats vying to shield you from the rain, though. Gorpcore’s popularity has given us waves of tech-y jackets, parkas, and anoraks all wrought from futuristic multi-layered materials that balance breathability with waterproof ability. The result is a cementing of this 21st century sportswear into must-have menswear. And let’s not forget the workwear-adjacent waxed jackets born from sailing the Scottish seas in 15th-century Scotland. With their rugged good looks and a lust for patina, they’ve become stylish staples when the weather’s all doom and gloom.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6689. Max Mara Is the Quiet Luxury Blueprint

For 75 years, the brand has put forth the idea that a foundational wardrobe—what we wear to move through the world—is far from boring. In fact, it can offer endless possibilities.

I stepped onto a crowded A train the other day, heading from Brooklyn to Manhattan, and was confronted with a microcosm of people with their different styles: contractors and construction workers (Carhartt and utility jackets), well-heeled, corporate pragmatists (slim suits, printed sheaths), fashion students (wearing their own creations), and art-world peacocks (prints on prints, layers atop layers).

There’s no better way to get a sense of what people really wear than on a morning commute. If you drop in at 8:00 a.m. on the Paris metro, the tube in London, the U-Bahn in Berlin, Singapore’s MRT, or the Shanghai subway, you’ll see a tightly packed sardine can filled with disparate modes of nine-to-five dressing. But recurring motifs appear, particularly on those women who look like they’ve really got it together: a sleek camel overcoat paired with crisply creased trousers and a great T-shirt, or a pair of jeans and a sharply tailored black blazer. This is the no-fail, get-it-done-and-look-good-doing-it city uniform, and much of its history can be traced back to Max Mara, which celebrates its 75th anniversary this year.

This is why the brand, despite its Italian origins, chose to show its resort collection in Shanghai this past summer. “Max Mara has always been a metropolitan phenomenon,” Ian Griffiths, the label’s longtime creative director, tells me on the eve of the show. “After 75 years, that’s what Max Mara is all about. It’s about urban chic; it’s about a woman who really wants to engage with a city.” For Griffiths, just as modernity defines Shanghai, so too does it underscore Max Mara’s longevity in fashion’s rapidly shifting ecosystem.

The show was held at Shanghai’s Long Museum West Bund, an art exhibition space housed inside a brutalist concrete building on the western side of the city. The skies that day were filled with dense gray fog and windy, misty rain, veiling the famously illuminated skyline just enough to look like a scene from Blade Runner.

“There’s something about Max Mara that works really well against the background of brutalist architecture,” Griffiths says. “It’s like the city itself, and Max Mara’s luxury is kind of a foil to this hard city landscape.”

Outside the museum, an entirely new neighborhood was going up. Luxury apartment buildings, restaurants, and gyms were all being erected by clusters of giant cranes placed precariously close together. Inside the Long Museum, guests were time-warped back to Max Mara’s beginnings in 1951, when Achille Maramotti founded the brand with one coat and one suit. He revolutionized sportswear in Italy by mass-producing classically tailored garments at a time when most men and women purchased their clothes directly from independent tailors and dressmakers. In many ways, Maramotti was an early proponent of modern sportswear and one of the first to translate it from its American origins to more distinctly European styles.

One of the most dominant themes on the runways in recent years has been this idea of wardrobing: effortless pieces that can be endlessly remixed, whether it’s a jean and a blazer accessorized with a printed silk scarf, a boxy knee-length skirt suit, or a fluid dress made from cotton jersey. Juxtaposed with recent trends like heavy embellishment, texture, and eccentric shapes and silhouettes, these updated takes on classics offer a way to play with your personal style if the more idiosyncratic stuff isn’t your thing. With Max Mara, though, it has never been about trends. Instead, the brand has held fast to the idea that real taste is inherent, not plucked from the internet, and that clothes should enhance rather than inform who you are or want to be.

It’s why Max Mara has long appealed to women in power who need to be heard and armored. See: Nancy Pelosi in the fiery-orange coat she wore following a confrontational meeting with President Trump in 2018 or Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, looking poised and polished in white jeans and a cashmere camel trench in 2023, a look built to withstand public scrutiny. Katie Holmes said at the show that she loves Max Mara because of its “classic elegance” and its ability to “fit into any wardrobe.” Fashion editor Tonne Goodman, who has styled many Max Mara shows and campaigns, is well known among fashion obsessives for her unimpeachable taste and rigorous uniform; she always wears some version of a chic silk scarf, sweater, and loafers.

“The clothes understand the realities of a woman’s life today,” says society fixture and designer Nicky Hilton, a longtime Max Mara client. “You can put on a beautiful coat or a perfectly tailored suit and immediately feel pulled together. But it never feels overly precious. The feeling of confidence and ease is incredibly consistent. The Teddy coats and camel coats have been staples in my closet for years.”

Max Mara clients wandered the exhibition space alongside newer Gen-Z acolytes like Olympic freestyle skier Eileen Gu and filmmaker and actor Maude Apatow. Laura Lusuardi, who has been the house’s fashion coordinator since the 1960s, was also there, dressed in a tunic, wide-leg pants, and sculptural statement jewelry. “Over 75 years, women’s lifestyles have changed dramatically, and Max Mara has always closely observed and accompanied that evolution, especially through pivotal moments such as the rise of the ‘working woman’ in the 1980s,” Lusuardi explains. “Our incredible archive serves as a constant source of inspiration, allowing us to rethink our heritage through a contemporary lens.”

In tandem with the resort show, the brand staged an exhibition in the same space, curated by fashion historian Olivier Saillard, that re-created its archive in Reggio Emilia, Italy. The space was packed with floor-to-ceiling industrial shelving that featured wooden shipping crates, shoe and hat boxes, spools of thread, and historic ephemera from the Max Mara universe, including Maramotti’s original sewing machines, advertisements dating back to the 1950s, and the original prototypes of some Max Mara coats. Through the archives, Saillard was able to highlight Maramotti’s fashion origins as the son of a mother who wrote sewing manuals and great-grandmother who started a dressmaking school in the 1850s. “Within that origin lies everything fashion has to say: transmission, true elegance, the timelessness of a garment one makes oneself or holds dear,” he says.

The show opened with a nod to streamlined glamour: a sequined ivory trench coat styled with a white turtleneck underneath and a pair of beige T-strap pumps. More monochromatic looks followed, including a boxy black miniskirt suit and a sumptuous white wrap coat cinched with a wide, decorative belt, which would appear in several playful iterations throughout the collection, including with black-and-white-striped sequined short shorts. Griffiths referenced the Bauhaus art and design movement (the original factory in Reggio Emilia was designed in a Bauhaus-inspired style) with dizzying graphic patterns applied to cardigans and pencil skirts, as well as injections of royal blue, mustard, and Max Mara’s signature red.

The Shanghai collection was a reflection of Max Mara’s unique ability to infuse newness and even some novelty (à la the short shorts, sequins, and belts) into its repertoire. As Griffiths explains, “It’s about offering a curated choice that allows every Max Mara woman to find her style, her look, her silhouette.” He adds, “Everyone has a desire for some kind of novelty, so you can’t erase it from the offer, but within the context of a wardrobe or within a collection, there can be one or two pieces, and hopefully those pieces have longevity too.”

Still, the aim, Lusuardi explains, is “not to be just ‘in fashion’ ” but to “go beyond trends.” She adds, “The essence of the Max Mara look lies in its essentiality.”

After the show, walking back out through the exhibition space, you could see their points articulated: young women wearing their ivory silk button-downs and tailored pants with multiple layered belts in mixed metals; older clients dressed in vintage Max Mara skirts and jackets, styled with a cardigan over their shoulders or a decorative minaudière. The brand was all around, but you noticed the people in the clothes.

“Over the years, creativity in fashion has evolved into something tied deeply to personal style,” Lusuardi explains. “It’s how a woman wears and interprets a piece that truly makes the difference. Max Mara offers a versatile foundation that adapts seamlessly to every woman’s unique lifestyle.” In other words, there’s no better—and more modern—uniform than one that’s truly your own, whatever city or subway car you’re making your way through.

Opening image top center: Max Mara Resort 2027. All others, surrounding: “The Max!” 75th-anniversary exhibition and behind-the-scenes images shown at the Long Museum West Bund, Shanghai.

There are few hair updates as simple, yet as impactful, as switching up your part. After several seasons dominated by center-parted lengths and deliberately undone styling, the side part is making a convincing return. The latest to make a case for its appeal? None other than Margot Robbie.

Attending Chanel’s Cruise 2026/2027 show in Australia, the actor and producer stepped out with a softly structured ‘buttercup bob,’ styled with a deep side part and flipped-out ends. The result was equal parts polished and quietly sophisticated. And while Robbie has recently been favoring the waterfall bob, this latest iteration feels notably sleeker, offering a more refined take on the trending cut.

“This bob is an effortless take on a classic jaw-length cut. It’s neat without feeling rigid, with soft ends and a clean shape that gives hair an expensive-looking finish,” Luke Hersheson, hairstylist and CEO of Hershesons previously told ELLE. In short, it trades lived-in texture for a more polished silhouette, with precise ends and subtle flicks upward that create a sharper finish.

Robbie’s latest style embodies the look perfectly, pairing a side part with softly sculpted ends for an updated take on the preppy bob. The part allows for a sweeping side bang, adding a touch of glamour to an otherwise classic cut.

When it comes to re-creating Robbie’s look, Talia Hurley, a stylist at Blue Tit London, recommends blow-drying the hair with a round brush for a glossy, classic finish. This will also help create added volume and the bend needed to achieve the look’s side-swept shape.

Luke Hersheson recommends finishing the look with a pea-sized amount of smoothing cream to add shine and tame flyaways without leaving the hair greasy, ensuring the style retains its polished, glossy finish.

#6687. The Fall Winter 2026 Fashion Trends to Know and Shop Now

If recent seasons have been defined by understated dressing, the fall-winter 2026 trends mark a shift toward a more expressive approach to style. However, there’s still a piece of the cake for every aesthetic to cut into. Across the runways, designers embraced the art of contrast. By pairing clean, minimalist silhouettes with rich textures—and reimagining classic wardrobe staples with unexpected details like a peplum or a voluminous shape—they proved that practicality and personality can coexist. The result is a season that feels both wearable and exciting.

Leading the conversation this season are six standout trends that capture fashion’s evolving mood. The Updated Lady introduces a fresh take on suiting for the modern woman, complete with feminine touches and softened structures. (Take a look at Chanel, Balenciaga, and Jil Sander for fresh inspiration, for starters.) Elsewhere, collections at Khaite, Kallmeyer, and Conner Ives nodded to the golden age of the 1920s, incorporating elegant Art Deco touches throughout. An unexpected take on proportions has entered the chat, too, with Tory Burch and Celine reconfiguring preconceived notions of size and shape. Designers, from Prada to Loewe, leaned on the power of styling, too, showcasing how layering and a close attention to detail can transform a wardrobe. For a more alluring take on the season, Alaïa and Valentino celebrated the female form through body-hugging silhouettes and delicate sheer pieces. Meanwhile, Dries Van Noten and Erdem embraced the spirit of fall with down-to-earth palettes of green and brown, punctuated by dark floral patterns.

Discover a shoppable first look at the key fall winter 2026 fashion trends before they fully take over. Don’t forget to come back to this story for more.

Unlike past seasons, there wasn’t one definitive silhouette for tailoring this fall. Let’s start with suiting. Designers don’t want you to stay within the lines. Many jackets were shown with mismatched trousers and skirts; lapel linings were exposed; traditional collared shirts were left undone and wrinkled; collars were turned up and styled with one in and one out. Some blazers shrank; some went long and lean. Others were cropped, nipped in, or even made sculptural.

In autumn’s sea of black coats and navy sweaters, choose color. This season, designers made it simple, showing a slew of head-to-toe looks in vivid monochrome hues. Take your pick! The runways offered a spin around the contemporary color wheel with splashes of color-drenched leather bags and footwear. From knits to denim, dresses to outerwear, we can’t think of a reason not to try this kind of energetic dressing.

This isn’t your grandmother’s lace! On the fall runways, designers from Altuzarra and Colleen Allen to Bottega Veneta, Dior, and Gabriela Hearst embraced a more dramatic kind of romance, with cascading layers, frothy ruffles, and sheer, sweeping silhouettes. Get the look with a delicate lace blouse paired with a tiered black skirt, or go all in with a floor-length lace dress. The effect is romantic, but anything but prim.

Photos: Courtesy of Kallmeyer, Khaite, Rabanne, Chanel, and Loro Piana

Although F. Scott Fitzgerald’s 1925 novel, The Great Gatsby, predates the height of the design style, its themes of 1920s luxury have permanently associated the story with the movement’s signature geometric patterns and overt opulence. From Khaite to Colleen Allen, designers embraced the era with richly detailed texture, glamorous shapes, fringe, gloves, and velvet. To quote the iconic host himself: “Can’t repeat the past? Why, of course, you can!” For 2026, the era returns with a modern, streamlined touch—ready for daily wear to elegant soirées.

Photos: Courtesy of Chanel, Stella McCartney, Givenchy, Jil Sander, and Chloé

The fall-winter 2026 runways showcased a sense of whimsy through bold proportions, featuring oversized designs, cropped styles, and exaggerated silhouettes. Cocoon-like tailoring, dramatic hemlines, and billowy pants and dresses create an expressive and eye-catching approach to fashion. This trend embraces a bit of drama (because that’s life!) while also maintaining a sense of balance. Unconventional silhouettes might feel daunting to incorporate into your daily lineup, so start with small touches. Destree’s jacquard blouse balances voluminous shoulders with a fitted waist that pairs easily with jeans, while Aflalo’s tapered white balloon pants feel airy and light—just add a layered knit and coat for transitional dressing.

Photos: Courtesy of Ferragamo, Loewe, Prada, Johanna Parv, The Row (middle)

Primarily inspired by the fall/winter 2026 Prada runway, the power of styling was a reminder that great style isn’t about owning more—it’s about seeing familiar pieces, like cardigans and tailored trousers, in a new light. Everyday wardrobe staples were transformed through unique pairings, layered basics, and unexpected accessories to create ensembles that demand a second glance. Styling, too, becomes a vessel for self-expression, allowing you to make each piece your own through personal touches and a careful attention to detail.

Photos: Courtesy of Dior, Chanel, Givenchy, Balenciaga, Proenza Schouler, Kallmeyer

Current, confident, and sophisticated, the Updated Lady emerged as one of fall-winter 2026’s defining archetypes, with houses like Chanel, Givenchy, and Balenciaga reimagining power dressing through a contemporary lens. Rather than rigid corporate suiting, the season favored softened structures, explored through gently sloping waists, sculpted jackets, and rich textures that balance strength with ease. The modern woman is multifaceted and full of contradictions, balancing polish with her own distinct edge—shouldn’t her wardrobe follow suit?

Photos: Courtesy of Gucci, Gorunway.com, Khaite and Alaïa

Bodies, bodies, bodies! The fall 2026 runways were an homage to the female form. From the second-skin dresses at Alaïa—some of which actually walked in flesh-colored nude—to Khaite’s sheer layers and Valentino’s lingerie-inspired slips, little was left to the imagination. Translating the trend into your own fall rotation may seem far-fetched, but by embracing it piece by piece, you can achieve an alluring look without going full naked dressing. Imagine Jil Sander’s knit bustier top with a slim trouser, Gucci’s cut-out leggings grounded by a crisp white tee, or one of Saint Lauren’s lace mini dresses beneath a sharp tailored blazer. To bring it back to one of the season’s strongest show notes—and one we outlined above: It all comes down to the styling.

It’s not unusual for fall trends to find inspiration in the countryside—whether it’s heritage plaids, khaki barn jackets, or some kind of cozy knit variation. As grounding as the source material may be, this season’s expression is more elaborate than ever. Nowhere is that more apparent than in the floral prints peppered throughout the collections: they’re richer, deeper, and even moodier than in years’ past. Par for the course, intricate floral brocades appeared at Dries Van Noten on everything from outerwear to midiskirts. Simone Rocha and Erdem also showcased their fair share of flora and fauna, from draped dresses to blouses, proving that the look can move between moods and occasions.

#6684. ‘VisionQuest’ Made Me Question Everything I Feel About AI

It’s hard to ignore how much AI has changed over the years and how it forces us to look at the WandaVision trilogy differently.

AI has always been one of the core parts of the Marvel Cinematic Universe. J.A.R.V.I.S.’s introduction in Iron Man has blossomed into a whole crew of AI characters who have joined in on the fun, although, usually always from afar. VisionQuest took it one step further, introducing us to new counterparts of different AI characters, turning them from digital assistants and the robotic arms that we’re used to seeing in the MCU to human-like avatars, giving them actual personas, allowing us to see more of their personalities and how they work together within the consciousness of Vision. Seeing their sacrifices (J.A.R.V.I.S., no!) and their triumphs (E.D.I.T.H., yes!) definitely had us feeling real emotions for these characters.

If this was five years ago, I would not even think twice about any of this. But, here I was, really questioning how I was feeling because of the current landscape. In a time where AI is taking over jobs, causing a new kind of mental health crisis, data centers are taking our water and resources, and increased fears of an AI takeover, there’s a certain kind of unsettledness when it comes to seeing the mixture of humanity, personality, and even memories being given to these AI characters and the fact that I am mourning over them.

VisionQuest makes it clear that what happened in Westview was not “real” and was all part of Wanda’s magic. While the current versions of Vision and Tommy didn’t actually live out those events, they cannot deny the connection they feel towards one another due to the “memories” they hold from that time. But are those memories just something that was programmed within them or something that has become real?

Of course, this is all gets blurry when you remember that this TV show is pure fiction. However, it’s the human parts of ourselves—the connection to life and emotion—that cannot help but process what we’re seeing as real. It’s also the humanity that is given to it by the human writers, actors, and those behind the scenes allow us to connect with this as an art form. And maybe that’s what makes this all so much more complicated.

The blurring of reality and AI is nothing new. Some people view AI as their real-life friends and partners. F.R.I.D.A.Y. notes that she lost “half of her world,” when she lost Tony Stark, showing how close she felt to him despite just being a program. Others have created AI personas of their loved ones who passed as a way to keep their spirit alive. Which brings us to the center of all of this, someone who is neither AI nor someone with broken memories: Wanda. Westview was an illusion created in her grief to help her mourn Vision and also create the future that she had always wanted, one with a husband, a house, and kids. She created a new kind of real, not only for herself, but for those around her.

So we have to ask ourselves, if something fake can make us feel something real, then what really is the truth? If we still don’t know, then AI certainly won’t either. In the case of VisionQuest, it’s clear that one of the important things needed to make something real is love. The love that Wanda has for her family. The love that these creators have for these stories. And the love that we, as viewers, have for these characters. That’s what makes it all feel real even though we know it’s fiction. And that’s what drives Vision and Tommy to finally recognize each other as father and son. Without love, it will never feel real. And I think—and I hope—that it will remain something that AI in real life will never learn how to replicate.

#6683. Men Are Outspending Women on Botox. Here’s What They’re Asking For

Guys are going to increasingly wild lengths to achieve their version of the idealized man. Looksmaxxing, as we’ve come to know it, has included surgical procedures to reshape their eyes, taking a hammer to their face to create a more chiseled jawline, and breaking their legs to gain a couple inches. But an OG in cosmetic procedures is seeing a resurgence in men, too.

Chances are you’re familiar with Botox: localized injections to smoothen wrinkles in common areas like the forehead, the eyes, or around the mouth. Long viewed as a treatment limited to the ladies, it’s increasingly becoming another form of male upkeep. Now we’re learning that men are outspending women on the popular procedure. According to an October 2026 report by Guidepoint Qsight, a medical aesthetics data and intelligence provider, men spent an average of $529 per neurotoxin visit in Q3 of 2026, compared with $455 for women. (The figures include not just Botox but also competitors like Daxxify and Xeomin.)

The potential explanation is simple: Botox is an easy way to look a little younger, more well-rested, and even less angry or severe. (As a built-in bonus, it’s virtually painless—especially compared to the barbaric looksmaxxing trends circulating as of late.) According to a 2025 survey of 2,900 aesthetic plastic surgeons, men accounted for over 15% of all Botox cases that year. It was also their top non-surgical treatment by a landslide.

The growing cohort of men opting into “Brotox” believe it’s money well spent. Nancy Samolitis, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in Los Angeles and co-founder of facile, has been treating men for years but has recently seen an uptick in male clientele, aged anywhere from 35 to 70. These days, “they’re more interested in skincare and more open to procedures,” she says. Many also book their first treatment nudged by their spouse or significant other who are existing patients. Others come in simply wanting to look better but not knowing what treatment to get. In many cases, Botox fits the bill.

While the uninitiated might think the injections make guys look surprised or less masculine, good work can be undetectable. Still you, just fresher.

Kyle Waldrop, a 37-year-old product designer in Los Angeles, first started getting Botox three years ago. “I’ve always been good about keeping up with a skincare routine and taking care of myself, so Botox felt like a natural extension of what I was already doing,” he says. His goal isn’t to change his face but to slow down wrinkles before they become obvious. He gets Botox for his forehead lines and crow’s feet, and recently started treating his neck lines, too.

But it’s not always about looking younger. Men are also using Botox in less obvious places. David Kim, MD, board-certified dermatologist and the founder of Soho Dermatology in New York City, treats the chin for more projection, as well as the underarms to combat excess sweating. Bell Yoo, NP, a board-certified nurse practitioner and the founder of Mimo Aesthetics in West Hollywood, adds that she injects the masseter (and sometimes temporalis) muscles for guys who struggle with jaw clenching or teeth grinding.

Aesthetically, men usually aren’t looking for the same thing from Botox as women. For starters, many want to soften their lines without erasing them. Preserving some natural movement is key. “My female patients often love that smooth, ‘glass skin’ appearance, whereas some of my male patients think it looks too waxy or oily,” Yoo says. Men also tend to opt out of a Botox brow lift, which many women request. “Men would much rather maintain a slightly heavier, lower-set brow than end up with an overly arched or ‘Spock’ brow,” Yoo says. Per Samolitis, this requires different injection points and doses tailored for guys. Kim, meanwhile, is careful not to overdo the crow’s feet. “It looks more natural when men have lines around the eyes, and it makes their face look better overall,” he says. These techniques quell the fears that guys have about looking less masculine or overdone. For most, the ultimate goal is to look relaxed and rejuvenated—not tight and taut. “When it’s done well and with the right amount, you look like yourself, just a bit more rested,” Waldrop says. “I still have all my natural movement and expressions, which is important to me.”

All that subtlety comes at a price. Men may end up paying more than women to treat the same areas, but the higher price tag is actually expected: Men often have larger, stronger facial muscles, which require more units to achieve their desired results, Yoo says.

While more men are embracing Botox, some remain tight-lipped about it. Yoo says that most of her male Botox patients are pretty discreet. “I think there’s still some stigma around men receiving cosmetic treatments, and many would rather keep it to themselves,” she says. Waldrop, however, is an open book. “I don’t really see it as something worth hiding or feeling that weird about,” he says. “Guys are already spending money on skincare, haircuts, hair transplants, working out, and all sorts of things to look and feel better, so I don’t really see why Botox should be treated any differently.”

For Waldrop, Botox is less a dramatic intervention than another item on his grooming checklist. He doesn’t see it as something that needs to be announced or apologized for. At the end of the day, “it’s really not that deep,” he says.
