#6662. GQ’s 13 Breakout Stars of 2026

Sometimes it’s fun to be early to the party. GQ launched the Breakouts portfolio in 2014 to celebrate the Hollywood upstarts who were poised to do big things. And not to brag, but we nailed it; that first group included Miles Teller, Shailene Woodley, Eddie Redmayne, and the late, great Chadwick Boseman. Over the ensuing years, we featured plenty more soon-to-be-superstars: Rami Malek. Brie Larson. Daniel Kaluuya. Riz Ahmed. Barry Keoghan. The kids from Stranger Things, when they were still kids. The cast of Succession before Succession became everyone’s favorite show.

In 2017, we put a baby-faced Timothée Chalamet on the list for his turn in Call Me by Your Name. (Our global entertainment director, Dana Mathews, fondly recalls him turning to her during the Man of the Year Party and saying, “This is the best party I’ve ever been to in my life.”) Since then, Chalamet has appeared on three GQ covers, earned four Oscar nominations, and become a household name (and maybe been to a few more great parties).

We took a few years off (okay, fine, seven), but 2026 feels like exactly the right time to revive GQ’s Breakouts portfolio—now through a wider lens. Yes, though we’ve got eyes on Hollywood’s next big things—like, say, Sly Stallone doppelgänger Anthony Ippolito; Gen Z class clown Owen Thiele, of Adults; Misty Green’s astounding leading woman, Rosalind Eleazar—not everyone is working the camera. We’re excited to introduce you to the West Coast’s hottest up-and-coming rapper in AZ Chike and put you on to Fcukers, whose debut album, packed with rowdy electro-pop bangers, made them first in our hearts and on our pregaming playlists. We’ve also got podcaster and journalist Pablo Torre, whose relentless reporting upended a $7.8 billion NBA franchise, and Jordan Firstman, an internet-born comedian who wrote and directed a film that commanded a lengthy standing ovation from Cannes audiences (right after they finished crying).

Point is, our Breakouts class of 2026 brings together 13 fully minted stars who did something that feels increasingly impossible: They captured our attention in a time when it feels like attention is more fleeting than ever. Welcome to their party.

Dress by Dior. Shoes by Jimmy Choo. Mask from Palace Costume Co.

Age: 25Breakout moment: Playing the queen bee on Ryan Murphy’s ’80s glam fever dream The Shards.—————

It’s a different kind of attention that I actually prefer. Because for so long I was getting attention, but not for a specific thing. And that was confusing and kind of messed with my head a bit. I was really young and people knew who I was, but I couldn’t really point to the work that they knew. And so it’s really fun for me to have people [now say], “I watched The Shards,” or “I watched Bottoms,” and then we have something to talk about.

Infinite Jest—no, I’m kidding, they’ve already read it, all of them. A Man’s Place by Annie Ernaux is very good and easily digestible. I think Just Kids is wonderful. What We Talk About When We Talk About Love. That one’s really great. Oh, and this is so classic, but Nine Stories by J.D. Salinger is really good. I know guys—male actors especially—love The Catcher in the Rye.

I got really worried the other day because I started getting a lot of followers. It was two days of so many followers, and I was like, “Oh my God, I’ve been doxxed.” The last thing I logged was Hitch. My top four are A Woman Under the Influence, The Dark Knight, Phantom Thread, and Eternal Sunshine. My Odyssey review has 112 likes. I don’t care how many followers I have on Instagram, how many likes I get. Letterboxd is truly a hit of adrenaline every time someone likes my review. —Frazier Tharpe

Jacket and jeans by Ralph Lauren Collection. Necklace by Chopard. Ring by Chanel Fine Jewelry.

On Wise: Jacket by Isabel Marant. Top by Gucci. Briefs by Araks. Boots by Herbert Levine. Sunglasses by McQueen. On Walker Lewis: Jacket by Balenciaga. T-shirt by Isabel Marant. Jeans by Gucci. Boots by Timberland. Sunglasses by Tom Ford. Jewelry, his own.

Ages: Wise, 28 | Walker Lewis, 29Breakout Moment: The NYC duo’s 2026 debut album, Ö, featuring indie-sleazy hits like “If You Wanna Party, Come Over to My House” and “Beatback.”—————

Wise: That was probably the most surreal thing I’ve ever experienced. We’re like, “This is what it feels to be like Led Zeppelin.”

Walker Lewis: It’s funny—a reel permeated my Instagram from a Brazilian influencer, and it was like, “Who is this controversial band that everyone’s arguing about opening for Harry Styles?” But I think by the last show, people got it.

Walker Lewis: Easy. The Cure. It’s unbelievable, to see somebody still sound that good and be able to play for two hours, and you know every single song.

Walker Lewis: When I was getting a root canal done and the nurse said, “Can I get a photo with you after?” I was like, “You couldn’t have asked before?” —Alex Pappademas

I cannot shut up about this, but it has to be throwing the first pitch out for the White Sox. I will remember that forever.

Yeah, it was. And I hadn’t thrown a baseball in a really long time.

I look forward to the moment where I get to really reflect and digest. Next month I have some time off, and I’m going to go home and eat sandwiches at my mom’s house and take my grandma for a walk. “Go on a walk with my grandma”.… That’s a weird way to put it.

Sadie Sink knew who I was, and that was kind of cool. I just love her. She’s so talented and so adorable. It’s like meeting the queen before she’s the queen.

I do watch the fan edits. They’re fun. Some of them pick the worst photos of me, and I’m like, “This is a hate crime, but thank you for putting it on TikTok.”

I got two very smart pieces of advice. One was, “Run. Don’t do this. Save yourself.” And then the other person said, “Stick with it.” I’m kind of doing both. It’s a beautiful bag—it’s quiet luxury, babe. It’s so quiet you don’t know it’s The Row. —F.T

Jacket and pants by Saint Laurent by Anthony Vaccarello. Boots by Giuseppe Zanotti. Sunglasses (throughout) by Louis Vuitton Men’s. Earrings (throughout), his own. Ring by Bvlgari.

Age: 38Breakout moment: Her riveting performance as the title character in Chris Rock’s Misty Green (and her role in Slow Horses).—————

I mean, the first time I watched it, I just thought, Oh—you’re going to be in every frame. [Laughs]

[In an American accent] “Murderer.” Mur-der-rer. I think every Brit finds that hard. I was like, “Can I say ’killer’ instead?” And “mirror.” It’s when you’ve got a double r. But I had a great dialect coach.

I would’ve loved to have been in a scene with Philip Seymour Hoffman. That would’ve been my dream. And I would love to work with Sandra Hüller.

I was onstage with Ralph Fiennes. We finished Misty Green—I did an overnight shoot on Friday into Saturday morning, got on a plane, arrived in London on Sunday, and went straight into rehearsals with Ralph. It was a pretty mad summer.

I was getting ready before the Misty Green premiere [at the Toronto International Film Festival]. And my mom came down. She sat there and she was just sending pictures and she just had tears in her eyes. Just seeing this whole period at TIFF—for her, it’s her little girl. And every now and again, I would just look at her and she was just happy and in awe in a way. It warmed my heart. —A.P.

Dress by Gucci. Hosiery by Wolford. Earrings by Cartier.

Shirt and pants by Brioni. Bow tie and cummerbund, stylist’s own. Vintage watch by Rolex from Foundwell. Vintage cufflinks by Cartier from Foundwell. Earring, his own.

Age: 35Breakout moment: The Cannes hit Club Kid, which he wrote, directed, and starred in as a party promoter navigating unexpected parenthood.—————

I still do, yeah, at the phone call scene at the end. But it feels very distant from me. I feel like I’m watching it more as an observer now, which is nice, and I feel different than when I made it. I was such an open wound.

Cannes was such an emotional experience. I’m 35, and I’ve always known that I had something to say and I knew how to say it, but I’ve never been given the opportunity. So, honestly, to feel like I was being seen and understood was like 20 years of validation that I didn’t get. And so something shifted, that week, in me. I’ve noticed myself not having to use humor as a shield anymore, as much. I’m less afraid to be vulnerable—and not just in my public life but in my personal life too.

Of course, you shouldn’t need the validation of anyone to feel like you’re worthy, but let’s be real.…

What gagged me this year? I would say, honestly, as a statement of ambition, the Javis’ movie [La Bola Negra]. You marvel at it because you’re like, “How the fuck did they pull this off?” To even want to tell that complex of a story, and to just do it and go balls to the wall, is very inspiring.

I was like, “This is too long. It’s embarrassing now.” —A.P.

Jacket and pants by Canali. Shirt by Amiri. Boots by Alessandro Vasini. Tie by Husbands.

Age: 41Breakout moment: Reporting on how the Steve Ballmer–owned Clippers were allegedly funny with money, on his podcast Pablo Torre Finds Out, leading to one of the most severe team penalties in sports history.—————

Two days ago, I walked into this event that The New York Times was holding…it was like the 175th birthday party [for the paper]. I walk out the elevator and literally the first person I see is [NBA commissioner] Adam Silver. I won’t say exactly what he told me, but the tenor of our conversation was like, This is the HBO series adaptation of what this moment would be.

As a first-generation American—my parents are from the Philippines—there’s always been a dream of mine to be cast as a white person. So…Andrew Garfield, come on. Let’s do this.

The funny part is that I’m not even done reporting this story yet. The federal government is now investigating the Clippers, and so I’m now investigating the government’s investigation in the era of Trump too, which is like its own rabbit hole inside of a rabbit hole, which is fucking wild. But at the same time, it feels like now our number is listed in the phone book…actual other NBA owners are calling me up saying, “Can you look into this?”

It’s hard not to be sappy about this, but the lesson I learned is that if you’re telling the truth, you can walk into any room and feel like that as a suit of armor. Even when the person you’re investigating is one of the 10 richest people in the world. —F.T.

Coat by Michael Kors. Vintage pajamas from Palace Costume Co. Socks by London Sock Company. Glasses by Jacques Marie Mage. Necklaces (throughout), his own.

Age: 37Breakout moments: Stealing scenes as a ’70s Provincetown line cook in the Anthony Bourdain biopic Tony, and his stand-up special Uncle Stav.—————

I just did The Drew Barrymore Show. That experience was so magical. I was so nervous to be around Drew Barrymore. I’ve done a lot of cool shit, and that’s the one where I was like, “I am actually nervous to the point where I’m not a professional. I’m just a stammering little boy who’s with the girl he had a crush on from The Wedding Singer when he was a fat 10-year-old, and I’m trying to keep it together.”

Last week I allowed myself an aimlessly wander around New York City day. Got a little stoned, walked around, stumbled into a movie. Walked along the water on the West Side. Sat down to a little random omakase. Rode a Citi Bike around. I call it the hero’s journey, where you leave your home at, whatever, 11 a.m. ,with just the bare provisions, and you’re not allowed to go home. You just have to keep moving and keep doing stuff.

I filmed this Judd Apatow movie The Comeback King, with Glen Powell, Cristin Milioti, Madelyn Cline. That comes out in February. I’m excited to do stand-up—for fun, not to explicitly work on another hour. I’m excited to go back to clubs and just like, “Can I be the funniest person in this club tonight?” And that’s my only goal.

To be honest with you, the last three years, it’s [been] all go. But you got to have these big years, or else GQ doesn’t talk to you at the end of the year. —A.P.

On Halkias: Jacket and pants by Brooks Brothers. Shirt by Many. Shoes by Louis Vuitton Men’s. Sunglasses by Valention. On Torre: Jacket by Tom Ford. Shirt by Factor’s. Pants by Louis Vuitton Men’s. Shoes by G.H. Bass. Sunglasses by Jacques Marie Mage. Ring, his own.

Shirts and pants by Dunhill. Underwear by Calvin Klein. Earrings (throughout), his own.

Age: 31Breakout moment: Storming the West Coast rap scene with collabs from Pharrell Williams and Tyler, the Creator on his major-label debut album, No Rest for the Wicked.—————

Not like I made it, but I have arrived. We went to Magic City on a Monday for the first time. They were playing the fuck out my records in that motherfucker. The DJ played “Look Like My Mama” in the strip club. You ain’t never heard Tyler, the Creator get played in a strip club. We crossing worlds that’s never been crossed before.

The day before the album came out, we were in Area 29 in Houston, doing our thing. Regular night, it ain’t too packed, throwing money. They tap me on my shoulder like, “My boy want to holler at you.” They take me upstairs to this private section, pull the curtain back…it’s Travis Scott.

It was epic, bro. N-gga came out from behind the curtain like Batman. The light hid half his face. He said, “I fuck with everything you got going on.” We go back down to that section, 15 minutes pass, then one of the owners came and grabbed me: “Look, look, look.” Travis was up there, playing [Chike’s song] “Packed Up.” —F.T.

Shirt by Lu’u Dan. Pants by Valentino. Bracelet by Cartier.

Age: 26Breakout moment: Being a dead ringer for Sly Stallone in I Play Rocky, the film about…Sly Stallone playing Rocky.—————

In the thick of prep. I was training at Gleason’s Gym with Stephan James, who plays Carl Weathers. We were beating the crap out of each other and figuring out how to box. I had gained a bunch of weight, and I was trying to actually cut a few pounds, so I was in those sweatsuits, like a garbage-bag type thing. On the way to the gym, I would listen to Stallone and on the way home.… Everything I could find up to 1980, 1985, every piece of Stallone footage that existed.

I [asked] Seth Rogen, “Dude, how do you handle this stuff?” And he said, “Just go with the flow.” It was such a simple answer, but from somebody like him, I was like, He’s got a good grip on this. The simplicity of it landed.

Philip Seymour Hoffman is one. Chadwick Boseman. Christian Bale, Heath Ledger.

[The first Rocky] is the best movie—but when I was younger, the one that caught my eye was four. Rocky IV is nuts. —F.T.

Jacket by Versace. Shirt by 73London. Pants by Umit Benan. Earring (throughout), his own.

(from l.) On Ambrossi: All clothing by Gucci. Shoes by Christian Louboutin. Pocket square by Brioni. Sunglasses by Ahlem. On Calvo: Jacket, pants, and boots by Tom Ford. Scarf, stylist’s own. Sunglasses by Jacques Marie Mage.

(from l.) On Ambrossi: Jacket and pants by Chanel. Shirt by Factor’s. Shoes by Marsèll. Pin by Cartier. On Calvo: All clothing, tie, and shoes by Ralph Lauren Purple Label. Watch by Cartier.

Ages: Ambrossi, 42 | Calvo, 35Breakout moment: Cowriting and directing La Bola Negra, the gay Spanish historical epic loosely based on an unfinished Federico García Lorca play.——————————————

Javier Ambrossi: Very important. We understood that sometimes people expect LGBTQ+ stories to be niche or for a specific audience. We wanted to do a queer story about universal love.

Ambrossi: It’s a way to put in context how different we are. We change a lot, and the story of our grandparents and our story is very different.

Javier Calvo: What do we do with the freedom our ancestors fought for, and died for?

Calvo: Isabelle Huppert. For me, she’s everything.

Ambrossi: I will go with Julia Roberts. My Best Friend’s Wedding is a very important queer story. The relationship between a woman and a gay man—it was the first time I saw that onscreen. And Rupert Everett was so bold, and I could tell in his eyes that he was gay. I was a kid and I was like, “He’s not faking it.”

How did you celebrate when you won best director at Cannes?

Ambrossi: I put the award on the table and went to sleep. And then Javi came over at 8 a.m.…

Ambrossi: “Give me the award!” And he took it! —A.P.

(from l.) On Ippolito: Sunglasses by Jacques Marie Mage. Necklace by Cartier. On Chike: Shirt and pants by Brioni. Sunglasses by Tom Ford. On Thiele: Jacket by McQueen. Shirt by Factor’s. Pants by Versace.

#6661. Meghan Markle Made a Subtle Change to Her Wedding Jewelry for a European Parliament Visit

Meghan Markle and Prince Harry visited the European Parliament in Brussels today to usher in the opening of the Lost Screen Memorial, which honors children who lost their lives after suffering harm from social media. For the solemn occasion, the Duchess of Sussex kept her look minimal, including her accessories and wedding stack. Meghan only wore her Welsh gold wedding band on her left ring finger, forgoing her engagement ring.

Meghan has a history of wearing just her wedding band while on trips abroad. Still, the piece is nearly priceless itself due to its material.

“Very little Welsh gold was ever mined, and it is traditionally used to make the British royal family’s wedding bands,” Hera Fine Jewelry founder and CEO Lauren Boc previously told ELLE while discussing Kate Middleton’s wedding stack. “Between its natural rarity and historic connections, I would consider her Welsh gold wedding band to be close to invaluable.”

Meghan accessorized her black Mackage coat with a few other gold pieces this morning, including her vintage Dior crystal earrings and Cartier Love bracelet.

Meghan has no other upcoming events that have been announced. Last month, following the Sussexes’ visit to Nottingham, a source close to the couple told The Telegraph that Meghan rarely joins Harry for engagements.

“They have different professional priorities,” one source explained. “Prince Harry’s is his philanthropic work and public service. Her focus is on her family and children, followed by her business, followed by rebooting her acting career. Her public appearances will be relatively rare. She is reading a lot of scripts at the moment. If she has time left after all of that, she will do some charity work. But she’s not a working royal; her day isn’t organized around a program pulled together by a private secretary. She’s a full-time mom and entrepreneur, and that alone takes up a lot of time and work.”

#6660. Balmain Resort 2027

“For me, the men’s and the women’s, they are kind of like one entity. I really want the men and women to be able to talk to each other.” Antonin Tron was riffing as we riffled the rails of his first pre-spring collections for Balmain, including his first-ever menswear collection for the house. “I don’t necessarily think of them as a couple,” he qualified: “but I think at Balmain the women are quite sexy and out there. And if I was to do something very different for men, it would be weird.”

Looking at his rails simultaneously, that relationship was manifest in substance as well as spirit: “We have a lot of overcrossing material,” Tron confirmed. The same embroidered surfaces, treated denim, and snakeskin jacquards traveled between the two wardrobes, but in womenswear their expression was differently calibrated. This was a more relaxed continuation of the luxuriously louche and wanton glamour of his last runway collection, which itself had been informed by the Californian desert. “With pre-collection I can explore a bit more the casual side of Balmain,” he said.

That meant injecting a dose of dishevelment into Balmain’s appetite for decoration. Sensuously draped dresses in snakeskin and beautiful, borderline-hallucinogenic florals came with cropped flight jackets, while satin tailoring, sheer lurex blouses, and embellished animalier were countered by washed denim and biker leathers. There were micro cardigans over exposed bras, skirts that succumbed into flowerings of asymmetric ruffle, and lavishly embellished pieces whose surfaces seemed weathered by weeks of sun exposure. What blurred in the haze of Tron’s gaze was much distinction between dressing up and down.

This dissolved tension was more than a styling proposition. Tron has little patience for the idea that luxury dressing must conform either to bourgeois standards of propriety, or fashion’s customary cringe of faux-intellectual snobbishness. “For me, this thing with sexiness is also a class thing,” he said of the physical ideals through which notions of elegance are policed. Balmain, in his view, offers a space to articulate sexuality rather than apologize for it.

He recalled meeting a client in Los Angeles while shooting the collection in Joshua Tree. When he mentioned his last show’s desert-and-hallucinogenics theme, she cheerfully volunteered that she had a house there and used to do exactly that. She was accompanied by her muscular husband. “They both wanted to be hot, and that’s it,” Tron observed. This seemed a pretty good expression of the collection’s carefully direct hedonism. Super-long leather boots and Lucite-heeled wedges provided the strut, while the tasseled Zabriskie bag offered easygoing swing.

His instinct is that luxury should enable freedom rather than impose rules. The filament that connects this new Balmain woman and the new Balmain man, in spirit as much as substance, is Tron himself. “I think slowly, I’m finding that line: I’m finding the woman and the man, basically.”

#6657. How To Crack Resale’s AI Algorithms

The next time someone asks ChatGPT to find them a designer handbag, the answer could be a previously owned version, even if they weren’t originally looking to shop secondhand.

Rémi Bouchez, who was appointed as Vestiaire Collective’s new CTO in March, says the resale platform is working to make its product listing available to OpenAI’s broader agentic shopping systems, which would allow secondhand pieces to appear alongside new products in AI-generated recommendations. The proposed plan follows Vestiaire Collective quietly launching a dedicated app plugin within ChatGPT last month, allowing shoppers to search its pre-owned luxury inventory and compare products using conversational prompts within the chatbot. A shopper searching for a new Prada bag could now conceivably be shown a pre-owned version at a fraction of the price, or an archival design that is no longer available firsthand.

At a time when luxury consumers are questioning rising prices, this could significantly impact the shopping journey. And this is just one part of a wider transformation in how secondhand fashion is discovered. Resale platforms are simultaneously rebuilding their own search and recommendation algorithms, using AI to understand product images, interpret shoppers’ tastes and determine which listings get seen. As a result, the rules of discovery are changing on two fronts: within resale marketplaces themselves, and through the AI assistants that could increasingly direct shoppers towards them.

Bouchez believes that if AI agents like Muse, Instinct and Duet reach mainstream adoption, it could fundamentally change how luxury shoppers weigh up their options.

“These agents are capable of ingesting a ton of information — way more than human shoppers can. They remember user preferences over time, and they can catch things like discreet terms and conditions or shady seller behaviors and put them in front of a user who would have otherwise missed them,” says Bouchez. He explains how an AI agent could compare a Prada bag across several platforms, assessing its condition, authentication details and seller reliability before recommending the best value option, raising the stakes for resellers.

It’s an opportunity resale platforms have long been waiting for. Finding a particular product secondhand has traditionally meant scrolling through multiple marketplace apps, deciphering inconsistent descriptions and comparing endless individual listings. AI now promises to take much of the legwork out of that hunt.

Across the resale industry, rival platforms are investing in both forms of discovery. Depop has enabled shoppers to search its marketplace through Apple’s Visual Intelligence on supported iPhones. Last month, The RealReal introduced its own AI shopping assistant, Ask TRR, built on Google Gemini AI that enables shoppers to search in natural language — or by uploading images of products they’ve seen for visual search — while learning shoppers’ preferences. Speaking on the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week, CEO Rati Levesque said Ask TRR’s early adopters spend 20% more per transaction than non-users. The RealReal is also preparing for shopping journeys that begin outside its own platform. A spokesperson tells Vogue Business the company is restructuring data on its 1.5 million listed items to make them easier for external AI agents to find and recommend.

Together, this represents an AI-driven sea change for resale. While AI may struggle to replicate the subjective judgement involved in fashion discovery, resale presents a more straightforward opportunity. A shopper searching for a particular archival bag doesn’t need their algorithm to have good taste, just to identify the right model and compare available listings by price, condition and authenticity.

Resale discovery is increasingly moving beyond keyword search. At Vestiaire Collective, visual search can now recognise multiple objects in an image and identify similar listings, while its search systems increasingly interpret natural language requests. AI can also extract information from photographs — including aspects of fit and visible defects — that previously depended on sellers filling in descriptions.

Poshmark is also using AI to bridge the gap between what sellers photograph and what shoppers can find. Its “Smart List AI” tool automatically generates searchable titles, descriptions and product categories from uploaded photographs. Chief product officer Heather Friedland says it makes listing creation less of a “heavy lift” once the photos are up, and that listing on Poshmark is now five times faster than before. Poshmark’s AI tool also automates offers, letting Poshmark negotiate with buyers on behalf of the seller, which she says makes selling 50% faster. “We want sellers to focus most on what they do best: source great items and have Poshmark take care of the rest,” she says.

At Depop, shoppers are increasingly browsing the personalized Suggested For You feed rather than starting with a search, says chief product officer Sonia Biddle. Its algorithm responds to individual preferences and emerging cultural trends, while AI identifies listings by category, color and style, making products discoverable even when sellers haven’t used precisely the right keywords.

“Fashion often starts with an idea: an era, an occasion or someone whose style you love, and that’s not always something you can put into words,” Biddle says. “AI helps us understand what you’re after, not just the words you type.” For sellers, that means some longstanding tactics like keyword hashtags may become less important, while product photography, pricing and reliability are becoming harder to ignore.

Depop’s visual search also allows shoppers to upload a photograph or screenshot — including of something spotted in a first-hand retailer — to find similar secondhand pieces. A new-season jacket might inspire a purchase, but not necessarily from the brand selling it.

Resale execs recommend sellers photograph items in natural light, capturing multiple angles and clearly showing any signs of wear. Photo: Courtesy of Depop

As images become more central to discovery, platforms are also investing in how listings look. Last month, Vestiaire announced a partnership with AI photography company Photoroom to standardise the main photograph of every new listing — around 40,000 items a day — bringing the often inconsistent images uploaded by individual sellers closer to the polished aesthetic of first-hand luxury retail.

The technology removes backgrounds, adjusts lighting, centres products and adds realistic shadows. According to results from a randomized A/B test conducted by Vestiaire Collective and Photoroom, listings processed using the new technology had a 5% higher sell-through rate than those using Vestiaire’s previous in-house photo-editing tool, while unique product page views increased by between 3% and 7%.

Next, Vestiaire is experimenting with much more ambitious AI image enhancements that can make the items themselves look more PDP shoot ready, Bouchez says, like digital ironing.

It’s a delicate balance: AI can make a pre-owned handbag look like something fit for a luxury DTC site, but an algorithm that makes a scuff disappear could also undermine the trust on which resale depends. Yet Bouchez says Vestiaire has seen an approximately 6% improvement in the proportion of enhanced listings selling within seven days since these AI image updates, without a corresponding increase in returns.

For sellers, getting discovered still depends heavily on the algorithms operating within resale marketplaces themselves. So what determines which listings appear first, and can sellers influence their ranking?

At Vestiaire, the answer isn’t simply the lowest price or the newest upload. Bouchez describes a three-stage ranking system that identifies relevant products, reorders them according to marketplace factors and then adjusts results to individual preferences. Those factors include condition, pricing, location and seller reliability. Because Vestiaire operates globally, proximity can matter: a nearby item may mean faster shipping, fewer customs complications and easier returns, which may mean it gets surfaced first.

Vestiaire assesses what constitutes a fair price according to factors including condition, location and whether the seller is a professional offering returns. An implausibly cheap luxury item may raise questions about authenticity, rather than look like an irresistible bargain. Bouchez says that analysing these factors is still a combination of humans and AI.

“Trust is a big pillar for Vestiaire — we invest a lot in that trust, on manual verification, on assessing a listing before it’s published,” he says. “Obviously, we want to keep the same level of trust but lower the investment with AI, but the more we can keep this USP high and even increase the trust, the better our position as a platform.”

Depop’s search algorithm prioritises how closely a listing matches a shopper’s query, including brand, category, size and color. Popularity signals — views, likes and additions to shopping bags — also matter, alongside seller history, location and personal shopping preferences. If a listing is underperforming, she recommends new photographs, a more detailed description and a pricing review.

Shoppers, meanwhile, are becoming more deliberate about influencing what appears in their feeds.

“It’s been really interesting hearing our community talk about ‘training their algorithm,’” Biddle says. “People know that what they like, view and save shapes what they see, and they’re becoming really deliberate about it.” But there’s a downside to this hyper-personalization: the more accurately a feed reflects established tastes, the less likely shoppers may be to encounter something unexpected.

Good product photography is increasingly important for visibility on resale platforms. Photo: Courtesy of The RealReal.

To counter AI’s tendency to reinforce existing preferences, Poshmark introduced a new “Tastemaker” programme in September, enlisting fashion figures including Courtney Grow, Colleen Allen and Jalil Johnson to curate shoppable edits from across its resale inventory. The platform has also established a dedicated human merchandising team to work alongside its AI and machine learning specialists, identifying emerging trends and bringing a more editorial approach to product recommendations.

“On trends, a purely algorithmic system tends to amplify what’s already popular,” Friedland says. “Human curation is our counterweight. Our tastemakers bring in new styles and AI then figures out which shoppers those styles will resonate with.”

For shoppers looking to escape their own personalized recommendations, Biddle suggests sorting search results by price or newest first, too. Visual search can also help uncover pieces that shoppers cannot easily describe. On Poshmark, Friedland recommends saving searches for specific archival pieces and liking items to help refine future recommendations.

And as AI agents take on more of the shopping process, the question of what consumers don’t see becomes even more significant. Vestiaire’s ChatGPT integration allows shoppers to compare up to three selected listings, asking the AI agent to explain differences in price, condition and seller information. But it also introduces another gatekeeper: instead of scrolling through hundreds of listings themselves, shoppers may increasingly rely on an AI assistant to decide which options are worth considering — and which never make it onto their shortlist.

For first-hand luxury brands, the implications go beyond losing the occasional sale to a cheaper pre-owned alternative. Resale platforms are accumulating information about which designs consumers continue to desire, years after they disappear from stores. Depop’s Biddle argues that these signals can be valuable for brands developing future collections.

“Resale tells brands something their own sales data can’t: what people still love years after it left the shop floor,” she says. “When we see searches spike for a particular era or label, it’s often an early sign that something’s coming back.”

Poshmark is similarly using AI to identify patterns across searches, listings, likes and transactions, tracking demand for particular designers, eras, silhouettes and price points. Friedland says combining these signals with scarcity and actual resale prices can help distinguish fleeting trends from enduring desirability — offering brands a measure of a product’s success beyond its initial sellthrough.

For luxury brands, the stakes are particularly high. If AI assistants can connect consumers with archival products as readily as current collections, brands may find themselves competing with their own past successes, without controlling how those products are presented or compared.

As sellers learn to level up their listings, shoppers train their feeds and luxury brands compete for attention, the question is how much influence any of them will retain over what an AI agent ultimately recommends.

#6655. No-Knead Pumpkin Focaccia

For those who fall into the pumpkin-should-be-savory camp, let us offer up a new recipe primed to become a seasonal staple: Pumpkin Focaccia. The iconic bread we know and love is ripe for the pumpkin treatment, lending it a golden hue and earthy sweetness. This version doesn’t require any kneading, making it straightforward enough to pull off in a single afternoon. You’ll perform a series of folds as it rises, simply pulling and stretching the dough to help it develop gluten. A showering of fresh rosemary and flaky salt on top is optional, but it takes crisp, plush focaccia from good to great. Serve it with a bowl of olive oil for dipping or a schmear of cream cheese to lean into the seasonal profile.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Mix one ¼-oz. envelope active dry yeast (about 2¼ tsp.), 5 cups (625 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. light brown sugar, and 1½ cups warm water in a large bowl until a dry, shaggy dough forms. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot 15 minutes.

Place a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough and moisten hands in water, shaking off excess. Stretch 1 side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat process 3 more times, turning bowl after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Remoisten your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat entire process 2 more times (folding and resting), about 1 hour more. By the last full fold, the dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Pour ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil into a 13x9" metal baking pan. Lightly oil your hands and punch down dough, then transfer to prepared pan. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Turn dough salted side down to coat both sides in oil. Press into an even layer with your fingers. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 450°. Unwrap focaccia and scatter rosemary leaves and more sea salt over if desired; drizzle with oil. Oil your hands and press fingers into focaccia several times to create dimples across surface, making sure to press fingers all the way down to the bottom of the pan. Bake focaccia, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until deep golden brown, 23–28 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let focaccia cool slightly in pan. Using a metal spatula, turn out focaccia onto rack and let cool completely.

Do Ahead: Focaccia can be made 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

#6653. The Most Extravagant Horseback Trips in the World

The horse girl is having a moment. Riding boots are officially trending. Kendall Jenner recently celebrated her 31st birthday with an equestrian-themed fête. And who could forget earlier this year in Paris, when Stella McCartney kicked off her winter 2026 show at a riding hall in the Bois du Boulogne by sending out 10 horses—five black, five white, all chic?

Fashion, it seems, has discovered the horse. But horses have never needed discovering: Gucci and Hermès built empires on saddles and tack long before equestrianism found its way back into the fashion conversation. It may be the lunar calendar’s Year of the Horse, but for some of us, every year is Year of the Horse. For those ready to graduate from dressing like a horse girl to living like one, here are some of the world’s most extraordinary horseback adventures, from Patagonian ridge lines to African safaris. Some of them are multi-day journeys across wild landscapes, and others allow for deep immersion into single properties that offer particularly exceptional horse experiences. Saddle up.

In the rolling pampas of Uruguay just inland from luxe-boho beach town José Ignacio, Estancia Vik offers horseback riding with a pretty spectacular dinner reservation. Guests saddle up on Criollo and Quarter horses alongside expert gauchos for an evening ride timed to the rising of the full moon. The ride begins at the stables before sunset, winds toward the José Ignacio River, and culminates in wine and a traditional Uruguayan dinner under the stars. The estancia also offers equine meditation, through which you can connect with the herd and experience just how intuitive these animals really are.

One of my personal favorite horseback experiences anywhere was in the vast, unending salt pans of the Makgadikgadi in Botswana. Here, at Natural Selection’s Jack’s Camp, guests visiting at certain times of year can ride alongside 30,000 zebras and wildebeest at the peak of their migration before the rainy season.

For experienced riders, Micato Safaris offers a nine-night “Riding the Wild Plains” equestrian safari through Nairobi, Laikipia, and the Maasai Mara. The idea is to experience Kenya’s wildlife from the saddle, crossing through conservancies alongside giraffes, elephants, and rhinos with little more than the sound of hooves beneath you. After two nights at the posh Hemingways Nairobi, guests head into the bush for a trip through some of the country’s top safari lodges. But you’re hardly roughing it. Think champagne breakfasts and sundowners overlooking the savanna.

Few travelers know Central Asia quite like explorer, author, and television presenter Alexandra Tolstoy. A relative of the novelist Leo Tolstoy, she has been traveling the region since the 1990s, when she and three friends embarked on a nine-month, 5,000-mile journey by horseback and camel along the Silk Road, from Turkmenistan to China. More than 25 years later, Kyrgyzstan remains her great love. Tolstoy leads journeys through the country’s dramatic Tien Shan Mountains, drawing on decades of relationships with local horsemen, nomadic families, and mountain communities.

“Kyrgyzstan is, quite simply, one of the most extraordinary and beautiful countries in the world to explore on horseback,” Tolstoy told us. “Horses are deeply woven into the country's history, identity, and everyday life. This is a place where horsemanship is not a recreational pursuit but an integral part of the culture, and that makes the experience particularly special.” Not ready to commit to a trip? Check out Tolstoy Dacha, her line of beautiful objects for home and travel.

Many come for the skiing and hiking, but real horse lovers come for the riding. Above the town of Merano, just steps away from Miramonti Boutique Hotel, the Sulfner riding stable is home to the region’s distinctive flaxen-maned Haflinger horses, with guided excursions, riding lessons, and carriage rides available. After a day in the saddle, there’s an outdoor Japanese-inspired onsen pool and forest sauna to look forward to.

For experienced horseback riders, Tswalu Kalahari Reserve offers a different way to explore the largest private reserve in South Africa—by riding across grass-covered plains, over rolling red dunes, and over seasonal riverbeds. With a stable of breeds including Thoroughbreds, Arabians, Appaloosas, and English Shires, Tswalu’s horseback safaris bring adventurous travelers closer to the landscape and wildlife, offering an immersive perspective beyond the traditional game drive.

Chile offers a compelling case for exploring on horseback. This neck of the continent is known for excellent hiking, yes, but horseback allows you to cover much more ground in a single trip. Luxury travel company Red Savannah offers a 10-night riding “Chilean Riding Adventure” that begins in the Atacama Desert, where guests ride across the otherworldly sands of Moon Valley before spending evenings stargazing under some of the clearest skies on Earth. The trip continues on to the Lake District and ultimately down to Patagonia, where you’ll canter along remote lagoons beneath the watch of Andean condors. You’ll stay in luxe lodges from AndBeyond and Explora along the way.

In the heart of France’s Camargue, where wild marshlands meet the Mediterranean, horses are as much a part of the landscape as the salt flats and flamingos. At Les Bains Gardiens, a countryside retreat with its own stables, guests can saddle up for guided two-hour rides through the wetlands and out to the beach. Experienced riders can even gallop along the shoreline. The estate is home to traditional Camargue horses and often stages “jeux gardians,” the horseback games that celebrate this region’s centuries-old riding culture.

#6652. These Wine Glasses Are the Only Ones That Can Survive My Clumsiness

I spent years living with roommates and making due with our collective assortment of mismatched dishware, throwing washed take-out containers haphazardly into a cupboard and reusing them until they were cracked and stained, and living with a pantry that was in a constant state of moderate disarray. But when I moved in with my boyfriend, I took the opportunity to get my shit together. I pride myself on being a relatively put-together person, and that now translates to my kitchen too. I’ve got a cabinet full of well-organized food storage containers with their corresponding lids, I keep my spices neatly stacked in deli containers with labeled with color-coded kitchen tape, I replaced my chipped water glasses with a matching set, and I have a special drawer that houses the linens, taper candles, and flatware I pull out when I’m hosting. It all feels very adult.

Until recently, though, there was one remaining aspect of my kitchen that still needed help. While I have more fun coupes and rocks glasses than I know what to do with, I haven’t owned a matching set of wine glasses since college—in fact, at the time of my move, I had two left to my name. It’s not for lack of trying: I’ve tested out glassware during my time at BA, bringing home countless options in the hopes that they’d be my forever stems. I’ve somehow managed to break every single one of them, which has become a running joke for those that know me.

But despite my clumsiness, I’m not willing to sacrifice style for durability. I want a thin-stemmed, thin-rimmed, elegant wine glass that won’t snap in two the minute I lay my hands on it. Is that too much to ask?

For the longest time, I thought it might be, and had resigned myself to sipping wine out of stemless tumblers—until I discovered Gabriel-Glas’s StandArt All Purpose Wine Glass. They’ve got a sleek, slightly conical shape that I find enhances reds, whites, and rosés alike, with a slight curve between the bowl and the rim that adds a touch of personality to an otherwise classic silhouette. The stem is thin enough to satisfy my desire for elegance without being so delicate that I’m scared I’ll snap it, and the laser-cut rim is a joy to sip from.

Because the glasses are machine-blown from a single piece of molten crystal, they have none of the weak points that tend to form where traditional multipart glasses are joined. The machine-blown construction also keeps the cost per glass low enough that I won’t mind replacing one if (let’s be real, when) I do drop and shatter it. But I’m pleased to report that as of right now, all six of my beloved StandArt glasses are intact and ready to take on my new apartment’s first season of holiday hosting and cozy weather hangs. Bring on the winter reds and festive bottles of bubbly.

#6651. RIP to LIV, the Golf League No One Ever Really Cared About

The most remarkable thing about the era of LIV Golf, a five-year run characterized by near-parodic blunders and missteps, is that leadership and its public-facing talent don’t appear to have learned any lessons from their many failures.

From the beginning, the upstart league, established in 2021 as a rival to the dominant PGA Tour, was plagued by its own ineptitude. It’s only fitting—after LIV’s newfound lifeline, private investment firm BC Partners, reneged on a $300 million investment—that the brand’s figureheads are now celebrating the end by taking a victory lap. Tone-deaf doesn’t begin to describe it.

LIV CEO Scott O’Neil—who took over for original boss and Major winner Greg Norman in January of 2025 and was faced with finding new cash flow after Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund announced in April that it would no longer finance the operation—clearly exists in a different reality than our own. “Together, our team delivered world-class individual and team competitions across five continents, built a global business, secured pathways to The Open and U.S. Open… and built a league capable of attracting both elite and rising talent from around the world,” he said in a statement late last week. It’s unclear if the farewell tour will continue, though, an even newer report suggests that BC is looking to purchase a bankruptcy loan from LIV’s current owners. If this Hail Mary works, LIV’s future would look much different than the one O’Neil has promised.

Another way to look at it? One of LIV’s biggest accomplishments was that the league, despite its intentions to diversify the game and bring fun back into a sport that had come to personify privilege and exclusivity, inadvertently consolidated the PGA Tour’s power as a monopolistic behemoth now primed to solidify its status as the only league in town. They helped usher in a new era of leadership and investment for the Tour, including the introduction of CEO Brian Rolapp, who is by all accounts the most well-liked and accomplished boss it’s had in quite some time.

LIV also managed to tarnish the reputations of its biggest stars. Jon Rahm, who was vehemently opposed to the dog and pony show when it was announced, only to sheepishly take a bag of blood money so big his great grandchildren will never have to work a day in their lives, is now one of the game’s great “What If?” stories. Prior to the US Open at Brookline Country Club in June 2022, the defending champion was asked about his thoughts on the upstart league. “Money is great,” he said. But Rahm and his wife thought about it further. “Will our lifestyle change if I got $400 million? No, it will not change one bit.” Just over a year later, he defected to LIV.

Then there’s Phil Mickelson, who was poised to become a fixture of the American Ryder Cup team and widely considered a shoo-in to hold a cushy job as an analyst for golf’s biggest broadcasting events. Upon joining the league, he admitted in a conversation with Alan Shipnuck that Saudi Arabia was a terrible bedfellow. (Shipnuck and Mickelson have disagreed over whether the comments were on or off the record.) “They killed Khashoggi and have a horrible record on human rights. They execute people over there for being gay,” he explained. But there was a caveat: LIV was simply a “once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to reshape how the PGA Tour operates.” Miraculously, he got that part right.

Prize money on the PGA Tour is greater than ever, the Tour’s main events have recalibrated, and its season-ending championship series has been completely reimagined. Mickelson won’t be allowed within 100 miles of it.

The league’s biggest attraction, Bryson DeChambeau, is theoretically the worst-situated of the game’s many turncoats, though he’s probably more excited about growing his YouTube channel than he is about playing golf anyway. No one’s put their reputation on the line for this gaggle of buffoons quite like DeChambeau, who spoke proudly about how LIV was “growing the game” and “bringing team golf to the world.” This past weekend, he shared a statement on the dissolution of LIV. “I still believe in team golf,” he wrote. “It may look different in the future, but I still believe it’s essential to growing the game.” A loyal foot soldier, even from the grave.

It was always about the money. Nothing more, nothing less. This was a cash grab of epic proportions, and golfers not good enough to earn their keep on the PGA Tour took a life raft and briefly found themselves in possession of luxury superyachts. Then, low tide left them holding bags of cash and not much else. Was it worth it? For most of these golfers, probably. They were past their primes when LIV began; they’re still past the primes now, and just a helluva lot richer.

The league positioned itself as a disruptor, and disrupted so poorly that they’ve turned the PGA Tour into the strongest version of itself we’ve seen since Tiger Woods was at his peak. All that bloviating about the good of LIV Golf from its loudest talking heads is a bunch of nonsense.

It’s hard to tell if these statements are one last line of defense or more genuine delusion from LIV’s last advocates. They came in with the idea of sticking it to the PGA Tour, which at the time was facing bleak circumstances, bogged down in nonsense before redirecting its energy towards batting this gnat into extinction. Ultimately, LIV helped the PGA Tour save itself.

Now it’s gone for good, and five billion dollars later, we’re not gonna remember a damn thing about it. Not the players, not the leadership, and surely not all the ways they supposedly grew the game while merely growing their own bank accounts.

#6650. Pumpkin Cheesecake Muffins

Loaded with pumpkin seeds, canned pumpkin purée, and pumpkin pie spice, these big streusel-topped muffins are every fall lover’s dream come true. And to make things even better, the inside of each muffin is stuffed with a soft, lightly sweetened cream cheese mixture. Make the cheesecake filling and the streusel ahead of time to pace things out if it’s helpful. Don’t, even for a minute, consider using anything other than Libby’s 100% pure pumpkin purée (not pie mix). Nothing is better. We promise.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Whisk ⅓ cup coarsely chopped raw pumpkin seeds, ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour, 2 Tbsp. light brown sugar, ½ tsp. pumpkin pie spice, and a pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl to combine. Using your fingers, rub in 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, until moist pea-size lumps form. Chill until ready to use.

Do Ahead: Streusel can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and keep chilled.

Vigorously whisk 6 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar, 2 tsp. all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. vanilla extract, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl until combined and smooth.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and chill.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Line cups of a standard 12-cup muffin pan with paper liners. Whisk 2 large eggs, 1½ cups (packed; 300 g) light brown sugar, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, ¼ cup whole milk, 1 Tbsp. pumpkin pie spice, 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth, about 1 minute. Whisk 1¾ cups (219 g) all-purpose flour and 1½ tsp. baking powder in a small bowl to combine. Add to pumpkin mixture and fold in with a rubber spatula until just incorporated and no large dry streaks of flour remain (don’t overmix; batter will be lumpy).

Bake muffins until streusel is crisp and muffins spring back when gently pressed, 24–27 minutes. Let muffins cool in pan 5 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack and let cool until just warm or completely.

Do Ahead: Muffins can be made 2 days ahead. Store airtight at room temperature.

#6649. 22 Best Airbnbs in Upstate New York for a Weekend Away from the City 2026

If you live in New York, pretty much anything qualifies as an excuse for a weekend Upstate. A clanging radiator blasting dry heat into your apartment when it’s still warm outside? Time to flee to greener pastures. An overwhelming work week spent mostly in the company of your inbox? You deserve to unplug. The very first hint of a reddening leaf in the park? A seasonal sign from above—get yourself to an apple orchard.

With most small towns within a few hours’ drive of the city (and several available on a train line, for those without a car), you don’t really need a reason to spend a few days in Upstate New York. And while there are plenty of boutique hotels dotting the Hudson Valley and the Catskills, for true relaxation, why not book an Airbnb?

This time of year is all about the outdoors. Spend your days hiking along mountain trails and creeks, exploring local markets to sample all the fresh produce (and the baked goods they inspire), or hitting a brewery in the evening for a glass of cider under twinkling lights. As the weather cools, the charm offensive continues: fire pits come out, farms open for pumpkin and apple harvesting, and following the foliage becomes a perfectly acceptable way to spend a lazy fall day. Some of our favorite Upstate New York Airbnbs are located in or within walking distance of quaint towns like Hudson and Woodstock; though if you prefer a truly off-the-grid experience, we found plenty of cabins and cottages surrounded only by meadows.

Ahead, the 22 best Airbnbs in Upstate New York.

Enjoy a slower pace at this newly renovated 1890s-era farmhouse in the Western Catskills. The home is set on 25 acres of rolling meadows and forest, which lead to two streams and a waterfall. While the home has been updated to feature all new appliances (including a Vitamix), details like reclaimed wood and a bread-baking wood-stove cement the snug vibes. The main area is one big room: an eight-person dining room table connects to the kitchen, where you can spend afternoons making the most of local ingredients you picked up from a nearby farmstand. And when you head upstairs, don’t miss the claw-foot tub—it’s reason enough to book this gorgeous stay.

Rooms: 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bathrooms; sleeps 5

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, window AC unit, heating, indoor fireplace, backyard, outdoor dining area.

This spot is billed as a “boutique nature retreat”—but let’s call it what it really is: an adult treehouse. It sleeps two, with a king-sized bed and hot outdoor showers. With no cell service or electricity, this is your chance to go fully off the grid; since the whole house is surrounded by forest, you’ll feel completely cozy and secluded. When you want to re-join society, the town of Phoenicia (and, more importantly, the local favorite Phoenicia Diner) is just a 10-minute drive away.

Amenities: Outdoor shower, fire pit, free parking

Best For: Fulfilling childhood treehouse dreams.

“Upstate” in perhaps only the most abstract sense of the word (it borders New Jersey, just about one hour out of the city), this lakeside spot is filled with sunlight, a far cry from the heavy wooden cabins that permeate the area. Outside, there’s a private garden with a waterfall and lily pond—and, of course, those unbeatable views of Greenwood Lake. There are plenty of wineries and antique stores nearby, as well as hikes for the adventurous weekender (the home is a five-minute walk from a path that connects to the Appalachian Trail) and a massive claw-foot tub to soak in when it’s time to unwind.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathrooms; sleeps 4

Amenities: HDTV, bathtub, record player, crib, board games, wood-burning fireplace, patio, outdoor furniture

Best For: Those who crave nature, but are afraid of the whole cabin-in-the-woods idea.

Renovated for modernity but restored with heaps of vintage touches befitting the older home’s roots, this light-filled apartment right in the heart of Hudson is great if you prefer to stay in a town rather than remote wilderness. From the zellige tiles to the antique stove, the kitchen is a particular star—anyone looking for style inspiration for an upcoming remodel will find several nooks to bookmark here. The Nespresso and tea station helps you start each morning off on a caffeinated foot, while in the afternoons, you’ll want to hang out on the porch or in the bubblegum pink claw-foot tub with a book.

Amenities: TV, sound system, crib, patio.

This new listing is the epitome of stripped-back country living: There’s no television and few amenities, so if you’re looking for a spot to indulge your off-the-grid dreams, this is it. (Though, lest you change your mind, the hamlet of Livingston Manor, with its concept stores and coffee shops, is walking distance away.) The house is a freshly renovated farmhouse, done in the Scandinavian style—from the antique furnishings to the original wood floors, every corner is steeped in character. There’s a bunk room for the youngest members of your travel party, plus a spacious kitchen for whipping up hearty breakfasts at home before heading out for the day.

Amenities: Air conditioning, pet-friendly.

Best For: Anyone looking to truly disconnect for a weekend.

Picture the prototypical lake cottage. Wood, everywhere, is a given; as is an A-frame silhouette, a fire pit and deck for grilling, and perhaps a wood-burning fireplace or two. Welcome to the Airbnb embodiment of that vision, complete with all of the above plus a few modern amenities (the Nespresso machine is a welcome addition). Sleepy Hollow Lake is a quick 10-minute walk down a trail away, for summertime guests. In the colder months, Hunter mountain and its ski slopes are a 45-minute drive away; and in between, you’ll have a third of an acre worth of land to explore on the property itself.

Amenities: Bathtub, record player, high chair, travel crib, board games, fireplace, beach/lake access, fire pit, pet friendly.

Distance from NYC: 2 hours by train, 2.5 hours by car.

No car, no problem: This charming one-bedroom is right in the town of Cold Spring, easily reachable from the city via the Metro North. You’ll be able to walk everywhere (Cold Spring Coffeehouse, a must-visit for your morning cappuccino and cardamom bun, is just 15 minutes on foot) and spend your weekend like a local. The home itself is clean and minimally decorated, with just enough original touches—including a gorgeous fireplace—to keep it from feeling too sparse. Remote workers will appreciate the spacious dining table, too, which doubles as a workspace you can spread out in in a picturesque alcove.

Distance from NYC: 1.5 hours by car, 1.5 hours by train.

Inspired by a Swiss Alpine home, this modern space is compact and minimalist, with oversized windows that really let the mountainside views seep in. Take it in up close and personal on the (covered) patio, which, in warmer months, is a great spot for a breakfast or dinner. Indoors, a colorful kitchen, shower skylight, and pellet stove all make for memorable decorative touches. It’s the right size for a solo traveler or a couple looking for a short-term stay; you’ll have all the necessities you need, but you’re encouraged to make the most of your surroundings.

Amenities: Outdoor shower, pellet stove, patio, fire pit, EV charger, pet-friendly.

Distance from NYC: Around 3 hours by train.

Best For: The no-frills traveler who still appreciates a little aesthetic effort.

Built in the ’80s by a master stonemason, this is one of the more unique options available to Catskills travelers. The home is actually a tower, with vaulted ceilings and wraparound windows offering sweeping views of the valley below. (The bathtub on the second floor is an especially great spot to take them in.) Just a quick seven-minute drive to the town of Woodstock, you’ll be left alone but not fully remote. And if it’s still warm enough, be sure to factor in enough free time for some evenings spent outdoors—the views are incredible, and between the hot tub and the deck, there are plenty of spots to take them in.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathrooms; sleeps 4

Amenities: Washer/dryer, bathtub, piano, record player, board games, air conditioning, fireplace, fire pit, hot tub.

Best For: Someone who read one too many fairytale books growing up.

This charming A-frame in Tannersville is full of lush plants, good energy, and nostalgic charm. The home dates back to 1971 and is right in the heart of the Catskills, just two hours north of New York City. While the interiors are supremely serene, the outdoor deck with its BBQ and twinkly lights is where you’ll probably spend most of your time—especially if you’re visiting in fall or spring, when the weather is its mildest. Prefer to stay in? The home comes stocked with a record player and board games, for cozy nights with the whole group that are probably why you booked an Airbnb Upstate in the first place.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, AC, heating, backyard, BBQ.

Best For: Plant parents who need a getaway.

If the idea of staying in a cabin in the woods with a cedar wood-fired hot tub sounds up your alley, book a stay at this bright home just 10 minutes from Woodstock. It’s not quite your old-school cottage: Aside from the light palette and modern decor, the bedrooms feature Casper mattresses, and the Breville espresso machine will make morning coffees on the deck all the more enjoyable. Outside, a fire pit and cedar wood hot tub and sauna make the case for ditching the dinner reservation in favor of staying in; plus, the house comes with a movie projector, for DIY movie nights.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, AC, central heating, backyard, fire pit, hammock, BBQ, hot tub.

Best For: A soak in the hot tub, beneath the trees.

From the wood-paneled A-frame ceilings to the forest green paint theme to the coffee-colored zellige tiling in the bathroom, there are plenty of decor ideas to steal from this Airbnb. Design aside, it’s well-located (hop in the car for a quick drive to the Ashokan Reservoir and little towns like Kingston and Woodstock) and surprisingly spacious. Come summer, we predict you’ll want to spend all your time on the sprawling front deck overlooking the trees—ditto the fall, as long as you pack the appropriate amount of wool sweaters to stay warm.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, sound system, indoor fireplace, fire pit, outdoor furniture, patio, pet-friendly.

We can already feel our blood pressure lowering simply admiring this tranquil Airbnb located on the outskirts of Kingston. The property offers numerous nooks for experiencing the natural surroundings—a fire pit encircled by Adirondack chairs, a tranquil pond best savored from the home’s swinging hammock, and even a screened porch just off the kitchen for early morning coffee. Inside is equally as dreamy, with plenty of natural light and cozy touches like exposed brick and a small fireplace. One perk: You can bring your pups for a small fee, so no member of the family is left behind for the next weekend Upstate.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathrooms; sleeps 4

Amenities: Washer/dryer, central AC, indoor fireplace, backyard, fire pit, hammock, BBQ.

Hide yourself away in this atmospheric cabin perched atop Bramley Mountain near Bovina Center, a great spot for cozy restaurants and country stores. The home has a spacious atmosphere thanks to the cathedral ceilings and open floor plan, but you never lose that innately cozy feel: a wood-burning stove, wood paneling, and an atmospheric porch are all there to remind you that you’re very much in the woods. Not that there’s a bad time to book a stay here, but if you have your pick, aim for the fall. The house is surrounded by trees that turn surreal shades of scarlet and persimmon come October.

Amenities: Bathtub, outdoor shower, washer/dryer, indoor fireplace, backyard.

Best For: Turning your phone on airplane mode.

There are two types of upstate getaways: the first, characterized by spending the entire weekend in one place, relaxing and recharging. The second is spent diving headfirst into the region’s many charms, exploring shops, restaurants, and markets in several small towns. This Airbnb is ideal for the latter sort of traveler, who wants friction-less access to destinations such as Woodstock, Saugerties, and Kingston.

It also happens to be impeccably designed, with highlights like an indoor fireplace, mid-century modern decor, and a backyard BBQ and fire pit you’ll have a hard time parting ways with—it even comes stocked with firewood.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, record player, indoor fireplace, fire pit, hammock, BBQ.

Best For: Exploring several nearby towns (and an impromptu game of chess to end the night).

Leaning into Wabi-Sabi design, this ranch-style home in the Warwick Valley is close to several lakes and hiking trails (as well as trendy breweries and restaurants). Natural materials and soft lighting set a relaxed tone for the space, and a trip to The Shed (the home’s meditation room) for a yoga session will begin each day on the right foot, as will the complimentary freshly-roasted bag of ground coffee from the owner’s favorite purveyor, Voyager Espresso. When you’re living in the foreground of the dense green forest, visible from most windows in the home, it’s impossible to not feel zen.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, yoga studio, central AC and heating, lake access, fire pit, backyard, BBQ, EV charger.

Best For: Coming back from your vacation actually recharged.

This secluded sanctuary in the Catskills forest sits on a hill overlooking an abundance of beauty, from woodlands and stream-fed ponds to a sprawling wildflower meadow. The cabin is petite (just 400 square feet) but a Wabi Sabi-inspired design lends a calming effect. A few standout details—and there are several—include the open floor plan with a winding spiral staircase in the center, natural earthy textures throughout, and a peaceful outdoor area complete with a fire pit, picnic tables, and twinkly lights. Even the bedroom is impeccably designed, with its antique chair nightstand and matching bedding; twin beds have never looked chicer.

Amenities: Toiletries, washer/dryer, record player, books and board games, window AC unit, indoor pellet stove, kitchen, fire pit, charcoal BBQ.

Best For: Reading your book beneath a canopy of trees.

Think of the typical log house, then flip that idea on its head. That’s what you get with Fox Ridge Chalet, which is anything but ordinary: A lot of it is white-washed, making it feel even bigger and brighter than it is, and the assortment of furniture is so eclectic, it has the air of a cool vintage shop. Situated on seven private acres of land, the picturesque property beckons to be explored. For the days when you decide you want to stay in, the movie screening projector, pool table, hot tub, exercise bike, and game collection should more than suffice.

Amenities: Hot tub, pool table, exercise equipment, fire pit, outdoor furniture, grill

Best For: Multigenerational summer getaways with the family.

Part of the National Register of Historic Places, this residence dubbed “The Gatehouse” was last restored in 2016—updated with more modern decor and comfy furnishings. Immerse yourself in scenic views of the Catskills Mountains and Hudson River from this historic French home while relaxing in the backyard, where a separate carriage house offers covered outdoor dining for the colder months. (Or the front yard—that storybook-perfect porch demands a few mornings or afternoons spend lounging on it.) Stay occupied with limitless activities such as hiking, biking, boating, and antique shopping, all of which can be found in the historic town of Hyde Park.

Amenities: Private balcony/patio, indoor fireplace, outdoor dining area, fire pit, BBQ grill

Best For: Staying in a home on the National Register of Historic Places.

The Pond House is a property with some serious art history cachet: It’s the former studio of social realist painter Reginald Marsh. An architect lovingly restored it into a single-family home that exudes country elegance: there are exposed beam ceilings, chandeliers, and floor-to-ceiling windows that look out onto the estate’s pond. Its most unique selling point is the main bedroom: With floor-to-ceiling glass windows slotted into wood paneling, you get a front row seat to the great outdoors from the comfort of your bed. It’ll be like sleeping in the world’s most relaxing fishbowl. (The adjacent bathroom, with its spa-like tub and equally oversized windows, is a nice companion.)

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathrooms; sleeps 5

Amenities: private balcony, bathtub, indoor fireplace, fully equipped kitchen

If you’re traveling with a large group (or looking for a spot to stay around a wedding), this home can fit over 16 guests. It’s the perfect luxurious weekend getaway—perched upon a sprawling 16 acres, this converted-barn home has a design-forward interior complete with 30-foot ceilings as well as five-and-a-half bedrooms. The service is also top-notch, as the property comes with a 24-hour digital concierge as well as a private chef upon request. You’ll only be a few minutes from Woodstock village, if you want to venture out for breakfast before heading out to traverse the area’s many hiking trails.

Rooms: 5 bedrooms, 3 bathrooms; sleeps 16+

Amenities: private hot tub, indoor fireplace, hammock, private balcony, patio and backyard

Best For: A grand fireplace that will take your breath away.

The sister property to the earlier Hudson home in our edit (all designed by New York design firm Zio & Sons), this three-bedroom offers a little more space. It’s a charming townhouse in the Hudson Valley right by the main stretch of shops and restaurants, chock full of antiques and old-world details like salvaged library doors in the bedroom and an 1840s-era mantel. This is a spot to save if you love design—from the cast iron tub to the copper pan-lined tile kitchen to the original wallpaper in the living room, the home is brimming with inspiration at every turn.

Amenities: private balcony/patio, bathtub, outdoor dining area,

Distance From NYC: 2 hours by car and train.

Best For: A design-driven stay in Hudson.

#6647. Farmers Market Salad With Miso Maple Dressing

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

The farmers market is my biggest hack for solo cooking. Instead of committing to a three-pound bag of carrots, you can buy just one, and choose your produce based on beauty or mere curiosity. That’s how I came up with this fall salad, comprising a single head of Little Gem lettuce and some crunchy produce, including that carrot we mentioned, cucumber, watermelon radish, and an Asian pear. Slicing those elements thinly with a mandoline and throwing them in an ice bath for a brief soak helps keep everything cold and crisp.

The dressing is equally important. I start with Kewpie mayo for its richness and savory depth—it’s made with only egg yolks and contains MSG, giving it a fuller flavor than standard mayonnaise. White miso brings even more umami, while rice vinegar keeps things bright. The result is a creamy finger-licking dressing that clings to every bite. Serve with a fried egg (or your protein of choice) and a piece of fresh bread to scoop up the leftovers. Make a double batch of dressing for dipping crudités or marinating salmon, chicken, or roasted vegetables.

Read More: The Farmers Market Is Built for Solo Cooking

Combine 1 small head of Little Gem or other crunchy lettuce, leaves separated, cut into 2"–3" pieces, 1 rainbow carrot, peeled, very thinly sliced lengthwise into ribbons with a mandoline or vegetable peeler, 1 Persian cucumber, thinly sliced, preferably with a mandoline, ½ small watermelon radish, peeled, halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, and ¼ medium Asian pear, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, in a large bowl of ice water. Let soak 10–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 2 Tbsp. seasoned rice vinegar, 2 Tbsp. white miso, 2 tsp. Kewpie mayonnaise, 2 tsp. pure maple syrup, and 1 tsp. toasted sesame oil in a small bowl until smooth and emulsified (or combine in a small glass jar, cover, and shake). Taste dressing and season with kosher salt.

Drain vegetables and run through a salad spinner or pat dry with a kitchen towel to remove excess water. Wipe out large bowl, return vegetables to bowl, and drizzle 2 Tbsp. dressing over. Toss, adding more dressing as needed, until evenly coated (reserve any remaining dressing for another use).

Transfer salad to a shallow bowl or rimmed plate. Top with a fried egg and serve with country-style bread if desired.

Do Ahead: Dressing can be made up to 3 days ahead. Cover and chill.
