#6611. I Tried the New AirDoctor 1500 Tower—And It’s the Perfect Size for Eliminating Kitchen Odors

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

It happens to the best of us. You’re minding your own business as dessert bubbles in the oven or dinner sears on the stove, then—bam! The smell of burning reaches your nose, and before you know it, you’re dragging out a stepladder to silence the blaring smoke alarm.

I hate to say that this is a fairly frequent scenario in my kitchen. While I do my best to prevent pans of lasagna from overflowing and exercise caution when searing steak, accidents still occur. The only difference is that I now have a solution to clear the lingering smell from my space.

I’ve been testing the AirDoctor 1500 air purifier for two months, and it’s a portable yet powerful option for eliminating pesky kitchen odors. Here’s everything you need to know.

Banish bad odors from your kitchen with this mini-yet-mighty air purifier.

The AirDoctor 1500 is a high-performance air purifier packed into a sleek, compact package. Unlike other air purifiers that can take up as much space as a dehumidifier, the 1500 measures less than 10 inches wide and 21 inches high. It features three filters: a pre-filter for trapping larger particles like pet hair, a carbon and VOC filter for filtering odors and an UltraHEPA for capturing everything else. It’s best suited for small-to-medium spaces up to 320 square feet and comes in black or white.

I’ve been testing the AirDoctor 1500 air purifier since its launch in September 2026. I’ve used it in my kitchen, entryway, office and family room.

The AirDoctor arrived on my doorstep in a sturdy brown box. It was well-packaged to prevent damage during shipping, and setup couldn’t be easier. All you have to do is lift the unit out of the box, remove the plastic bag, peel off a few stickers and, most importantly, set up the filter.

The filter housing snaps off easily, and installation is as simple as removing the filter from its packaging and popping it back in. In all the air purifiers I’ve tested, AirDoctor has the most seamless filter access, thanks to built-in magnets in the housing. This is important not only for changing the filter but also for cleaning it.

After completing setup, I plugged in the AirDoctor and turned it on. It immediately whirred to life, starting at high speed with a red light and working its way down to a low-speed setting. The control panel is reactive to a simple touch, with options for speed (auto, one, two, three or four), ion, dim and timer. The interface also includes a light that signals when the filter needs to be checked or replaced.

As the air purifier got to work, I was impressed with how little sound it produced. On level one, you can barely hear it. It’s a slightly audible white noise that blends easily into the background. Level four is obviously the loudest, similar to a fan on high speed. If you’re very sensitive to noise, you might find any air purifier, including the AirDoctor, too loud to sleep with. But in a kitchen, the whir blends right into the din of cooking, a running dishwasher and other ambient sounds.

Within a week of the AirDoctor being in my space, it faced its first real challenge. I had a potpie galette in a 425-degree oven, and some of the filling started to leak onto the pizza steel it was baking on and burn. Within minutes, my oven filled with smoke. I managed to get the galette out without setting off the alarms, but my space was filled with an unpleasant, burning-vegetable odor.

I turned on the AirDoctor, set it to auto, and it immediately kicked into high gear. The light turned red—a sign that it senses poor air quality—and the fan worked overtime to cleanse the air. After about 15 minutes, the light turned yellow—moderate air quality—and I could already sense a difference. Within an hour, it was back to a blue light, which signifies good air quality, and it’s like the accident never happened.

Over the next few weeks, the AirDoctor helped clear the air after I burnt some toast in the toaster and cooked cruciferous vegetables. It also helps combat day-to-day odors, like a full trash can or a garbage disposal ready for a scrubdown.

What I like best is that the AirDoctor isn’t just masking these scents; it’s actually removing them from the air. As an allergy sufferer, I’ve also noticed fewer symptoms (especially sneezing) when the air purifier is running. Thanks to the 1500’s portable size, it’s easy to tote it around my downstairs living area, too.

The AirDoctor’s filters are designed to last—but the exact lifespan depends on many factors. How long you run the air purifier each day, for starters. Along with what kind of baseline air quality is in your home. Pets, for example, are an obvious culprit for added dander and hair. Luckily, the 1500 includes a built-in sensor light that tells you when it’s time for a refresh.

You can also pop off the housing and give the filter a good vacuum. I like to do this once a month or so, but again, buildup may be more or less severe depending on your home’s air quality conditions.

I’ve had the opportunity to also test the AirDoctor 1500’s larger cousin, the AirDoctor 3500. But how do these models compare?

Size is the most obvious difference. The 1500 is six inches slimmer than the 3500 and weighs roughly half as much. I find that the 1500 blends more seamlessly into my space than the 3500, taking up less footprint. The round tower design is also very easy to slip into a corner.

That said, the 1500 covers rooms up to 320 sq. ft., while the 3500 covers up to 630 sq. ft. This makes the 1500 a great option for kitchens, offices, laundry rooms and small bedrooms, while the 3500 is a better choice for large living rooms and open-concept homes.

Beyond that, performance is very similar. Both models are quiet and easy to operate. They use a 3-stage filtration system, including an UltraHEPA. They’re both high-quality machines that are built to last. And that quality does come at a premium. The 1500 retails for $399, while the 3500 costs $659.

My spouse likes to joke that I’m like a basset hound given how sensitive I am to smells. That’s why the AirDoctor 1500 is an obvious choice in our kitchen. It efficiently rids our space of odors from cooking, pungent foods and even the occasional smoke-induced accident. Not only is this machine reducing odors that would otherwise linger for days, but it’s also cleansing our air of other contaminants.

This way to cleaner air! I love this air purifier's slim footprint, low noise level and triple filter design.

The AirDoctor 1500 air purifier is available from the brand’s website or Amazon. It retails for $399.

#6610. This Christmas, Harrods Is Doing Things Differently

There are few signs that Christmas has arrived in London quite like the Harrods store lighting up for the festive season. Every year, thousands of visitors descend upon Knightsbridge to see the store’s holiday transformation, and this year, the heritage retailer is giving them even more reason to stick around — and return again and again.

Unveiled on Tuesday, Harrods’s iconic terracotta façade has been revamped once again into a celestial spectacle, complete with 600 handcrafted stars, four kilometers of gold leaf, and more than 17,000 lights. The difference this year, however, is that the holiday campaign, Where the Stars Align, is the first wholly Harrods-created festive concept in several years. This follows a spree of collaborations with luxury houses, including Dior in 2022 and Loro Piana in 2024, which placed the retailer as secondary in its own Christmas storytelling.

This time, Harrods has brought multiple brands under its complete creative direction: each of its 24 Christmas windows feature unique installations from houses including Ralph Lauren, Van Cleef & Arpels, Chopard, Dior, Graff, Cartier, and Chanel Beauty.

“I wanted to create joy, but I also wanted that feeling of childhood — those moments where you stop and just look up, whether that’s with your friends and family,” says Alexander Wells Greco, Harrods’s creative visual director. “There’s that moment to pause in such a busy climate.”

For Michael Ward, the store’s managing director, the façade is also an important gateway to the wider Harrods experience. “Our façade is one of London’s most recognizable landmarks, and at Christmas, it becomes a destination in its own right. It attracts people who may not have planned to visit the store, creating an opportunity to introduce them to everything Harrods has to offer,” he says.

That invitation continues inside. Customers can take part in luxury engraving, leather personalization and bespoke calligraphy, alongside gold-leaf and bauble personalization with Acqua di Parma. A Dior cinema activation will screen a new film from its creative director Jonathan Anderson, while family programming includes snow globe making, arts and crafts, and biscuit decorating. Children can also collect and post letters to Father Christmas from dedicated Harrods post boxes throughout the store.

The scale of the program reflects the commercial importance of the festive period. A 2025 Microsoft Advertising survey found that 60% of small and medium-sized retailers consider the holidays their most important trading period, with 44% expecting it to account for more than a quarter of annual sales. For Harrods, the stakes are particularly high: more than a third of its customers visit during the festive season, according to Ward. The campaign, therefore, is an opportunity to engage existing customers while drawing in visitors who might initially come for the spectacle.

However, success is not measured by footfall and holiday sales alone. Harrods is also looking at the quality of the experience and the longer-term relationships it can build with customers. The aim for every touchpoint, from the windows and the lighting to the restaurants, is to reinforce the wider Harrods proposition. “If someone comes to see the lights, discovers something unexpected inside the store and experiences the exceptional service that defines Harrods,” Ward says, “that is incredibly valuable to us. These are investments in the long-term strength of our brand, as much as in the Christmas trading period.”

Having spent several years investing in the lighting infrastructure that now connects its Knightsbridge façade, windows and surrounding public spaces, Harrods is using this year’s campaign to bring that investment to life. Every evening from 6pm, the façade will host a choreographed light show, repeating every 30 minutes and encouraging visitors to stop by and take in the display.

But while technology provides the scale and the spectacle, the installation is equally defined by the craftsmanship behind it: 600 handcrafted stars, bespoke moons and illuminated elements, brought together by more than 60 specialists and over 40,000 hours of work, with the majority of production taking place in the UK.

“Craftsmanship is fundamental to luxury, and it reflects the same commitment to quality and attention to detail that we expect across everything we do at Harrods. As technology and AI continue to transform the world around us, I believe there is something increasingly valuable about human creativity and the ability to create physical experiences that people can genuinely connect with,” says Ward, noting that recent holiday campaigns from brands such as Prada and Dior have also embraced illustration and craft. “There is a renewed appreciation for the human touch and the sense of wonder that is thoughtfully made.”

For Greco, championing local suppliers was a no-brainer, reflecting both the depth of creative talent available in Britain and the retailer’s responsibility to platform that talent. “We have such huge creative talent in the UK from a production standpoint, across all aspects,” he says. “We have such a vast platform that can really enable and enhance the visibility of these wonderful local crafters.”

“Christmas is such a tactile seasonal moment,” continues Greco. “Irrespective of opening gifts or whatever, you’re with your loved ones, you’re socializing, and I think it’s that tactility that enabled us to make the right decision at the beginning of the year and say, ‘Let’s maintain that. Let’s support the human touch.’”

Rather than concentrating all of its activity around the initial campaign launch, the department store is rolling out a rotating program of retail theater throughout the six-week festive period to reflect the changing priorities of customers as the season progresses, as well as giving them reasons to return.

“In November, we see customers start to prepare for the festive calendar, whether that means finding something to wear for a special occasion or getting their homes ready to entertain. As we move into December, gifting naturally becomes a priority. But gifting today is not simply about buying for others,” says Ward.

Harrods is programming its in-store experiences accordingly. November’s line-up includes live fashion illustration in the store’s Eveningwear and Occasion Room, beauty gifting experiences with Clé de Peau Beauté and personalized Christmas card calligraphy, alongside opportunities to have festive purchases engraved or customized. As the season progresses, the focus broadens to family experiences, with a weekend of snow globe making, arts and crafts and Marcato biscuit decorating on December 12-13. Letters to Father Christmas can also be posted at dedicated Harrods post boxes from November 10 to December 24.

The strategy comes at a time when physical retailers are having to work harder to justify the journey into store. PwC found that 64% of UK festive purchases were expected to take place online in 2025, including home delivery and click-and-collect. Meanwhile, McKinsey’s latest retail research found that 65% of consumers cite immersive environments as a driver when choosing a store for discovery-led visits.

“We are operating in an environment where customers are increasingly thoughtful about how and where they spend their money, and luxury retailers need to recognize that. Customers have high expectations, particularly at Christmas. They are looking for exceptional products, but also for service and experiences that make their time worthwhile,” says Ward. “Harrods is well positioned because we offer far more than a traditional retail experience. Whether someone is looking for a very special gift, preparing for an occasion or simply spending time with family, we can offer something that feels personal and memorable. Ultimately, our focus is not simply on encouraging customers to spend more, but on giving them compelling reasons to choose Harrods.”

There is also a wider ambition to create a sense of community around the store. Harrods has been part of London’s retail landscape for more than 175 years, and Greco sees this as carrying a responsibility beyond its commercial operations. “We are the beacon of Knightsbridge,” he says. “We have a duty of care to make sure that we are delivering exceptional retail theatre, even more so throughout these seasonal moments.”

#6609. If You Didn’t Already Think CrossFit Was a Cult, This Book Will Convince You

CrossFit could easily hold the distinction of being the most popular—and certainly the most universally recognized—fitness movement ever. At its peak, the company, founded in 2000, boasted over 15,000 affiliate gyms, or “boxes,” in more than 150 countries and was enlisting nearly 50,000 coaches each year. Somewhere along the line, to many people (including my mom), the word CrossFit became synonymous for working out.

But you may have noticed that people don’t talk as much about CrossFit nowadays as they used to. Following an assorted variety of allegations against its mercurial founder Greg Glassman in 2020, and the tragic and seemingly avoidable death of an athlete at the 2024 CrossFit Games, the company has been gradually losing its chalky grip on popular culture.

But the storytelling around CrossFit’s rise and fall is anything but done and dusted, as I learned while reading Calum Marsh’s new book, The Glass Box—a fascinating, staggeringly detailed account of not only CrossFit’s rocket-propelled rise and spectacular flame-out, as told by insider sources including Glassman himself, but a trove of previously unshared anecdotes that make it hard to put down.

A few days after the book’s late-October release, I spoke to Marsh about airing CrossFit’s dirtiest laundry, how the cultishness of CrossFit has spread to other fitness crazes, and why an old-fashioned barbell snatch is the ultimate kryptonite for the modern performative male.

Calum Marsh: The first 50 people I spoke to were basically warning me off the subject, telling me that it was going to be an uphill battle and that if the people that I was writing about were unhappy with how I wrote about them, they would criticize me or attempt to defame me. They have a long history, which I've chronicled in the book, of creating campaigns of bad will towards their critics. They are really experienced at mobilizing the internet and mobilizing social media in order to discredit people that they consider critics or, as I sometimes frame it in the book, heretics.

But, on the other hand, I knew that I was going to be approaching this from a journalistically rigorous perspective, and that it was going to be an account of what actually happened, from the people who were involved. It wasn't going to be a book about my opinion or my personal take on CrossFit. So I felt quite secure that the things I was writing in the book were the best possible representation of the truth.

There's been a lot of focus on some of the more, shall we say, sordid details. There was an article in the New York Post that basically pulled all that out and made the book seem like it was some scandalous hit piece. That's not the book I tried to write, and it's not the book I think I wrote. The book I wrote is a very fair, even-handed assessment of a man and the business that he created. It includes true stories about his behavior that may not be the most flattering, and it includes, I think, testament to the brilliance of what he created and all of the great things that he did.

It's been amusing to see the reception somewhat split among some hardcore CrossFitters. They're upset because they think it's a takedown of Greg Glassman that's biased against him. And then other critics think that I'm way too generous to him, or way too flattering. Someone said I was too affectionate towards him. It's funny to me that two different people can read it and have polar opposite views. But hopefully that means that it's just objective.

It’s something that is always mentioned in relation to CrossFit. There’s actually another book that came out while I was writing my book, called The Cult of CrossFit by Katie Rose Hejtmanek. It's an academic study of the history and sociology of cults, and how CrossFit is a cult by definition. I thought that was really illuminating. There are a lot of similarities that go beyond all the joking, and there are a lot of things about the cult-like nature of CrossFit that have made it intoxicating for some people, and maybe painful in other ways as well.

The thing that struck me was how a lot of people, especially earlier CrossFit enthusiasts or devotees, talked to me about the difficulty they had leaving CrossFit. Greg has said many times, and will still say, that they weren't a cult because you could leave at any time. And I always found that to be a fairly unconvincing argument, because many cults say the same thing. A lot of CrossFitters had this experience where they felt like they had really close friends—sometimes even family members or partners—who essentially excommunicated them—cut them off, iced them out, however you want to phrase it—after they either left CrossFit or spoke out against CrossFit. That, to me, is the strongest cult-like parallel.

It really wasn't. I had heard from people that Glassman was generous, and so I knew stories about him spending lavishly on dinners, for example. But it all seemed pretty much within the realm of normal spending for someone who's massively wealthy. It wasn't until I started speaking to people who were more familiar with CrossFit’s finances when I started to learn about the degree to which the spending was out of control. The amount of money they spent relative to what they earned is the most shocking thing to me, because it's not like they were spending that much money while wildly out-earning it. They were almost spending more than they were making. And they were not slowing their spending when the earning slowed. That, to me, as a business reporter, is very, very interesting, because you start to wonder how they let that happen. Was no one there to say, ‘Hey, we need to pump the brakes a little bit?’ As it turned out, there really wasn't.

A lot of people had this reckoning in 2020 after [Glassman’s George Floyd tweet] and some of the accusations that came out about Glassman then. A lot of gyms deaffiliated from CrossFit, and Greg, of course, stepped down and sold the company. I personally know many people who had a kind of personal reckoning with their level of comfort in supporting the company. But I think that was, at least in some cases, answered by Greg's departure.

Others went through this process of divorcing themselves from the CrossFit identity as a brand, but continuing to practice CrossFit as a methodology. There are thousands of gyms all over the world that are CrossFit gyms in all but name. They probably call themselves cross-training or functional fitness now, but if you go in, they still have a Rogue rig, they still have wall balls, they still do snatches—everything you'd expect to see if you walked into a CrossFit gym. The people there are still CrossFitters at heart. They've still given themselves over to the transformative power of the methodology that Greg Glassman invented. But they are no longer endorsing or supporting the brand or the company at large.

I would be willing to bet that if you walked into any CrossFit gym in North America and asked them what the difference is between when Glassman was in charge and when corporate private equity took charge, they wouldn’t know that even happened. The average person, who just goes to CrossFit to get fit and doesn't follow the CrossFit news and isn't obsessed with CrossFit Games, would not have any idea. And this is partly a consequence of the fact that the affiliate model is so loose.

I first started going to a box in 2018. I was doing personal training with someone at what I didn't realize was even a CrossFit box. I was doing that personal training for probably about a year before I realized I was doing CrossFit, and then I started doing classes in 2019.

I do! In fact, I coached a CrossFit class earlier this morning.

Yeah. Well, they don't allow you to call it a certification with the one I have. They're very clear about that language. But I do have my CrossFit Level 1 certificate. I did the course and passed the test.

I think that part of it is just the nature of fandom. If you become enthusiastic about something, you want to identify as an enthusiast, and that means wearing the T-shirt. I went to a Bob Dylan concert on the weekend. I bought a Bob Dylan hat. It's just part of the experience of being a fan of something. I think Hyrox is super interesting, because it does have a lot of cult-like similarities with CrossFit. But the really toxic side—the side that's a bit more nefarious, that involves really giving your life over to it—I haven't seen with Hyrox, at least yet. I feel like there's something missing at the center, possibly the guru figure that Greg Glassman was for CrossFit. Hyrox doesn't really have that. So maybe that missing ingredient has stopped it from being as intense. But, on the whole, I think it's just this level of fandom that is baked into everything in culture now.

There's a journalist named Hannah Singleton, who writes about fitness a lot. She recently wrote a piece about how athleticism is the new flex for people, and I think that’s sort of the direction we're moving in. For example, Hyrox. It's in the same vein as running a marathon or doing an ultra race, where it's an achievement that you can brandish. You can put it on your LinkedIn. You can say that you've done this and that. Maybe it's on your resume. You're almost putting up points on your scoreboard. And I think that we're probably going to find either more events along those lines, where it's something that you can be proud of because it's so difficult, or a system in which you can have an overall fitness score. I think people really want to show that they put in the work. They want to impress people with how fit they are. In the same way that people who are into running are obsessively posting about their marathon time or their 10K time, and those milestones are universally understood in running—everyone knows how impressive it is to run a sub-10-minute 5K or a sub-three-hour marathon—the fitness equivalent of that, I think, is still coming.

This is one of the things I find interesting in light of CrossFit—and I know that some people are going to think this is not true—but I really do think CrossFit, or let’s say functional fitness, is an antidote to this whole performative thing. It's so hard that it's humbling. You can’t really show up and pretend you did it. You cannot performatively do barbell snatches. If you see someone on social media snatching heavy, it's because they've worked at it for hundreds, if not thousands, of hours, and because they're really strong, really mobile, and really fit. And I say this as someone who both has a copy of Infinite Jest on my bookshelf and wears Satisfy.

You can ‘perform’ your sport of choice by posting about it, but things like snatches or ring muscle ups are so physically demanding that it kind of cuts through that bullshit. And I think that we're probably going to increasingly value things that we know on-site are authentic, because there's an authenticity built into it. There's no shortcut there. And that authenticity will become more and more valuable.

#6608. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

#6607. Bill Hader Has Highbrow Taste in Children’s Movies

You can trust Bill Hader on movies. From gushing about John Ford and Akira Kurosawa in the Criterion Closet, to spoofing Errol Morris and D.A. Pennebaker in Documentary Now!, to creating, directing and starring in four seasons of HBO’s Barry—the SNL alum’s cinematic expertise is well-documented. Hader knows a thing or two about kids’ movies in particular, having lent his iconic voice to animated tentpoles like Inside Out and Cloudy With a Chance of Meatballs. This week, you can hear Hader in The Cat in The Hat, a new adaptation of the 1957 Dr. Seuss classic, in which he voices the titular troublemaking feline.

Written and directed by Alessandro Carloni and Erica Rivinoja, this new iteration of the beloved children’s story is an inviting romp that is mischievous enough for kids, grounded enough for grown-ups, and teeming with gags and good nature that all can enjoy. The film is an ideal showcase for Hader’s gymnastic vocal talents, and also boasts Quinta Brunson, Matt Berry, and Giancarlo Esposito among its cast. (It’s a more family-friendly—though no less amusing—take on the Cat than when Hader last played the character, in a 2014 SNL sketch.)

A father to three daughters, Hader has seen it all—from Frozen and Tangled to Off Campus—and does his part, when possible, to pass down the classic films that were formative during his own childhood. “You don’t want to push it too hard,” he tells GQ on a recent call. “For every one I show them, there’s 10 that I start and they go, ‘Ugh, Dad, this is boring.’” The rest of us, however, are eager to take note. Below, Hader shares some of his favorite quote-unquote “kids’ movies” whose cinematic merit makes them a must-see at any age.

“When I was young, my dad told me that was a movie that he watched as a kid. I didn't grow up in a time when there were a lot of Westerns, but [for] my dad and uncles, that was all that was on TV.

What I was moved by was the relationship [between] Alan Ladd as Shane and this little boy [Brandon deWilde] enamored with a gunfighter. It has this heroic sensibility to it, but underneath was this honesty of, ‘You don't want that life,’ which I thought was interesting. To me, Van Heflin, the dad, was the cooler guy. So it upended those expectations of what the movie was going to be.

It has this ending where it's poignant and kind of sad, but I remember thinking, ‘Oh, that's good that that's what happens at the end of the story.’ It's a good coming-of-age story… It's kind of sneaky. You could see it on the face of it just being this cut-and-dry, Western-hero type of movie. But when you really think about it, even as a kid, I got a sense that there's a lot of depth to it.”

“Buster Keaton is one of my favorites, and that was one I showed my kids. I have three daughters. Now they're 17, 14, and 12, but at the time, they were very little. I'm a movie nerd, so I was gonna show them some silent movies, and I was like, ‘I know. Everybody's gonna roll their eyes at me for showing the kids silent movies. How pretentious.’ But they really responded to Buster Keaton, specifically Sherlock Jr. and Three Ages, his take on the movie Intolerance by D.W. Griffith. They just loved it, and it was fun getting to watch it through their eyes.

I recently took my youngest [to see] it at the Aero Theater in LA, and it still was great. To see a movie that was made over a hundred years ago still work on all [levels], like… it works better than most movies now. It's just very simple. [Keaton] wasn't some kind of auteur guy. He was a vaudeville comedian that was curious about filmmaking; what you could do with editing, what you could do with shots. And I think he ended up making the blueprint of how you shoot physical comedy and action. It’s pretty amazing.

What's interesting about some of those silent movies is that they don't really know what they're doing. The best stuff comes out of, ‘I don't know, I had this idea, let's figure it out in a really open, curious way.’ And in doing that, you invent the language.

Charlie Chaplin, too. [I’ve shown] them City Lights and The Circus and The Gold Rush. But they were really drawn to Buster Keaton, I think, because he was kind of dry and you didn't really know what he was thinking, and so you could put all your feelings onto him.”

“That's one that my parents showed me when I was a kid. It's a long movie, but it has so many crazy [moments] and a lot of physical comedy. I just love all those comedians in the movie. Every time someone pulls up, you're like, ‘Oh my God, it's Jonathan Winters. I love Phil Silvers. Oh my God, Spencer Tracy's in this movie!’ Dick Shawn is my personal favorite in that movie, the guy who's the real mama's boy.

It's kind of the one Stanley Kramer movie I like. Stanley Kramer movies tended to be, I don't know, a little sentimental, or overtly didactic or something, [but] this movie is just having a ton of fun. I have very fond memories of watching it with my parents and my grandparents. My dad was in town recently, and when I came home, he was watching it with my kids, and they were all laughing really hard and telling me scenes from it.

They really loved it, but [just like] with the silent movies, you don't want to push it too hard. For every [classic movie] I show them, there's 10 that I start and they go, ‘Ugh, Dad, this is boring,’ and I go, ‘Alright, we can watch Nobody Wants This or Off Campus.’”

“The Secret of NIMH was one that I loved as a kid, because it was ostensibly a kid's movie, but it was incredibly dark and disturbing. It has stuff that I still find really frightening. And I loved the mythology of it. As a kid, I liked the idea that in your backyard [there] could be this whole kingdom that you don't even know about.

There's specifically a shot in it with the crow, played by Dom DeLuise, and in the distance they see this cat. There's this long shot [of] this field, and then suddenly, just really quickly, you see this cat pop up and go back down under [as] it's trying to catch a bird or something. That shot had a huge effect on me. I thought, ‘Oh man, that's so terrifying.’

And then the story of the rats and NIMH, and they're all being tested on, and they fall into this abyss, and the whole ending where they're having this sword fight… I just thought it was fantastic. Everything was high stakes. And it wasn't Disney. I liked Disney, but Disney never went that dark.

Maybe not a lot of people agree with me, [but] I’m definitely someone [that] likes when something's scary for a kid, within reason. A lot of people are like, ‘No, no, no, they can't see that.’ And it's like, ‘No, let them see it. Get scared. That's good.’ I was happy that I was scared.

I'm sure if The Secret of NIMH came out now, they would have a whole room of executives going, ‘You can't have the owl with its head upside-down, turning around and with cobwebs all over him. It's just too scary.’ But for me, it scared me to death, and then I would keep watching it, and then it became less scary, and then I started to appreciate it. I think it's good for kids to be scared.”

“That movie came out when I was a freshman in high school. I got a job on the school paper, and my first job was to write a review of all the new movies, and it was the week that that movie came out. And so I remember I went with a notebook, I was writing my thoughts down, and then I ended up writing a pretty bad [review]. I liked [the movie] a lot, but my actual writing was terrible. The editors took it and rewrote it all.

But I loved it. I love Tim Burton. I loved the music in it, specifically the song that Catherine O'Hara sings as Sally; I think it's such a moving song. And Henry Selick’s direction in it is amazing. People always think Tim Burton made that movie. He didn't. It's Henry Selick. He spent every day there with those animators making that thing work.

I love the scope of it and how grand it is, from the beginning—that ‘This Is Halloween’ song, there's something almost operatic about it. And it's its own thing. The best stuff, to me, is always when the filmmakers and the writers [are] doing a thing that they want to see, and they trust an audience will get it.

When it came out, I remember it wasn't what it is now. It was kind of this weird oddity. And then as time went on… I remember moving to LA, and it was the 10-year anniversary of it, and they had a screening someplace, and I drove past all these people dressed like the characters, they had Jack Skellington t-shirts on and all that stuff, and I went, ‘Wow, that's crazy.’ Cause I was a huge fan of it, and had the soundtrack, and I absolutely adored that movie.

[Once] I had kids, it was one of the first movies I showed them, and they watched it every Halloween and every Christmas. My youngest daughter [recently] played Sally in a school play, and she got to sing that song, and so it was full circle. I got very emotional. I was like, ‘Oh my gosh, there she is, singing that song.’ And I had become friendly with Catherine O'Hara, and she passed away, and it was really… Yeah, I was a blubbering idiot when she started singing that song.”

#6606. ‘Wanted’ Stars Solea Pfeiffer and Liisi LaFontaine on Their Long and Winding Road to Broadway

Solea Pfeiffer and Liisi LaFontaine have been waiting to get Wanted to Broadway since 2018. Back then, the rollicking Broadway musical, which opened Sunday at the James Earl Jones Theatre, was slowly being developed from Angelica Chéri and Ross Baum’s grad school thesis. Though LaFontaine had broken out as Deena in the West End premiere of Dreamgirls two years earlier, as Pfeiffer reminds her, she was intimidated to be costarring with someone hot off the original Hamilton tour.

“Then on our first day of rehearsal, our voices blended like crazy and we had the same sense of humor,” LaFontaine remembers. “I was like, This is going to be my first New York friend.”

Their voices still soar divinely when combined—this is probably the best-sung show on Broadway right now—but the intervening eight years have been as winding as the musical’s inspiration: Chéri’s family lore that her great-great-aunts Mary and Martha Clarke were able to pass as white in Reconstruction-era Texas and might have gotten into some outlaw hijinks.

Wanted has gone through its own transformations, from a title change (it was formerly Gun & Powder) to significant retooling across two different stagings, starring either Pfeiffer or LaFontaine—never together. And the theater landscape itself has completely changed since the pandemic, in ways good and bad. What’s stayed firm is the remarkable talent of these leading ladies, whom time and hard-earned opportunities have made young industry veterans.

A few days before their big night, Pfeiffer and LaFontaine got together to discuss the show’s evolution and how significant it is for them to lead an original musical as performers who, like their characters, are mixed race.

Vogue: Does it feel like you’re in a different industry now from the one you walked into?

Solea Pfeiffer: There’s kind of a shift happening in the industry right now. A lot of development is starting in London before it comes here—a lot of shifting in the gestation process of musical theater at the moment. It’s strange. This season, this moment on Broadway…. I think we’re going to learn a lot about the state of the art in the next few months. There’s so much Black art that’s happening all over New York, and at the same time producers and the discourse are saying, “Broadway is dying, Broadway’s so alive, we’re grossing more than ever.” There are so many statements out in the ether about the state of musical theater and whether it’s doable or profitable or worth it. Depending on how this season goes, I think we’re gonna learn a lot about who’s right about what.

Liisi LaFontaine: The stakes in everything just feel higher. I think we’re all still processing and unpacking the pandemic—and sometimes I can’t believe we have phrases like pre-COVID in our vocabulary. So much has changed, and the need for art and live entertainment has also changed. I think, right now, what we do is genuinely vital to the health of the country, giving people a space to go and feel something.

Pfeiffer: I think making art during a second Trump term feels pretty different. It feels strange to be doing “frivolous art” right now. Wanted is this combination of escapism and a very galvanizing statement about getting out in the world and remembering that freedom is not free. It feels amazing to be part of a show that is platforming such Black excellence and saying, “Look at America.” This little microcosm of a story is the blueprint for a lot of what we are experiencing.

The show hits all of these ideas without ever feeling like homework. I keep telling people that it just feels like a big old musical.

Pfeiffer: One of the first book musicals was Show Boat, which dealt with the exact same themes: a woman who is passing during the Reconstruction era. This is kind of the modern, centennial answer to all the questions raised by Show Boat [which premiered in 1927]. It’s just true to the form—this American story in this American art form—and it’s not pretending to be anything besides a big old musical. At the same time we get to really dissect these American traditions of assimilation and sacrifice. It feels like we’re contributing to the canon.

The show’s been in development for so many years. How have conversations around race changed in the room?

LaFontaine: Oh my God, the reckonings. I think the best part is that our writer is a Black woman, so naturally the conversations will be different than if it was anyone else in that lead role, a little more sensitive. Having a Black woman tell a story that is specifically true about her family, having a Black director [Stevie Walker-Webb], mixed race people starring in the show, our choreographer [Chelsey Arce] is mixed race…. It’s a very brown room, a very female-heavy room, and all the men in the room are very receptive. A lot of the men that we’re around these days, we say they feel like they’ve been written by women.

Solea and I have learned how to talk about our race and things we never even realized we needed to talk about. Last night at the stage door, we met a woman in her 50s who is mixed race. She was crying to us, talking about how complicated it is, how each generation, older and older, had less and less language. Us ’90s babies were born in this golden era where it was like, America’s on the up and up and race? We’ve never even heard of her. Obama’s coming. But I think about the Mariah Careys and the generations above us who had to either hide their Blackness or completely assimilate into one side or the other.

Pfeiffer: Miscegenation was literally a crime during our parents’ lifetime. Doing the show in 2018 and 2020, I remember it felt like an important development in feeling whole as a mixed person and that I didn’t have to dissect myself to make sense of myself. Now, as we’re seeing people have their citizenship questioned in the street based on look alone, there’s something really important about naming American whiteness. The Reconstruction era is when this American identity of whiteness was codified into law. Now, we have slave catchers in the streets doing this again—it’s like the American playbook. It’s nothing new, and we don’t get taught this, or it’s getting written out. That’s what I think is so exciting about telling this story in 2026. All the roadblocks that pushed our timeline of getting the show to Broadway…. Like, Oh my gosh. But we get to do it now. We get to say something not just for the Black experience but for anyone who doesn’t fit into that clear “American identity.”

You’ve both spoken about how meaningful it’s been to work on a show that acknowledges your own mixed race identities. Has that been a grounding experience?

LaFontaine: This is the first time I’ve played a specifically mixed race person. Any other time it’s been kind of open to interpretation. Dreamgirls is a very Black show. In Moulin Rouge!, I was considered the first Black Satine. There’s always this feeling of leaning into one side or the other, dependent on how people perceive you. I feel, in my adult life, there’s even less language for being mixed. As a kid, my parents made up words to help us identify ourselves and it felt a lot more like there was space for both. But as I entered the real world, I was like, Okay, I’m just—I am a Black woman. It’s the one-drop rule: If you look Black, if you have a Black parent, then you are Black. And I’m down for it. I love being Black, but there is an erasure that happens to half of you. My dad’s white, my mom’s Black, and he passed when I was 14, so I really only had my Black parent around for my whole adult life. I didn’t realize how much I needed something like this to be able to fully self-realize.

It’s making me feel like a whole person instead of someone who’s been fragmented down into what makes the most sense. It is incredibly grounding and really special. It’s amazing to meet other mixed race girls at the stage door who say, “This really got me.” Even if certain things aren’t being said, certain conversations we wish we could lean into a little bit more…. Just seeing it on stage, there’s so much that makes people see themselves. I think for anyone with a biracial heritage, there’s a very complex feeling of, Where do I fit in? The show asks that question over and over and allows us to find the answers. Being inside of it for so many years, it’s been amazing and complicated and hard sometimes, like maybe I want to stop thinking about this a little bit. But it’s really special to be able to play myself fully.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

#6605. Hidden in the Viral Last Ditch Debacle: How to Keep Lesbian Bars Alive

By September of this year, Jackie Matellian had spent months living in her truck while working several jobs to keep Last Ditch, a lesbian bar in Greenfield, Massachusetts, open. She was the last remaining original founder, and the bar was in deep financial trouble. According to reporting by The Boston Globe, workers had gone unpaid, Matellian was carrying a $50,000 start-up loan, and the landlord wanted $3,900 in overdue rent.

Last Ditch had been built to do things most bars don’t even attempt. It welcomed lesbians, transsexuals, and other queer people who couldn’t afford the cover, offered a free store with food, clothing and harm-reduction supplies, and required KN95 masks or better. For immunocompromised patrons, those precautions made it possible to have a night out without gambling with their health. The bar’s radical inclusiveness was part of why people cared about it—and part of what its owners were struggling to finance it.

Desperate for cash, the bar’s management announced a policy shift with a cheery Instagram post: Saturday nights would become mask-optional. The gamble backfired. By treating accessibility as negotiable, the bar alienated immunocompromised regulars without attracting enough new customers to pay the rent. Follow-up stumbles culminated in a marathon three-and-a-half-hour community meeting that collapsed without a resolution. Rather than saving the venue, the policy pivot left Last Ditch with the worst of both worlds: fractured community trust and an unresolved financial crisis.

The drama became national entertainment, right up until October 26, when Last Ditch announced its soft closure.

The spectators moved on, but one issue remains: expecting one struggling lesbian bar to compensate for the failures of an entire social infrastructure is absurd. The irony is that Western Massachusetts built the blueprint for combating exactly this.

Women in the area have been finding ways to share the costs of lesbian social life for decades. UMass Amherst documents more than 400 lesbian and feminist groups active in the region between 1968 and 1978. Northampton had the Common Womon Club, Lesbian Gardens, Womonfyre Books, and the Nutcracker’s Suite self-defense dojo. These were places women built to make their social lives and organizing possible outside institutions that routinely excluded them.

In 1976, the women behind Common Womon pooled money to buy property through Ceres Inc., the nonprofit they’d formed, then financed renovations with help from donations and a loan. The adjacent storefront provided rental income and housed the Nutcracker’s Suite, then Womonfyre Books, so control of the property also gave the women a way to make room for other projects and help pay for the place they shared. Common Womon also collected sliding-scale membership dues, while the Valley Women’s History Collaborative lists benefits for the Common Womon Club that helped keep it going.

The womon-spelling and the names are fun to inherit; I also want us to inherit the ability to put actual premises under our control. For Last Ditch, that begins with finding out whether a new set of owners can remain in the building on terms the business can afford.

Matellian had already told the Globe she planned to turn the bar into a cooperative. For that to relieve the pressure on her, new members would need to take responsibility for work she’d been doing and agree on how the existing debt would be handled. But calling it a cooperative wouldn’t do much for Matellian if she was still the person everyone called whenever something went wrong. Sharing authority has to include sharing responsibility for the work, with limits on what any one person is expected to carry.

Sharing ownership would give people more power over decisions and occasions to disagree about them. Common Womon closed in 1982, while Womonfyre lasted until 1989. Womonfyre faced harassment and threats from outside the lesbian community as well as conflicts over sexual politics and what the shop should sell. Its archive preserves those disputes alongside bank statements and instructions for running the store.

A cooperative at Last Ditch would need procedures for making decisions in tandem with conflict resolution. Which is why I like that the Womonfyre archive makes room for instructions on running the shop alongside political disputes. A disagreement over how to run a bar doesn’t become abuse because people are arguing. Treating every conflict as a verdict on someone’s character makes it harder to agree on a change, because the argument can continue long after the conduct has stopped or the policy has been reversed.

Making that possible at Last Ditch requires paid training and a written account of all this work. A cooperative whose members can debate the mission for four hours but can’t cover a shift or pay its debt will end up crushing the same woman behind the bar.

If Last Ditch is to survive, its next incarnation must trade endless character trials for operational infrastructure: shared labor, transparent books, and creative financing strategies.

If one thing the Globe’s reporting revealed, it is that one commercial bar bearing the weight of an entire community’s social safety crushes everyone under impossible expectations. Instead, we must look for ways to anchor the politics in practical economics, share the burden, and build a room strong enough to hold the argument without tearing down the house.

Anyone asking the community to save Last Ditch needs to be prepared to share control of what survives.

#6604. To Penny, or Not to Penny?

Few shoes are as essential in the modern menswear landscape as the classic leather loafer. Whether you’re dressing up or dressing down, it is the “the Swiss Army Knife of shoes,” an any-occasion solution to many footwear conundrums. But within the broader loafer genus, one particular species—the penny loafer—includes a divisive design feature: a small, coin-shaped slot in the leather strap “saddle” across the vamp of the shoe.

As the lore goes, Ivy Style pioneers and sock-hopping teens in the mid-20th century liked to store a penny in their shoes as “payphone change.” But now that payphones are a thing of the misty-eyed past and the American one-cent penny is no longer minted for circulation, is it still cool to put a penny (or any other coin, or coin-shaped object) in your penny loafers? What is the line between timeless and passé?

We invited two of GQ’s most well-heeled staffers, associate grooming and wellness editor Tyler Chin and senior style commerce writer Gerald Ortiz, to ponder the pros and cons of the penny loafer.

Mahershala Ali, an ostensible penny proponent, in London on October 19.

Tyler Chin, associate grooming and wellness editor: Sure! I’ve seen so many guys wearing loafers these days, and yet still haven’t seen any of them harking back to the shoe’s origins with a penny in them. Maybe I’m not looking hard enough or I’m not in circles where they are doing that, but it’s an inoffensive and easy way to accessorize the shoe. Plus, I had an English teacher in high school who did it, and while she wasn’t particularly cool, I did think the sartorial choice was neat.

Gerald Ortiz, senior style commerce writer: No. I feel like guys who put pennies in their loafers are either try-hards, or just learned about that particular piece of prep trivia. The only acceptable instance to wear a penny in your loafers is if you’re really about that prep/Ivy style, like Preppy Pete, or the guys who frequent Alfargo’s Market (shout out).

TC: I think the penny would be the most boring and obvious choice. If a quarter could fit in there, I think it’d be so funny if you were at a vending machine and short a few cents and settled up with the coin in your shoe. One time, the button on my pants fell off on the street and I lost it, but imagine I had a spare button in my shoe? I could reattach it right there and then! In the hypothetical I’d also need to be toting around a sewing kit, but hey, I’d love to think I could be MacGyver in that scenario.

GO: It doesn’t have to be anything at all. But if you’re going to do it, I don’t see why it couldn’t be another coin or object. It could be a Chuck E. Cheese token. Whatever you put in the slot, it would still be wack.

TC: I just got back from a trip to Tokyo, and I had a lot of leftover yen coins. Two of them—the five and 50 yen—have a hole on them, which differentiates them from your boring American coin. I’d throw one of them in my shoe and be one of those people who never stops talking about their travel abroad.

GO: I saw on Instagram someone stick a hundred dollar bill into their loafer and that was funny for a second. Then I scrolled on to the next meme.

TC: I’m pretty sure a coin that is that close to the ground will surely have a patina before the end of the day. Also, I can’t remember the last time I’ve seen a shiny new coin—who carries loose change these days anyway?!

GO: You know, it might be kind of cool to see a penny completely covered in verdigris slotted into your loafers. But maybe the coin should match the sheen of your loafers. I dunno, just don’t do it and you won’t have to think about it.

TC: Everyone I know is very familiar with my love of penny loafers. Lately I’ve been wearing them with bootcut jeans that are just a little longer than usual, so they have a nice drape over the shoe. Top-wise, I’d go with a tucked-in button up, T-shirt, or sweater. Pretty much anything that would go well with sneakers would be equally suited for wearing with loafers. Which is nearly all outfits.

GO: Penniless or not, a pair of wide khakis with a clean-to-slight break and a striped button-up is a failsafe outfit. It wouldn’t be very inventive, but it would pass muster for most conceivable situations. Vintage straight-leg jeans with good fades, a fucked-up band tee, and a sportcoat is also a great look. But the best looks are always the unexpected pairings.

TC: It’s sort of like how guys will go on and on about having functional sleeve buttons on a suit jacket. Is there any situation where you’ll actually need to unbutton those or do you just leave one or two undone to “stunt” on your unimpressed bros? If you really want to put a coin in your shoe for the sake of accessorizing your footwear, then by all means get a shoe with a functioning penny slot and use it! But if you’re doing it just so you can say “Yeah, these joints are the real deal!” and use it as an excuse to talk about the history of the shoe and why yours are superior, then I’d rather you wear lace-ups.

GO: I think it’s fine, even preferable to have a faux penny slot. It’s like how jeans still come with the watch pocket. It’s purely vestigial at this point, but would feel incomplete without it.

TC: One of these days, I’ll be telling my great-great grandchildren about the origins of the penny loafer and they’ll be confused because they would’ve never heard or seen the one-cent coin before. I’ll whip one out of my shoe and instead of being impressed they’ll chalk it up to another one of Old Man Ty’s tales from his youth, and tuck me back into the nursing home they checked me into.

GO: Lol. I guess it’ll make the penny more covetable. But it’ll be a long time before the penny becomes that desirable. That said, I love this British brand Six 95 that’s designing cool pieces using coins, so I can absolutely see more labels farming pennies for their clothes and accessories.

TC: Men will break up anything other than a toxic relationship. Loafers did nothing wrong and sometimes it’s just the person wearing them that needs to hit the curb.

GO: It makes sense. It’s like any trend, really. Even if they’re as versatile as we’ve been propping them up to be, loafers reached an inflection point where, for some guys, they’re just not the vibe anymore. But I don’t think they’ll dip so low to be thought of as cringe or as an emblem of the 2020s. They’re as classic as it gets and they’ll go through their own ebbs and flows.

TC: A quarter to increase my net worth 25-fold.

#6603. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#6602. Why Valentino’s Chairman Is Betting on Türkiye’s Oldest Retail Giant

Most luxury retailers rely on international custom, but not Beymen. Now 55 years in business, Türkiye’s answer to Harrods — located across the country — is growing rapidly, boosted by local demand. And last weekend, the retailer held an opulent two-day event to celebrate the first anniversary of its flagship Tersane location, alongside the opening of a new luxury handbag exhibition, “Timeless Treasures”. As part of the program, Beymen invited guests including interior designer Harry Nuriev, as well as fashion designers Giuseppe Zanotti, Giuseppe Santoni and Antonin Tron, to a black-tie gala for a dedicated speech from Beymen Group CEO Elif Çapçı and a special performance from Diana Ross, alongside other festivities.

As the lavish party suggests, despite a recent luxury slowdown, Beymen has fared well, according to Çapçı. This year, the group is close to making €1.5 billion, growing at 15% in the first nine months. (The group — a privately owned company — declined to share further figures.)

Following investment from Mayhoola — the Qatari fund that owns Valentino and Balmain — in 2019, Beymen Group has staged a national expansion in multi-brand retail, as well as direct-to-consumer (DTC) partnerships with major European luxury brands.

Beymen’s Tersane store sits at the intersection of Europe and Asia.

What attracted Mayhoola? “The Turkish market is a very important and pivotal market between the Middle East and Europe,” says Rachid Mohamed Rachid, Mayhoola CEO and chairman for Valentino and Balmain, noting the country’s size and relatively strong luxury consumption and youth presence. “The way the country is growing economically — quite an aggressive growth in the last 20 years — has given this market a level of importance.” It’s the Sunday morning following the gala and the executive sits opposite me, beside Çapçı. The three of us are inside a plush personal shopping salon on the top floor of Beymen’s Tersane location, a bespoke flagship situated on the northern shore of Türkiye’s Golden Horn — a historic waterway dividing the old and new city.

At present, Beymen owns 290 stores in various formats across Türkiye and Egypt (a small operation): 25 multi-brand, around 60 franchise stores with leading designer brands, and three of its own brands, with stores across the region. And progress is ongoing. Current investments include a third Valentino store, as well as a Ferragamo, Pucci and Toteme store. This year, Beymen also opened a new multi-brand beauty outpost — under the Beymen Beauty Stores name — following two new additions last year. (Beauty is a fast-growing category for the business, confirms Çapçı.)

Now, the retailer is capitalizing on its national market share through enhanced clienteling, store experiences and cultural programming, while navigating the nation’s limited supply of luxury products. “Over the last [few] years with Mayhoola at the helm, we have been increasing our focus on becoming a true luxury player and raising the bar in how we offer luxury, our customer experience, the value proposition,” says Çapçı, noting the firm’s expertise and support in enhancing store renovations, brand partnerships, as well as VIC clienteling and customer management. “It’s not only how you do stores and visual merchandizing, but how you do events, how you become more associated with culture, art, and social responsibility.”

Beymen Group CEO Elif Çapçı believes in the power of domestic expansion.

Beymen is about to celebrate the Tersane store’s first anniversary, and has mounted “Timeless Treasures” to mark the moment. The showcase features 55 global brands’ interpretations of the Anatolian envelope-shaped bag, including Ganni and Louis Vuitton, plus some carefully selected student designers. The company considers this a positioning exercise, bridging the gap between local consumers and international luxury houses, while signaling Beymen’s investment in local heritage and creative industries. “Timeless Treasures” follows another landmark exhibition rooted in heritage, “Golden Opulence” (2023). This cultural programming, Rachid tells Vogue Business, helps showcase the last 500 years of Türkiye’s history. “I think the Turkish consumers are very proud of their country,” he says.

According to Çapçı, every multi-brand store in the Beymen portfolio has been built from scratch. This localized approach reflects a local consumer base. Indeed, 85% shoppers are domestic, bolstered by a small percentage of foreign visitors from Gulf countries, Russia, and ex-Russian republics. “We are not a big believer of multi-brand luxury traveling well,” Çapçı says.

Inside the new “Timeless Treasures” exhibition at Beymen’s Tersane location.

Beymen has a strong market share in Türkiye, counting only a handful of competitors that specialize in international luxury. Communité is one, offering a brand assortment that spans Willy Chavarria and Proenza Schouler through to Dries Van Noten and Carolina Herrera. Vakko is another, stocking Comme Des Garçons Play, Oscar de la Renta and Thom Browne. Besides these, Türkiye’s fashion landscape is more typically associated with its factories and fabrics, and a strong domestic market for demi couture, dominated by DTC brands such as Özgür Masur and Amor Garibovic. Beymen’s range spans Christian Louboutin, Prada and Fendi to Canali, Kiton and Tod’s.

Rachid invested because he saw white space. “Although the country had been historically a very important supplier of fashion in terms of textiles and leather goods, [it wasn’t as] developed in the design and the luxury segment,” he says. “It was really an opportunity for us to define that, while also tapping the market’s consumption potential.”

Beymen’s OMA-designed Tersane location spans 12,000 square meters.

Per Euromonitor, luxury goods in Türkiye demonstrated stable growth last year, as the sector recovered despite macroeconomic challenges. Inflation — exacerbated by the Middle East crisis — remained elevated, eating into discretionary spending among middle-income groups. As in other markets, high-net-worth individuals (HNWIs) are leading spending. And Beymen is able to harness them to weather the retail storm.

In-store sales represents 70% of Beymen’s revenue, with the remainder coming from e-commerce. For its Beymen brand chains, the split is 80% in-store versus 20% online. In tune with global consumer sentiment, the group’s wealthiest shoppers expect distinguished shopping experiences.

In this vein, the Tersane store has been designed as a destination retail experience. Beymen partnered with the Office for Metropolitan Architecture (OMA) — the Rem Koolhaas-founded firm behind several Prada locations — to create a refreshingly bright and airy department store, channeling sunshine from the adjacent waterway. Despite its clean, modular design spread across nine distinct sections, the Ottoman-era shipyard building has kept many of its heritage features. Throughout the 12,000-square-meter space, Beymen has placed works from its own art collection.

Inside one of the nine galleries spread across the Tersane flagship.

“We believe that success is dependent on both understanding a market and your roots in that market,” says Rachid. “I believe department stores are local businesses. I don’t believe that you can take a department store and move it from one country to another. You have an experience when you go to Beymen in Türkiye, another experience when you go to Harrods in London, and another when you go to Galeries Lafayette in France.”

Çapçı compares Beymen to big European businesses that rely on fluctuating foreign income. She doesn’t cite specific examples, but it’s widely understood that London’s West End — Harvey Nichols, Selfridges, Harrods — rely heavily on Chinese and Middle-Eastern custom. For Çapçı, it’s a risky approach, which is why she’s keen to keep expansion plans domestic. (To her point, China’s spending has slowed following a real-estate crisis, and Middle Eastern spending has dipped following ongoing conflicts.)

Beymen plans to double down on client experience over future expansion.

While VICs lead luxury spending at Beymen, the company particularly values its aspirational and accessible luxury shoppers, despite the smaller ticket sizes. Beymen’s VIC clienteling has been enhanced by Mayhoola’s investment and its savoir-faire gleaned from brand-specific experience. (Mayhoola owns 100% of Balmain, Beymen and Pal Zileri, and 70% of Valentino.)

Well before the acquisition, however, Beymen had established itself on intergenerational client relations. “This used to be a much smaller business, where you knew the clients by name. We are still keeping that,” says Çapçı, noting Türkiye’s culturally recognized heritage in hospitality. “We know the families. We go into their homes. If they like something, [we] just send it. They keep what they like. They send the rest [back]. They pay later.” Some clients have shopped with Beymen for multiple decades, adds Çapçı.

Beymen estimates its target consumer at 35-plus, however the company focuses on communicating and selling to Gen Z, perceiving this cohort as an investment for the future. The company also sees Gen Z as the opinion leaders who influence older generations. Rachid emphasizes that the Turkish population is young and dynamic, sitting on the intersection of the Middle East, Europe, Central Asia and the Mediterranean. “You can feel it,” he says, taking a sip of Turkish tea. “I think that that has a strong impact on the character of the consumption here. People are open to new ideas, they are open to diversity.”

The Beymen consumer is discerning on craft, and the retail strategy matches this.

On a granular level, Rachid adds, the Turkish consumer comes to stores with a strong understanding of workmanship and quality. The proximity to traditional craft and textile design makes the Beymen consumer discerning. “They’re not only going after flashy, big names,” he explains. “They have a very strong appreciation and knowledge. Don’t forget that one of the biggest attractions in Istanbul is the Grand Bazaar.”

Looking ahead, Rachid wants to prioritize the service each consumer receives over international and national store expansion, focusing on interactions and experience. “I think this is really the competitive advantage of Beymen,” he says.

#6601. We’re in a James Bond Fever Dream Now

“Next James Bond ‘REVEALED,’” reads a headline published by The Sun last week. “After a loose-lipped co-star blabs secret after ‘a few lagers.’” The article suggests that Josh O’Connor, who has recently been named in the wider press as a last-minute hopeful in the race to find the next Bond actor, is the shoe-in to be 007—all based on what one of O’Connor’s cast mates in the theater production Golden Boy might have maybe told a stranger while drunk at The French House in London.

“They said that he had confided in them about getting the role when the cast of Golden Boy had celebratory drinks after the play finished its run on Halloween,” the article continues. So, there it is: we have our next Bond! Source: someone told someone else down the pub. No, really, honest!

This is nothing against O’Connor, mind. As Ben Allen argued in the latest edition of GQ’s Intermission newsletter, he would make for a killer, surprising pick, suggestive of an “actually new direction” delineating from the hyper-machismo that defined Bond through to the end of the Craig era. His characters tend to be quieter and more introspective; his performance style is similarly subtle. (The hipster choice? Maybe, but obviously a great one.) But the article is a symptom of how utterly insane the maelstrom of reports around the next Bond have become as we seemingly enter the casting endgame, with screen tests reportedly taking place in October. Further, producer Amy Pascal has said that we can probably expect an announcement to come before the end of the year.

Over the past weekend, Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult emerged out of nowhere as having taken part in those aforementioned screen tests. Both would’ve come as whiplash to anyone who has had a passing interest in the endless Bond casting conversation: sure, they’ve been in and around the pack over the years, but given neither are called “Callum Turner” or “Jack Lowden,” the only speculated names taken seriously for much of 2026, they’re big—but both welcome!— shocks. I’m as much of an RPatz supremacist as anyone else who likes to think they know ball about films, the actor routinely being the best thing about his projects, from Nolan’s Tenet and all of his zany arthouse movies to both The Odyssey and Primetime this year. Much love to our man Hoult too, an underrated cornerstone of franchise cinema writ large, from X-Men to the new Superman. But still: what the hell?

In their own article about Pattinson and Hoult joining the race, Variety might’ve actually buried the most baffling lede: according to them, Harry Styles has “had discussions about the part,” while they also note that The Gentlemen’s Theo James—long thought out of the running—is actually yet to be ruled out. No shade on Styles, but he hasn’t been in a film since he briefly dipped a toe in acting in 2022’s Don’t Worry Darling and My Policeman, neither of which exactly kickstarted his movie career. And, like, he’s Harry Styles. Bond song? Yeah, we can see the vision. But the idea of him actually being 007 feels more like the product of an ayahuasca fever dream.

Regardless, Styles’s suitability for the role isn’t really the point. What’s more insane is that the Bond casting conversation only seems to have hit a level of psychosis as it nears the finish line: every other hour, the reported frontrunner switches from Lowden to Turner to O’Connor or Pattinson, a fever pitch of speculation and rumor-mongering that was tired before it was tired. Gary Oldman reckons it should be Lowden! Pierce Brosnan backs Turner! As one person astutely put it on Threads: “OH MY GOD JUST PICK A JAMES BOND. DO ANY JAMES BOND, JUST JAMES BOND A JAMES BOND.”

But it’s not just Bond himself, it seems. As I sat down to write this piece, an email hit my inbox from the publicist for a betting company. Subject line: “Maya Jama odds slashed to star in the next Bond film.” Damn it. Just bring back Pierce.

This article originally appeared in British GQ.

#6600. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.
